**Calls** (CALLING-SERVICE §6; §10.10):

- `call.offer` carries a fresh ephemeral KEM `ek`, generated by the
  calling device, which keeps its private half.
- The answering **device** runs
  `SetupBaseS(ek, info = "vettid/vms/2/call" || call_id)` and returns the
  resulting `enc` in `call.answer`. Both devices derive
  `K = ctx.Export("vettid/vms/2/call-key", 32)`, and from it
  `k_call = HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = K, salt = "vettid-call-v1", info = call_id)`.
  The vaults relay `ek` and `enc` and never hold `k_call`.
- (0.28.0) `k_call` is never a frame key: each device derives two
  direction keys from it, bound to the negotiated media suite, and from
  those the frame keys (§10.10 "Media suites and keys").
- Offers carry `exp`, 45 s by default.
- `call.offer`, `call.answer` and `call.end` are durable. `call.ice`,
  `call.ringing` and (0.28.0) `call.keepalive` are ephemeral.
- A locked callee cannot answer, so the call times out.

### 10.1 Common rules and `sync.event`

- Bodies are JSON objects (§5.3). Unknown members are ignored. Strings are
  at most 4 KiB unless stated. Timestamps in bodies use the inner `ts`
  format; invite and pairing expiries (`exp` in responses) are RFC 3339 in
  whole seconds.
- Error codes: `bad_request`, `not_found`, `forbidden` (the sender's role may
  not send this type; (0.51.2) also a holder-only type of §3.5.9 from an
  app that is not the holder, and any type but the recovery path's from
  a recovering app, §11.11.5; (0.52.0) to a holder-only type of §3.5.9
  it means only that another live app holds the credential), `unsupported_type` (§5.3), `internal`, `relay_error`,
  `ttl_not_allowed`, `claim_unavailable`, `accept_failed`, `approve_failed`,
  `connection_unavailable`, and (0.4.0):
  - `conflict`: the request's `version` is not the current one (§8.4);
  - `exists`: the object already exists (`credential.create`; since
    0.10.2 also `connection.invite.accept` of a vault already connected
    or requested, with body `{connection_id}`, §6.4);
  - `limit`: a count or size limit of the feature would be exceeded.
    Since 0.21.0 (owner decision of 2026-10-08, §15 item 29) its body
    names the limit: `{limit: <name>, max, size?}`, where `max` is the
    bound (a count, or bytes for a `*_size` limit) and `size`, only for
    a size limit, the size the refused request would have reached as
    the vault counted it. A vault never sends `limit` without this
    body; an app shows a name it does not know as a generic "limit
    reached". The names:

    | `limit` | `max` | Reached by |
    |---|---|---|
    | `items` | 2,000 items, critical ones included | `item.put`, `wallet.create` (§10.7, §10.18) |
    | `critical_items` | 1,000 critical items (also the credential's 1,000 entries, §3.5.2) | critical `item.put`, `item.sensitivity`, `wallet.create` |
    | `item_size` | 65,536 bytes, or 12,288 for a critical item (§10.7 Size) | `item.put`, `item.sensitivity` |
    | `credential_size` | 131,072 bytes of the credential's `inner` (§3.5.2) | a credential operation that adds to it |
    | `profile_items` | 32 items tagged `@profile` | `item.put`, `item.tag` (§10.8) |
    | `profile_size` | 196,608 bytes of `profile.update`, counted with maximum-length names | `profile.set`, `item.put`, `item.tag` (§10.8) |
    | `tag_registry` | 512 registry entries | `tag.set` (§10.8) |
    | `app_settings` | 64 `app.*` keys | `settings.set` (§10.8) |
    | `share_rules_subject` | 64 rules per subject | `share.rule.set` (§10.12) |
    | `share_rules` | 512 rules in all | `share.rule.set` |
    | `share_pending` | 4,096 pending items | `share.rule.set`, `item.put`, `item.tag`, `tag.merge` |
    | `grants_given` | 1,000 active given grants | `grant.decide`, and every change that includes items by an `auto` rule or a decision (`share.rule.set`, `share.decide`, `item.put`, `item.tag`, `tag.merge`), shared actions (§10.12, §10.14) |
    | `grant_requests` | 1,000 requests the asking vault keeps | `grant.request` |
    | `catalog_requests` | 64 outstanding catalog requests | `grant.catalog` |
    | `grant_fetches` | 64 outstanding fetches | `grant.fetch` |
    | `held_approvals` | 8 held requests per device | a request held for approval (§6.8) |
    | `connection_requests` | 256 outgoing connection requests | `connection.invite.accept` (§10.4) |
    | `blocks` | 1,000 block entries | `block.add` (§10.4) |
    | `auth_challenges` | 8 outstanding challenges per connection | `connection.authenticate.request` (§10.4) |
    | `agent_grants` | 32 grants per agent | LEASH grants, agent share rules (§10.11) |
    | `critical_use_requests` | 64 outstanding outgoing requests | `critical-secret-use.request` (§10.13) |
    | `action_invocations` | 256 outstanding outgoing invocations | `action.invoke` (§10.14; the reference's bound, first stated here) |
    | `introductions` | 16 open introductions | `intro.create` (§10.15) |
    | `location_shares` | 64 outgoing shares | `location.share.start` (§10.16) |
    | `location_requests` | 1 per connection per 10 minutes | `location.request` (§10.16) |
    | `wallets` | 16 wallets | `wallet.create` (§10.18) |
    | `wallet_addresses` | 2,000 addresses per wallet | `wallet.address.new` (§10.18) |
    | `push_registrations` | 20 registrations that reach the gateway per 24 hours (0.24.0); every registration the gateway answered over HTTP counts, refusals included (0.24.1); (0.30.0) a `push.confirm` does not count | `push.register` (§14.1) |
    | `attachment_storage` (0.32.0, release A) | 1,073,741,824 bytes of stored attachments, content and thumbnails, sent and received | `message.send` with an attachment (§10.5.1) |
    | `attachments` (0.32.0, release A) | 4,096 stored attachments | `message.send` with an attachment |
    | `attachment_fetches` (0.32.0, release A) | 2 `content` fetches in progress per device | `message.attachment.get` |

    A count that is part of a request's shape is `bad_request`, not a
    `limit`, and has no name: more than 64 fields in an item, for every
    sensitivity (§10.7; 0.21.1), as more than 16 tags or 500 ids in a
    list. Limits on what another vault sends (received grants, pending
    requests per connection, offers) are not error responses: those
    messages are dropped and audited as their sections say, and (0.23.0)
    a connection's asks are bounded by §10.4.1's constants;
  - (0.18.0) `too_soon`: `account.name.set` within 30 days of the last
    applied name change, with body `{allowed_after}` (RFC 3339, §10.8);
    (0.52.0) also a `credential.utk.get{"resync": true}` within 10
    minutes (scaled, §3.5.4) of the device's last resync, with the same
    body;
    (0.32.0, release A) also a peer's `relay.token.refresh`
    after `quota_exceeded` within 24 hours of the last fresh standing
    token that refreshes gave that connection, and (0.33.1) any other
    refresh within an hour of it (§7.2; 0.32.1);
  - (0.42.0) `way_not_allowed`: an agent's `item.get`, `item.run` or
    `item.proxy` for an item whose settings do not allow that way, with
    body `{ways}`; `program_not_allowed`: an `item.run` whose program
    the item is not bound to (§10.11 "Ways to use a secret");
  - `bad_password`, `backoff`, `stale_credential`, `utk_invalid`: §3.5.3,
    §3.5.4. Since 0.17.0 a `backoff` error response's body is
    `{retry_after}`: the whole seconds, rounded up and at least 1, until
    the backoff that refused the request ends (the PIN backoff of §11.8
    or the password backoff of §3.5.3), as in the unlock result
    (§11.4). The app shows it as a countdown and does not resend
    before it ends;
  - `credential_required`: the vault has no credential (§3.5.7), or a
    recovery needs one (§11.11.5). (0.51.2) It may answer an owner
    device's request, the daily check and the credential operations
    included, before the type's handler: then no PIN or password is
    tested and nothing is counted. (0.52.0) A UTK the request presents
    is spent (§3.5.4), as for every refusal; this replaces 0.51.2's "no
    UTK is spent". Also a vault with a credential but no holder
    (§3.5.9), to the holder-only types, to `vault.delete` (0.54.0) and
    to every request a restricted vault refuses, with body
    `{"reason": "no_holder"}`; a vault without a credential sends no
    body. An app shows `no_holder`
    as a vault this phone cannot use, not as a passing fault;
  - `bad_pin`: the current PIN given to `pin.change` is wrong;
  - (0.33.0, release R) `weak_password`: a password being set breaks a
    rule of §11.14.7, with body `{reason}` (`short`, `repeated`,
    `common`, `same_as_pin`, `guessable`); `counter_unavailable`: the
    change needs the recovery attempt counter, which could not be
    reached, and nothing was changed (§11.14.3); `busy` also answers an
    operation that needs the heavy key derivation when the enclave has
    no room for it, with nothing changed (§11.14.3); `retry` answers
    `pin.change`, `credential.password.change`, `credential.reset`,
    `vault.secret.renew` and `device.transfer.approve` when the first
    header write of a DEK replacement could not be stored and read back,
    with nothing changed but the spent UTK (§11.14.2);
  - and (0.5.0):
    - `session_required`: a desktop or agent has no access session
      (§6.8);
    - `denied`: an app denied a held request, or the device's access
      session ended while it was held (§6.8);
    - `approval_timeout`: no app decided a held request in time (§6.8);
    - `busy`: `call.start` while a call is ringing or active (§10.10);
      (0.32.0, release A) also `message.attachment.get` when
      no transfer could start within 30 s (§10.5.1); the device tries
      again later;
    - `calls_off` (0.28.0, release C2): `call.start` to a connection
      whose calls the member turned off (§10.10);
    - `credential_locked`: the operation signs with the credential key
      and the unlock window is closed (§3.5.3, §10.4);
    - `blocked`: `connection.invite.accept` of an invitation from a
      blocked identity (§10.4);
  - and (0.6.0) no new codes: `forbidden` also answers an agent's request
    that no LEASH grant covers (§6.8, §10.11), and `credential_locked` a
    signed LEASH grant outside the unlock window. Refusals between vaults
    are not error responses but `status` or `error` members of the
    answering event (§10.12–§10.14);
  - and (0.7.0) `in_use`: `tag.delete` of a tag a share rule names
    (§10.8), and (0.8.0) `item.put` or `item.sensitivity` of a wallet's
    item (§10.18);
  - and (0.8.0):
    - `invalid_psbt`: a PSBT the wallet refuses to sign; `message` holds a
      short reason (§10.18);
    - `unavailable`: the operation needs something this release does not
      have, such as a vault-side chain source (§10.18);
  - and (0.56.0) `cap_exceeded`: `wallet.sign`, or the approval of
      `wallet.request-payment`, would take more out of the wallet than
      its spend caps allow; body `{reason, limit_sats, remaining_sats?,
      allowed_after?}` (§10.18 "Spend caps");
  - and (0.9.0):
    - `one_app`: `device.pair.create{role: "app"}`; the vault already has
      its app (§6.7);
    - `credential_frozen`: a clone alarm is open and awaits the holder's
      confirmation, or the request presented a clone (§3.5.9);
    - `rotation_required`: the alarm is confirmed; only
      `credential.rotate` runs until the forced rotation (§3.5.9);
    - `credential_lost`: removed in 0.16.0. It answered
      `credential.recover` when the vault kept no copy of the latest blob
      (backup off); there is no recovery with the backup off, which the
      enclave refuses before any recovering app exists (§11.11.1,
      §11.11.5);
    - `transfer_pending`: reserved; unused since 0.10.3, when the
      approval of a transfer completes it at once (§6.7.1);
  - and (0.13.0) `owner_check_required`: the vault is held (§3.6.3); the
    request waits for a successful `vault.owner-check`. Answered to every
    owner-device request outside the hold's allow list, to requests held
    for approval when the hold begins, and to a `settings.set` that
    would turn the hold off, which only a check may do (§3.6.7);
  - and (0.32.0) `response_too_large`: the response could
    not be sealed within §5.5's bound (§8.1); no body;
  - and (0.24.0) `gateway_error`: `push.register` could not complete at
    the push gateway (unreachable, timed out, `5xx`, the gateway
    refused the vault's attestation, or, 0.24.1, any other answer but a
    well-formed `202` (0.30.0; a `201` until 0.29.x) and §14.1's three
    `400` codes), with body `{retry_after?}`; the app tries again
    later, after `retry_after` if present (§14.1). (0.30.0) Also
    `push.confirm`: the challenge expired (message
    `challenge_expired`), the gateway refused the code (message
    `challenge_invalid`), or the gateway could not be reached; the app
    registers again (§14.1).
- (0.51.2) **Error codes are not secret.** An app may show the member a
  code it does not map (and SHOULD, rather than a text that names no
  cause), so that the member can report it. It shows the `code` alone,
  never the response's `message` or body, which may name items, ids or
  gateway details.
- A request answered with an error changes no state, except the password
  backoff, the spent UTK and the audit log and feed entries of §3.5.3,
  and, for a failed owner check, the PIN backoff and the check's
  `failures` (§3.6.4), and, for a failed `push.register` that reached
  the gateway, the `push_registrations` window (§14.1, 0.24.1), and,
  for a failed `push.confirm`, the erasure of the pending registration
  where §14.1 says so (0.30.0).
  Objects that several
  owner devices can edit carry a `version` (an integer from 1, `0` before
  the first write); a change MUST name the version it was based on, and
  the vault answers `conflict` if it differs.
- Ids the vault assigns (`item_id`, `rule_id`, `entry_id`) are ULIDs.
- A type sent by a principal whose role is not listed for it is answered
  with `forbidden` (requests) or dropped and audited (other messages).
- Side effects reach the owner's other devices (§9.1) as `sync.event`
  `{kind, ...}`. Kinds:

  | `kind` | Members |
  |---|---|
  | `message.receipt` | `connection_id`, `message_id`, `receipt` (`delivered` \| `read`) |
  | `message.read` | `connection_id`, `message_id` |
  | `message.attachment` | `connection_id`, `message_id`, `state`, `reason?`: an attachment's state changed (§10.5.1; 0.32.0, release A) |
  | `device.paired` | `device_id`, `role` |
  | `device.unlinked` | `device_id` |
  | `device.transferred` | `device_id` (the new app), `old_device_id` (§6.7.1) |
  | `device.transfer` | `transfer_id`, `state` (`aborted`), `reason` (§6.7.1) |
  | `credential.alarm` | `alarm_id`, `state` (`frozen`, `rotation_required`, `resolved`) (§3.5.9) |
  | `owner_check` | `deadline`: a check succeeded, and a hold, if any, ended (§3.6, 0.13.0) |
  | `vault.release` | `release` (PCR0 hex), `release_number`; sent once after a vault first runs under a new release (§11.10.6) |
  | `account.changed` | `version`: a newer account snapshot arrived from the host (§11.13, 0.15.0), or (0.18.0) the `name_request` changed (§10.8); for a `name_request` change alone, `version` is the stored snapshot's, unchanged (0.19.0) |
  | `credential.changed` | `version` (§3.5.5) |

  | `connection.changed` | `connection_id`, `version` (`connection.update`, §10.4; since 0.23.0 also a change of the connection's ask state, §10.4.1) |
  | `connection.request` | `pending_id` (incoming) or `connection_id` (outgoing), `state` (`approved`, `peer_approved`, `declined`, `peer_declined`, `expired`) (§6.4); `peer_approved`: the peer's `connection.approved` arrived (0.10.3); `declined`: the member declined; `peer_declined`: the peer's `connection.declined` arrived and ended the request (0.10.5) |

  | `approval.decided` | `approval_id`, `approved` (§6.8) |
  | `leash.grant.changed` | `grant_id`, `agent_id`, `version` (§10.11) |

  These go to the owner's app and desktops other than the sender (not agents), never with

### 10.2 Lifecycle and sessions

| Type | Request body | Response / event body |
|---|---|---|
| `vault.enrolled` | — | §11.3 |
| `vault.enroll.confirm` (app) | `{}` | `{}` |
| `vault.status` (app, desktop, agent) | `{}` | `{vault_id, state_seq, header_seq, provisional, devices, connections, owner_check}`; 0.29.0, release L: also `unlock_id` (to the app and desktops, not to agents or a recovering app) and, inside `owner_check` for the app and desktops, `idle_lock_at` (RFC 3339: when the vault will lock itself if no check is passed, §3.6.8; absent for a vault without a credential); `owner_check` (0.13.0) is `{state: "ok" \| "due" \| "held", deadline, interval_seconds, failures, hold, hold_off_until?, waiting?}` to apps and desktops and `{state}` to agents (§3.6, §3.6.7). `waiting` (0.19.0) is `{messages, requests, calls, other}`, the counts of `vault.held` since the deadline (§3.6.3), present while the state is `due` or `held` for a device that receives `vault.held` (the app; desktops with an access session while `held`) and absent otherwise. (0.32.0, release A) To the app and desktops also `attachments: {count, bytes, max_count, max_bytes}`: the stored attachments, their bytes counted as for `attachment_storage`, and the two bounds (§10.5.1). A recovering app (§11.11.5) gets only `{vault_id, state_seq, header_seq}` (0.16.0): nothing about the vault's devices, connections or owner check before it has proved the credential password. (0.33.0, release R) To the app also `recovery: {state, attempts, present_recorded_at, counter}`, to desktops `recovery: {state}` (§11.14.11). (0.41.0) To desktops and agents also `session: {session_id, expires_at} \| null`: the calling device's own current access session, never another device's (§6.8). (0.43.0, approved by the owner 2026-10-18) To the app and desktops also `time_scale`, the release constant of §11.10.8 (1 in production) |
| `vault.owner-check` (app: the holder) | `{credential, utk_id, sealed{pin, password, hold?, hold_off_until?}}` | `{credential, version, utks, deadline, interval_seconds, hold, hold_off_until?}` (§3.6.1, §3.6.7); (0.33.0, release R) also `recovery: {state, present_recorded}` (§11.14.5); `bad_pin`, `bad_password`, `backoff` (body `{retry_after}`, §10.1), `utk_invalid`, `stale_credential`, `credential_frozen`, `rotation_required`, `forbidden` (not the holder), `bad_request` (a PIN that is not 6–32 digits) |
| `vault.held` (V→D, to the app and desktops in an access session) | — | `{deadline, waiting: {messages, requests, calls, other}}` (§3.6.3); 0.29.0, release L: also `idle_lock_at` (§3.6.8) |
| `vault.lock` (app, desktop) | `{}`; 0.29.0, release L: `{unlock_id}` ("Locks", below) | `{}`; then `vault.locking`. 0.29.0, release L: `stale_lock` when `unlock_id` does not name the current unlock (nothing is done); `bad_request` when it is not 32 lowercase hex characters |
| `account.get` (app, desktop) | `{}` | `{account: <snapshot, §11.13> \| null, version, received_at, name_request?}`; `null` (and `version` 0) before any snapshot arrived (0.15.0); the snapshot carries the member's full `email` (0.20.0), which only this type returns and only to the app and desktops (§11.13); `name_request` (0.18.0) is the latest `account.name.set` request (§10.8). A change of `name_request` alone sends `sync.event{kind: "account.changed"}` with the stored snapshot's `version` repeated, not incremented (0.19.0): `version` counts snapshots only, so a device MUST NOT skip an `account.changed` whose `version` it already holds |
| `vault.delete` (app: the holder, or the enrolling app before a credential exists) | `{confirm: "delete my vault", credential?, utk_id, sealed{pin, password?}}` | `{}`; then the deletion of §12.5. `bad_request` without the exact phrase or a needed member; `bad_pin`, `backoff`, `bad_password`, `credential_frozen` / `rotation_required` (holder during an alarm), (0.54.0) `credential_required` with body `{"reason": "no_holder"}` (a vault with a credential but no holder, §3.5.9), `forbidden` (a recovering app since 0.16.0: it completes the recovery first, then deletes as the holder; a member without the credential uses §11.11.9) |
| `vault.locking` (ephemeral) | — | `{reason?}` (0.29.0, release L: `{reason?, unlock_id}`, the unlock this lock ends), with `exp` = now + 60 s; an app ignores one whose `ts` is not later than its latest successful unlock result's (§11.4, 0.23.3); `reason` is `"recovery"` when a recovery request locked the vault (§11.11.1), `"owner_check"` when ten consecutive failed owner checks did (§3.6.4, 0.13.0), `"idle"` for the idle lock (§3.6.8; 0.29.0, release L) |
| `relay.token.issued` | — | `{kind: "standing" \| "reconnect", token}` |
| `relay.token.refresh` (req) | `{}` | `{kind: "standing", token}` |
| `identity.rotate` | — | `{rotation: <identity.rotate statement, §3.4>}` |
| `relay.address.update` | — | `{relay: {url, mailbox, pk}, token, reconnect_token?}` |

**Locks (0.29.0, release L; approved by the owner 2026-10-12,
VAULT-LOCK §3).** A lock from a
device belongs to the unlock it ends.

- **`unlock_id`.** Each time a vault opens (a successful
  `vault.enroll` or `vault.unlock`, §11.3, §11.4, or (0.56.1) a
  successful recovery open, §11.14.6) its process makes 16
  random bytes, written as 32 lowercase hex characters. The value is
  kept in memory only: it is in neither the state nor the header, and
  it ends with the process, so every earlier value is stale after any
  lock, restart or move. It is not a secret and authorizes nothing by
  itself. The app has it from the enroll, unlock or (0.56.1)
  recovery-open result; any app or desktop can read it in
  `vault.status`.
- **A bound lock.** `vault.lock {unlock_id}`: the vault compares the
  value with its current unlock's.
  - Equal: it answers `{}` and locks after the batch (§12.3), sending
    `vault.locking {unlock_id}`.
  - Different: it answers `stale_lock` and does nothing. The device's
    unlock is over; the vault is open under a newer one. The device
    treats its own lock as finished and does not repeat it on its own
    (a new lock the member asks for is a new lock, "What ends a
    device's lock" below).
- **Without `unlock_id`** (a device from before release L): the lock
  is carried out as before 0.29.0, while such devices are supported;
  after that it is answered `bad_request` (VAULT-LOCK L2). Devices
  that implement 0.29.0 MUST send the value to a vault that announced
  one.
- **Idempotent.** A repeated `vault.lock` for the current unlock locks
  once: the first locks the vault, and a locked vault collects nothing
  (§12.1), so a later copy waits at the relay until its `exp`. If the
  member unlocks again first, the copy names an old unlock and is
  answered `stale_lock`.
- **`vault.locking {unlock_id}`** names the unlock being ended, for a
  lock from any cause. A device that holds that value knows its unlock
  is over. A device MUST ignore a `vault.locking` whose `unlock_id` is
  not its current one; for a notice without the member (a release
  before L) the rule of §11.4 stays (`ts` not later than the latest
  unlock result's).
- **What ends a device's lock.** The vault's `{}` to its `vault.lock`
  and a `vault.locking` naming its unlock confirm that the vault is
  locked; these are the vault's word. `stale_lock` ends the device's
  lock without confirming it: the unlock the lock was for is over and
  the vault is open under a newer one. The device does not repeat that lock
  on its own; a new lock the member asks for (bound to the current
  opening when the device knows its `unlock_id`, otherwise
  unconditional, §8.6) is a new lock. The device reads the status
  (MEMBER-API `GET /api/vault/status`), and says the vault is locked
  only if that status was read and is not `unlocked`. The member API's
  answers (§11.5) are the host's (§13.3): for a bound lock its `locked`
  and `not_running` confirm it (VAULT-LOCK L6), and its `stale` is read
  as `stale_lock` is. A device that holds no current `unlock_id` (a new
  process before its first status read) handles a `vault.locking` by
  the time rule of §11.4: its `ts` later than that of its latest
  successful unlock result (§11.4).
- **Other owner devices.** A desktop locks with the value from
  `vault.status`. Agents cannot lock.

### 10.3 Devices (§6.7)

| Type | Request body | Response / event body |
|---|---|---|
| `device.pair.create` (app) | `{role: "desktop" \| "agent"}` | `{pairing_id, link, exp}`; `{role: "app"}` is answered `one_app` (§6.7) |
| `device.pair.pending` (to apps) | — | `{pairing_id, pending_id, role, name, sas}`; `name` is the new device's self-asserted `profile.name` |
| `device.pair.approve` (app) | `{pairing_id, session_seconds?, grants?}`; `session_seconds` (60–86,400) only for a desktop or agent: its first access session (§6.8); `grants` only for an agent: 1–32 LEASH grant specifications (§10.11), signed at the approval (`credential_locked` outside the unlock window) | `{}` |
| `device.pair.reject` (app) | `{pairing_id}` | `{}` |
| `device.pair.rejected` (to the new device) | — | `{}`: the owner rejected the pairing or transfer after its `hs.fin` (0.10.5); sealed under the handshake's epoch, on the device's token from `hs.init`, as `device.paired`; the device stops waiting (§6.7) |
| `device.paired` (to the new device) | — | `{device_id, role, vault_id, release, release_number, token, session_expires_at?, transfer?, credential_version?, user_guid?}` (the release the vault runs under); `token`: the device's standing token (§7.1); it replaces the request token of a pairing's or transfer's `hs.resp` (0.10.3), and after enrollment or recovery, whose `hs.resp` already carries one, it is a fresh one (0.10.4); `transfer: true`, the credential's `credential_version` and (0.17.0) the member's `user_guid`, which its unlocks need, for a transferred app only (§6.7.1) |
| `device.list` (app, desktop) | `{}` | `{devices: [{id, kind, state, name, ik, profile?, created_at?, last_active_at?, session_expires_at?, push?, signer?}]}`; `push` (0.24.0) only on the app's entry while it has a registration: the push state of §14.1; `signer` (0.27.0) only on an Android app's entry with a recorded signer: `{class: "vettid" \| "google_play" \| "development", digest: "<64 hex>"}`, the vault's signer binding (§11.7.1) |
| `device.unlink` (app) | `{device_id}` | `{}`; `forbidden` for the app itself (0.9.0: it leaves by a transfer or a recovery) |
| `device.unlinked` (to the unlinked device, best effort) | — | `{reason?}`: `"transferred"` for the old app of a transfer (§6.7.1), `"replaced"` for the old app of a recovery (§11.11.5); (0.33.0, release R) a transfer's also carries `transfer_id`, and is sent only after the new phone's first unlock from storage (§11.14.10) |
| `device.transfer.create` (the holder) | `{}` | `{transfer_id, link, exp}`; `exists` while a transfer is open; `credential_frozen` or `rotation_required` during an alarm (§6.7.1) |
| `device.transfer.pending` (to the holder) | — | `{transfer_id, name, sas, signer?, signer_changed?}`; `name` is the new app's self-asserted `profile.name`; (0.27.0, Android) `signer` is the attested class of the new app's signer and `signer_changed` whether its digest differs from the vault's binding (§11.7.1) |
| `device.transfer.approve` (the holder) | `{transfer_id, credential, utk_id, sealed{password, pin}, signer?}` | `{}`: the transfer is complete (0.10.3; was `{exp}`); (0.33.0, release R) `{"unlink": "after_new_unlock"}`, and also `busy` and `retry` with nothing but the UTK spent (§11.14.10); `bad_pin`, `backoff`, `bad_password`, `stale_credential`, `credential_frozen`, `utk_invalid`; (0.27.0) `signer`, the new app's class, is REQUIRED when the pending said `signer_changed: true`, else `signer_unconfirmed` (§11.7.1) |
| `device.transfer.reject` (the holder) | `{transfer_id}` | `{}`; cancels the transfer before or after the scan, until the approval; after the new app's `hs.fin` it gets `device.pair.rejected` (0.10.5) |
| `device.session.request` (desktop, agent) | `{seconds?}` (60–86,400, default 3,600) | `{request_id, exp}`; (0.40.0) `too_soon` (body `{allowed_after}`) within 10 minutes of the device's last accepted request (§6.8) |
| `device.session.pending` (to apps) | — | `{request_id, device_id, role, name, seconds, exp}` |

- `last_active_at` is when the vault last processed a durable message from
  the principal, to the minute; `session_expires_at` is present while an
  access session lasts.
- A held request that is approved is executed when the decision arrives,
  so `approval.decide` answers with its outcome; the requester gets the
  request's own response.

| Type | Request body | Response / event body |

| `connection.invite.cancel` | `{invite_id}` | `{}` |

| `connection.request.pending` (incoming, to apps and desktops) | — | `{pending_id, invite_id, sas, remote, state, exp, profile?, introduced_by?}`, once `hs.fin` has checked out; `state` is `pending`, or `approved` under in-person auto-approval (§6.4) |
| `connection.request.outgoing` (to apps and desktops, the accepting device included) | — | `{connection_id, sas, remote, exp, name?, introduced_by?}`, once the vault has sent `hs.fin` and knows the SAS (0.10.3), whichever device accepted or for an introduction (§10.15) |

| `connection.update` | `{connection_id, version, alias?, note?, tags?, favorite?, archived?}` (at least one) | `{version}` |
| `connection.remove` | `{connection_id}` | `{}` |
| `connection.rotation.resolve` (0.33.0, release R; the holder only) | `{connection_id, new_ik}` | `{}`: keeps that successor of the connection's identity key and drops the other (§3.4); `not_found` when the connection has no conflict or `new_ik` is neither candidate; `forbidden` to a desktop or an agent |
| `connection.removed` (V↔V) | — | `{}` |
| `connection.event` | — | `{connection_id, event: "added" \| "removed" \| "stale" \| "rekeyed" \| "reconnected" \| "failed" \| "profile", pending_id?, reason?}`; `profile`: the connection's shared profile changed (§10.8); `failed`: an outgoing request ended without a connection other than by its member's decline (§6.4, 0.10.4); `reason`, only with `failed`: `declined` when the peer declined (0.10.5), absent for an expiry or an aborted handshake; `pending_id` with `added` on the inviter's side names the request it came from (on the accepter's side `connection_id` is the accept's) |
| `block.add` | `{connection_id \| pending_id, note?}` (exactly one of the ids) | `{block_id}` |
| `block.remove` | `{block_id}` | `{}` |
| `block.list` | `{}` | `{blocks: [{block_id, ik, name?, note?, created_at}]}` |

```json
connection: { "id": "<id>", "kind": "connection", "state": "active", "name": "...", "ik": "<b64>",
              "profile": { }, "created_at": "<ts>", "last_active_at": "<ts>",
              "version": 2, "alias": "...", "note": "...", "tags": ["family"],
              "favorite": true, "archived": false,
              "asks": { "muted": false, "paused": false, "cooldowns": 0 } }
```

- **Requests** (0.10.2, §6.4; states 0.10.3). In
  `connection.request.list`, an incoming request is listed once its
  `hs.fin` has checked out; its `state` is `pending` (awaiting the owner)
  or `approved` (the owner approved, awaiting the peer's approval). An
  outgoing request's `state` is `waiting` (no `hs.resp` yet; `sas`
  absent), `pending` (the SAS is known, awaiting the member) or
  `approved`. `peer_approved` is whether the peer's `connection.approved`
  has arrived; a request with both approvals is a connection and leaves
  the list. `exp` is when the request is dropped (§6.4 "Request expiry
  and retention"); `created_at` is when the vault received the `hs.init`
  or sent it. Both lists are newest first; a vault holds at most 256
  requests of each kind (more are refused: an `hs.init` is dropped and
  audited, an accept is answered `limit`). `introduced_by` is the vault's
  connection id of the introducer (§10.15). Approvals, the peer's
  approval and declines reach the other devices as
  `sync.event{kind: "connection.request"}`, and so do an incoming
  request's expiry and (0.10.5) the peer's decline (`peer_declined`, to
  every app and desktop).

The D→V types above are sent by `app` or `desktop` devices, except
`connection.invite.create`, `connection.invite.accept` and
`connection.approve`, which only the app sends (`forbidden` to a
desktop, §6.4 "Who approves"); for desktops, `connection.remove` and
`block.remove` are step-up types (§6.8).

- **Metadata.** `alias` (at most 128 bytes), `note` (at most 1,024 bytes),
  `tags` (at most 16 distinct tags matching `[a-z0-9_.-]{1,32}`),
  `favorite` and `archived` are the owner's own metadata. They are never
  sent to the peer, are versioned as one object per connection (§10.1;
  `version` is `0` before the first update) and are announced to the
  other devices as `sync.event{kind: "connection.changed"}`. `""` clears
  `alias` or `note`; `tags` replaces the list. `name` and `profile` remain
  the peer's values (§10.8).
- **`name` and `profile`** (0.18.0). `profile` is the peer's latest kept
  `profile.update` body (§10.8): `{version, first_name, last_name, ik,
  name?, photo?, items}`, absent only before the first, in the moment
  after activation; the inviter's side then has the request's
  `{first_name, last_name, name?}`. `name` is the peer's display name,
  from that profile or, before it, from the peer's `hs.init` or the
  bundle's `hint.name`; absent without one. Apps title a connection from
  the names as §10.8 says, never from `name` alone, and show the
  fingerprint of `ik`. In `connection.request.pending` and
  `connection.request.list`, `profile` is the requester's `hs.init`
  profile (`{first_name, last_name, name?}`, §6.2).
- **`last_active_at`** is when the vault last processed a durable message
  from the connection, to the minute; `created_at` is when the connection
  was made.

**Block list.** `block.add` blocks a connection or the sender of a pending
connection request:

- A connection is removed as §7.4 "Peer blocked" says (the peer gets a
  best-effort `connection.removed`, never a reason) and its `ik` and relay
  key are recorded in a block entry.
- A pending request is declined, which sends `connection.declined`
  (§6.4, 0.10.5; never a reason, so a block looks like a decline), and
  its `hs.init` identity (`from.ik`, `from.relay.pk`) recorded.
- An identity already blocked is answered `exists`; the list holds at most
  1,000 entries (`limit`). `note` is at most 256 bytes.
- A vault MUST refuse (drop and audit as `drop.blocked`) a connection
  `hs.init` whose `from.ik` or collect `sender` is on its block list, and
  answers `connection.invite.accept` of a blocked identity's invitation
  with `blocked`.
- A block entry follows neither the peer's identity rotation nor a new
  relay key of the peer: it guards against reconnecting by accident, while
  reaching the vault at all always needs a new invitation from its owner
  (§6.4).
- `block.remove` deletes the entry. The owner may then connect with the
  same peer again through a new invitation and approval (§7.4).
- Changes are announced as `sync.event` `block.added` / `block.removed`,
  and audited (`connection.blocked`, `connection.unblocked`).

**Member authentication.** The handshake (with the SAS, §6.3) authenticates
a connection's *vault*. `connection.authenticate.*` asks the connection's
*member* to prove that they are present now: their app approves, and their
vault signs a fresh challenge with the member's **credential key**
(§3.5.1), which only the member's password unlocks.

| Type | Request body | Response / event body |
|---|---|---|
| `connection.authenticate.request` (app, desktop) | `{connection_id, context?}` | `{request_id, exp}` |
| `connection.authenticate.challenge` (V↔V) | — | `{request_id, nonce, context?}`, with `exp` |
| `connection.authenticate.pending` (V→D, apps and desktops) | — | `{connection_id, request_id, context?, exp}` |
| `connection.authenticate.approve` (app) | `{request_id}` | `{}`; `credential_locked` outside the unlock window |
| `connection.authenticate.deny` (app, desktop) | `{request_id}` | `{}` |
| `connection.authenticate.response` (V↔V) | — | `{request_id, status: "signed", key, sig, signed_at, rotations?}` or `{request_id, status: "denied"}` |
| `connection.authenticate.rotated` (V↔V) | — | `{rotations: [<statement>, ...]}` (1–32 credential-key rotation statements, §3.5.5) |
| `connection.authenticate.key` (V→D, every owner app and desktop) | — | `{connection_id, key}`: the pinned key followed a rotation |
| `connection.authenticate.result` (V→D, every owner app and desktop) | — | `{connection_id, request_id, authenticated, key?, key_changed?, reason?}` |
| `connection.authenticate.list` (app, desktop) | `{}` | `{states: [{connection_id, key?, verified_at?, last_result?, last_at?}]}` |

- `nonce` is 32 random bytes; `context` is at most 256 bytes and shown to
  the member. A challenge lives 10 minutes (`exp`). A vault keeps at most
  8 outstanding challenges it sent per connection (`limit`) and 4 it
  received (more are dropped and audited). Since 0.23.0 a received
  challenge is an ask (§10.4.1).
- To approve, the app opens the credential's unlock window
  (`credential.unlock`, §3.5.3) and sends `connection.authenticate.approve`;
  the use extends the window. The vault signs

  ```
  m   = challenger_ik (32) || responder_ik (32) || nonce (32) || request_id (26) || context
  sig = Ed25519(credential key, "vettid/vms/2/conn-auth" || m)
  ```

  where `challenger_ik` is the requesting vault's `ik` and `responder_ik`
  the signing vault's, each as the other side has it on record. `key` is
  the credential key's public key.
- The requesting vault checks that the response answers an outstanding
  challenge it sent to that connection, verifies `sig` under `key` over
  `m`, and tells every owner device the verdict: `reason` is `denied` or
  `bad_signature`. It pins `key` at the first success. A later success
  under another key sets `key_changed: true` and re-pins, unless the
  pinned key leads to it through valid rotation statements (below); apps
  MUST show a key change.
- **Following a credential-key rotation.** A vault records, per
  connection, the credential key it last signed a response with (the key
  that connection pinned).
  - At `credential.rotate` (§3.5.5) it sends every active connection with
    such a key `connection.authenticate.rotated` carrying its statements
    from that key to the new one, in order.
  - A signed response whose `key` differs from the one recorded for that
    connection carries the same chain as `rotations`, so a requester that
    missed a delivery catches up.
  - The receiver follows the chain from its pinned key: each statement's
    `old_key` MUST equal the previous one's `new_key` (the first's the
    pinned key), both signatures MUST verify, and the chain is at most 32
    statements. On success it pins the last `new_key` and tells every owner
    device with `connection.authenticate.key` (a delivered chain) or with
    `key_changed: false` (a response).
  - **Failure.** A chain that does not verify (forged, unsigned, broken or
    too long) changes nothing: it is dropped and audited
    (`connection.authenticate.rotation_rejected`), and the next
    authentication under the new key reports `key_changed: true`. A
    receiver with no pinned key ignores `rotated`.
- Approvals, denials and verdicts are audited
  (`connection.authenticate.requested`, `.signed`, `.denied`,
  `connection.authenticated`, `connection.authenticate_failed`,
  `connection.authenticate.key_rotated`,
  `connection.authenticate.rotation_rejected`); an incoming challenge is a
  feed item.

#### 10.4.1 Asks from a connection: no approval fatigue

(0.23.0; owner's review of vettid.org #181, 2026-10-09, §15 item 31.)
A connection must not be able to wear the member down with repeated
requests until one is approved by mistake. An agent is bounded by
cooldowns, a referral cap and suspension (§10.11); a connection is
bounded here, in the member's vault, by the same ideas.

**Asks.** An **ask** is a message from a connection that, if accepted,
waits for the member's decision:

| Ask | Arrives as | Reaches the member as | The member's decline answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| A grant request, `item` or `category` entries (§10.12) | `data.request` | `grant.pending`, feed `grant.request` | `data.decided{approved: false}` |
| A critical-item use (§10.13) | `critical-secret.use` | `critical-secret-use.pending`, feed `critical-secret.use.request` | `critical-secret.result{status: "denied"}` |
| An invocation of a `prompt-each-time` action (§10.14) | `action.invocation` | `action.pending`, feed `action.request` | `action.result{status: "denied"}` |
| A member-authentication challenge (§10.4) | `connection.authenticate.challenge` | `connection.authenticate.pending`, feed `connection.authenticate.requested` | `connection.authenticate.response{status: "denied"}` |
| An introduction offer, from the introducer (§10.15) | `intro.offer` | `intro.pending`, feed `intro.request` | `intro.answer{accept: false}` |
| A location request (§10.16) | `location.requested` | `location.request.pending`, feed `location.request` | (none: §10.16 has no decline message) |

Nothing else a connection sends waits for the member. Share-rule
questions (`share.pending`, §10.12) come from the member's own rules,
never from a connection, and are not asks. Actions in `allowlist` or
`default-allow` run without the member and are bounded by §10.14's
limits only. Connection requests (§6.4) come from not-yet-connections
and keep their own limits.

**Constants.** Fixed for v1 by this specification (defaults; a later
version may make them settings):

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| Decline cooldown | 7 days |
| Ask rate | 5 asks per connection per 24 hours |
| Pending asks | 8 per connection, all kinds together |
| Pause | after 3 declines from one connection within 30 days |
| Batch | 10 minutes |
| Neutral answer delay | 1–20 minutes, uniformly random (below) |
| Held neutral answers | 16 per connection |

These are not `limit` errors (§10.1): the requester is another vault,
which never gets an error response for them.

**Checks.** For each ask that passes the checks its type already makes
at once (malformed, a duplicate id, an item that is not usable or a
field that is not suitable, an action not offered, the per-type caps;
§10.12–§10.16), the member's vault checks, in this order, and
**suppresses** the ask at the first that applies:

1. **Muted.** The member muted this connection's asks (below).
2. **Paused.** This connection's asks are paused (below).
3. **Cooldown.** The member declined the **same** ask from this
   connection within the last 7 days. The same means: for a grant
   request, an entry with the same `kind` and `ref` (the same `item_id`,
   whatever its `fields`, or the same category); for a critical-item
   use, the same `item_id` and `field_id`, whatever the operation and
   payload; for an action, the same `action_id`; for authentication, any
   challenge; for an introduction, any offer from that introducer. A
   grant request in which only some entries are in cooldown reaches the
   member without those entries (the member's decision, and so the
   answer, covers only the others); one in which all are is suppressed.
   Location requests have no decline and no cooldown.
4. **Pending.** This connection already has 8 asks waiting for the
   member, all kinds together. The per-type caps of §10.12–§10.16 stay
   as a backstop.
5. **Rate.** 5 asks of this connection have reached the member in the
   current window. The window is a fixed 24-hour window that starts at
   the first ask that reaches the member, as §10.12's rate limits are
   (Rate limits for connections); suppressed asks do not count.

An ask that passes reaches the member as before and counts in the
window.

**Declines.** A **decline** is the member's explicit refusal of a whole
ask: `grant.decide{approve: false}`, `critical-secret-use.deny`,
`action.respond{approve: false}`, `connection.authenticate.deny`,
`intro.decline`. An expiry, an approval of only some entries, a
suppressed ask and a desktop's request that an app denied are not
declines. Each decline starts the cooldown of that ask (point 3).

**Pause.** When a connection's third decline falls within 30 days of
the first of those three (the vault keeps the times of its last three
declines; this is a count of events, not of throughput, so it is a
sliding 30 days), its asks are **paused**: later asks are suppressed
until the member resumes them. The member gets **one** high-priority
feed item, `connection.asks_paused` (`connection_id`), and
`sync.event{connection.changed}`; the app says "<First>'s requests are
paused after you declined several" and offers to resume them or to
remove the connection. Asks already waiting stay and can be decided.
Pausing is per connection and has no end of its own.

**Mute.** The member may mute a connection's asks at any time, and
unmute them. While muted every ask is suppressed with no feed item and
no notification; asks already waiting stay. Muting does not pause or
remove the connection: messages, profile updates, grants and shares go
on.

| Type | Request body | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `connection.asks.mute` (app, desktop) | `{connection_id, muted}` (`muted` boolean) | `{}`; `not_found` |
| `connection.asks.resume` (app, desktop) | `{connection_id}` | `{}`; `not_found` |

- `connection.asks.resume` **always** clears the connection's decline
  times and cooldowns, and ends its pause if it is paused (so that a
  member who declined by mistake can be asked again at once, and the
  next three declines are counted afresh). It is audited
  `connection.asks_resumed` and sends `sync.event{connection.changed}`
  every time, also on a connection that is not paused or has no
  cooldown (0.23.1, owner decision of 2026-10-09; 0.23.0 said that it
  changed nothing there). Unmuting does not resume a pause. Neither type
  is delegable (§10.11).
- **State.** Per connection, in DEK state: `muted`, `paused_at`, the
  times of the last three declines, the cooldowns (one per ask
  identity, at most 64 per connection, the oldest dropped first, each
  with its end), the current window's start and count, the open batch
  and the held neutral answers. It goes with the connection (§7.4).
- **Shown on the connection.** `<connection>` carries
  `asks: {muted, paused, paused_at?, cooldowns}` (`cooldowns` the number
  in force), and changes send `sync.event{kind: "connection.changed",
  connection_id, version}` (`version` the connection's, as for
  `connection.update`; 0.23.1) to every owner device (apps, and desktops
  within their access session, §9.1). The app shows a paused or muted
  state on the connection's page with the action that ends it.

**Batching.** Asks from one connection that reach the member within 10
minutes of the first of them form one **batch**: the first creates its
feed item as before; each later ask of the batch creates no feed item
and instead updates the batch's item (a new `seq`, the same `item_id`),
whose `count` (0.23.0, present from 2) is the number of asks in the
batch. If the member has read or archived the batch's item, a later ask
of the batch still updates its `count` and `seq` and leaves its status
as the member set it; if the member deleted it, the batch ends and the
ask starts a new batch with a new item (0.23.1). The per-type `.pending`
events are still sent. Apps MUST present
a batch as one approval entry and one notification ("Dr Lee asks for 3
things"), listing its asks from the per-type lists, and MUST NOT raise a
notification for each ask of a batch in progress.

**What the connection learns: nothing it could tell apart.** A
suppressed ask is answered exactly as the member's decline of that kind
is (the table above: `approved: false`, `denied`, `accept: false`), with
the same members, never with a code or a `retry_after` of its own, and
not at once: after a delay drawn uniformly at random from 1 to 20
minutes, so that its timing does not tell an automatic refusal from a
person's. Exactly (0.23.1): the answer is due at min(now + d, `exp` − 1
minute), d the random delay, and never earlier than now (an ask whose
`exp` is less than a minute away is answered at the vault's next send).
Held answers are kept in DEK state (State, above); one that falls due
while the vault is locked is sent after it is unlocked. A location
request gets no answer, as when the member does not share. The vault
holds at most 16 such answers per connection; asks beyond that are
dropped without an answer, as an unanswered ask. So a connection cannot
tell a decline from a cooldown, a pause, a mute, the pending cap or the
rate. Apps on the asking side MUST show every refusal neutrally ("Not
accepted"), never as "declined by <First>".

**Audit.** Every suppressed ask is audited `drop.ask_muted`,
`drop.ask_paused`, `drop.ask_cooldown`, `drop.ask_pending` or
`drop.ask_rate` (`connection_id`, `ref` = the ask's `request_id`,
`invocation_id` or `intro_id`), and each entry removed from a grant
request its own `drop.ask_cooldown` with the same `ref` (0.23.1: one per
removed entry, written even when the reduced request is then suppressed
by a later check, which adds its own `drop.ask_*`); History shows them
on the connection. The changes are audited `connection.asks_paused`,
`connection.asks_resumed`, `connection.asks_muted` and
`connection.asks_unmuted` (`connection_id`). Only a pause is a feed
item.

### 10.5 Messaging

| Type | Request body | Response / event body |
|---|---|---|
| `message.send` | `{connection_id, text}`; `text` 1 byte to 16 KiB (larger content uses the blob flow, §5.5). (0.32.0, release A) `{connection_id, text?, attachment?}`: with `attachment` (§10.5.1) `text` is optional, 0 bytes to 16 KiB (a caption) | `{message_id, sent_at}`; (0.32.0, release A) with an attachment also `att_id`, answered once the request's checks passed; the attachment's progress follows as `sync.event{message.attachment}` (§10.5.1 "Sending") |
| `message.deliver` (V↔V) | — | `{message_id (ULID), text, sent_at}`; idempotent by `message_id`. (0.32.0) A message with an attachment travels as `message.attachment.deliver` instead (§10.5.1) |
| `message.receipt` (V↔V) | — | `{message_id, receipt: "delivered" \| "read", at}` |
| `message.new` | — | `{connection_id, message_id, direction: "in" \| "out", text, sent_at, delivered, read}`; (0.32.0, release A) also `attachment?`, the device view of §10.5.1 with `thumb` (to a desktop without `thumb` and `name`; never to agents); `text` is `""` for an attachment without a caption |
| `message.list` | `{connection_id, limit?}` (1–500, default 100); (0.32.0) also `before?` (§10.5.2) | `{messages: [<message.new body>, ...]}`, oldest first; (0.32.0) at most 131,072 bytes, with `next_before?` (§10.5.2); attachments without `thumb`; volatile (§8.2) |
| `message.get` | `{connection_id, message_id}` | `<message.new body>`; (0.32.0) an attachment without `thumb`; volatile (§8.2) |
| `message.read` | `{connection_id, message_id}` | `{}`; the vault sends a read receipt |
| `message.delete` | `{connection_id, message_id}` | `{}`; local only; (0.32.0, release A) erases the message's stored attachment (§10.5.1 "Deletion") |
| `message.attachment.get` (app; 0.32.0, release A) | `{connection_id, message_id, part?: "content" \| "thumb"}` (default `content`) | `content`: `{blob: {id, key, sha256, size, mime, name?}, expires_at}`, a blob the vault uploaded to the requesting device's mailbox; `thumb`: `{thumb}` inline. §10.5.1 "Fetching". Volatile (§8.2) |
| `message.attachment.discard` (app; 0.32.0, release A) | `{blob_id}` | `{}`: the vault deletes a blob its device uploaded and will not send, unless an attachment names it (§10.5.1 "Sending") |
| `message.attachment.deliver` (V↔V; 0.32.0, release A) | — | `{message_id (ULID), text?, sent_at, attachment: <peer view>}`: a message with an attachment, and a fresh upload of the same attachment after `missing`; idempotent by `message_id` and blob `id` (§10.5.1) |
| `message.attachment.status` (V↔V; 0.32.0, release A) | — | `{message_id, status: "stored" \| "missing" \| "refused" \| "withdrawn", reason?, at}`; `withdrawn` from the sender, the others from the recipient (§10.5.1 "Receiving", "Delivery to the peer") |

The D→V messaging types are sent by `app` or `desktop` devices.
(0.32.0, release A) Attachments are app-only: a desktop sends none
and fetches none, and `message.attachment.get` and `.discard` are the
app's alone (§10.5.1 "Desktops"). An agent may send some messaging
types under a grant (§10.11), but never with an attachment, and does
not learn that a message has one (§10.5.1 "Agents").

**Links** (0.24.0, owner review of 2026-10-10). `text` is plain text;
the vault neither parses nor rewrites it. Clients make only `https://`
URLs tappable; before opening one they show its host and ask, then hand
the URL to the operating system, so an Android App Link or an iOS
Universal Link opens the app verified for that domain and any other link
opens the browser. URLs of every other scheme, custom app schemes
(`someapp://`) included, are shown as text and never opened: any app can
claim a custom scheme. This is how connections, and later services
(their service vaults), reach the member through VettID's notification
channel (PUSH-GATEWAY §12).

#### 10.5.1 Attachments (0.32.0, release A)

*Approved by the owner 2026-10-15 (vettid.org #288; owner decisions
of 2026-10-15, §15 item 38). It applies from a vault release that
implements it, called "release A" here, and an app release, which are
not released; it binds nothing before.*

A message may carry **one attachment**: in this version, a photo. The
member's phone uploads it to its own vault, which keeps a copy for the
member's history and sends a fresh copy to the connection's vault,
which keeps its own copy for its member. A phone never stores one: it
fetches the photo from its vault when the member opens it and keeps it
in memory only (ANDROID-PLAN "Photo attachments"). Relay blobs are a
transfer mechanism only (RELAY-PROTOCOL §6.8): every blob is deleted by
its recipient once fetched, good or bad, and expires after
`blob_ttl_seconds` (7 days) otherwise.

**One per message.** A message has at most one attachment; a member who
sends several photos sends several messages (the app sends them in
order, the caption with the first). One per message keeps a message's
state one value (sent, delivered, failed), keeps every limit below a
single check per message, and keeps each message to one transfer of at
most 8 MiB. Several would need partial failure states, a quota check
over a set and a message larger than one transfer slot. A later
version may add an array member without changing this one.

**Kinds.** `kind` is `"photo"`, the only kind of this version. Other
files are for a later version (owner decision 4); a vault refuses any
other `kind` (`bad_request` from a device; `refused` with reason `type`
from a peer).

**Constants** (release constants of release A):

| Name | Value | What |
|---|---|---|
| `attachment_max_bytes` | 8,257,532 at vettid.org: the largest content whose blob (§5.5: 41 bytes plus the padded plaintext) fits the relay's `max_blob_bytes` (8,388,608) | `size`, the content's length |
| `thumb_max_bytes` | 32,768 | a thumbnail's decoded length (owner decision 5) |
| `photo_types` | `image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/webp` | the types a vault and an app accept, by sniffing (below) |
| `photo_max_side` | 8,192 pixels | `width` and `height`; recipients decode nothing larger (ANDROID-PLAN) |
| `attachment_storage` | 1,073,741,824 bytes (1 GiB) | per vault: the stored content and thumbnails of every attachment, sent and received (owner decision 3) |
| `attachments` | 4,096 | stored attachments per vault (bounds the index in vault state) |
| `peer_storage` | 268,435,456 bytes (256 MiB, a quarter of `attachment_storage`) | stored attachments received from one connection, an attachment whose fetch is in progress counted at its declared size (0.32.1, 0.33.1: a waiting one by its thumbnail only) |
| `peer_attachments` | 64 attachments and 268,435,456 bytes (256 MiB) per rolling 24 hours | accepted from one connection (§7.3) |
| `peer_reuploads` | 64 uploads and 268,435,456 bytes per rolling 24 hours | uploads the sender's vault makes again for one connection on its `missing` |
| `attachment_transfers` | 2 per vault; per enclave instance by memory (below), at most 4 until measured | blob transfers in progress at once |
| `attachment_fetches` | 2 per device | `content` fetches of one device in progress |
| `attachment_window` | 7 days | how long a sender's vault waits for the peer's `stored` before it tells its member (owner decision 8) |
| `missing_window` | 30 days | how long a sender's vault answers a `missing`, from its own `sent_at`; and how long a recipient waits for an upload, from the message's arrival in its own vault (never from the peer's `sent_at`) |
| `missing_backoff` | 10 minutes, doubling to 24 hours | between two `missing` for the same attachment |
| `missing_turn` | 24 hours | how long a recipient keeps asking for one attachment of a connection before it moves to the next one waiting (round robin) |
| `attachment_reoffers` | 3 | uploads of one attachment after the first; so at most 4 fetches of it by the recipient |

**The views.**

```json
blob:        { "id": "<blob_id>", "key": "<b64 32>", "sha256": "<b64 32>", "size": 812345,
               "mime": "image/jpeg", "name": "photo.jpg" }
device send: { "blob": <blob>, "kind": "photo", "width": 2560, "height": 1920, "thumb": "<b64>" }
peer view:   { "blob": <blob>?, "kind": "photo", "size": 812345, "width": 2560, "height": 1920,
               "thumb": "<b64>", "expires_at": "<ts>"? }
device view: { "att_id": "<ULID>", "kind": "photo", "mime": "image/jpeg"?, "size": 812345,
               "width": 2560, "height": 1920, "name": "photo.jpg"?, "state": "stored",
               "reason": "<code>"?, "thumb": "<b64>"? }
```

- `blob` is §5.5's claim-check reference: `id` the relay's `blob_id`,
  `key` the fresh 256-bit blob key, `sha256` the SHA-256 of the
  uploaded bytes, `size` the content's length (1 to
  `attachment_max_bytes`), `mime` the sender's claim (a string of at
  most 64 bytes; never used to decode, below), `name` optional, at most
  255 bytes of UTF-8 (apps send none for a photo). A blob key is used
  for one blob only.
- The **peer view** carries `size` itself, and `blob` with
  `expires_at` only when the sender's vault uploaded one: without them
  the recipient asks for the upload when it can take it ("Delivery to
  the peer").
- `width` and `height` are integers from 1 to `photo_max_side`: the
  sender's claim, for laying out a placeholder; recipients decode with
  their own bounds and never trust them.
- `thumb` is the thumbnail, base64, its decoded length 1 to
  `thumb_max_bytes`, one of `photo_types` by sniffing. It travels
  inline, inside the encrypted message, never as a blob.
- The **device view** never carries a blob key or a blob id. `size` is
  the declared size until the content is stored, then the stored one
  (they are equal, or the attachment failed). `mime` is present only
  once the content is stored, and is then the type **the vault
  sniffed**, never the sender's claim. `name` is present only when the
  sender sent one, as stored. `thumb` is present in `message.new` and in
  `message.attachment.get{part: "thumb"}` only; `message.list` and
  `message.get` leave it out (§10.5.2).
- `state` and `reason`:

  | Direction | `state` | Meaning |
  |---|---|---|
  | out | `preparing` | the message is stored; the vault is fetching the device's upload and checking it |
  | out | `sending` | stored in this vault; being uploaded to the peer, or waiting for the peer's request or its `stored` |
  | out | `delivered` | the peer's vault reported `stored` |
  | out | `failed` | `reason`: `bad` or `type` (the device's upload failed the checks of "Sending"), `unsupported` (the peer's release has no attachments), `refused` (the peer refused it; then also its reason when the peer gave one: `refused:rate`, `refused:type`; a refusal because the peer's store is full carries none and reaches the member as a generic "couldn't be delivered"), `missing` (the peer could not use any upload, after `attachment_reoffers`), `unconfirmed` (no `stored` within `attachment_window`), `removed` (the connection was removed or blocked first) |
  | in | `fetching` | the message is stored; the vault is fetching the attachment, or waiting to ask for it or for its upload |
  | in | `stored` | stored in this vault; `message.attachment.get` serves it |
  | in | `failed` | `reason`: `full` (`attachment_storage`, `attachments` or `peer_storage`), `rate` (`peer_attachments`), `type` (not an accepted type), `bad` (hash, length, padding or decryption failed on every fetch, at most `attachment_reoffers` + 1), `expired` (no usable upload within `missing_window` of its arrival), `withdrawn` (the sender said it will not upload it: `withdrawn:deleted`, `withdrawn:limit`, `withdrawn:expired`), `removed` (the connection was removed or blocked first) |

  An `unconfirmed` attachment becomes `delivered` if a `stored` still
  arrives, and `sending` again on a `missing` within `missing_window`.

**Sniffing.** Wherever this section says "by sniffing", the type is
decided from the content's first bytes and nothing else: `image/jpeg`
starts `FF D8 FF`; `image/png` starts `89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A`;
`image/webp` starts `52 49 46 46` (`RIFF`), any 4 bytes, `57 45 42 50`
(`WEBP`). Anything else is not an accepted type. The vault does no
other parsing of the content: no image decoder runs in the enclave.

**At rest.** Each stored attachment has a fresh 32-byte key `k_att`,
kept only in the attachment's index entry (DEK state, §3.3), and two
objects under the vault's prefix (VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.2), the
content and the thumbnail, framed and padded as a blob's plaintext
(§5.5), so that the host sees the same coarse sizes as the relay:

```
object = 0x01 || nonce (24, random) || XChaCha20-Poly1305(k_att, nonce, aad, framed)
framed = §5.5's padded plaintext of the content (part "c") or the thumbnail (part "t")
aad    = "vettid/vms/2/att" || 0x00 || vault_id || 0x00 || att_id || 0x00 || part || 0x00 || object[0]
key    = vaults/<vault_id>/att/<lowercase att_id>      (content)
         vaults/<vault_id>/att/<lowercase att_id>.t    (thumbnail)
```

`att_id` in the AAD is the canonical ULID, upper case as everywhere in
this document (§5.3); only the store key spells it in lower case,
because store keys allow lower case only (VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.2).
The stored objects never reuse a blob's key or bytes. Thumbnails are
objects, not state: vault state is rewritten whole at every flush
(§8.3), and 4,096 thumbnails of 32 KiB would make it 128 MiB. A
thumbnail is held in its entry only until its object is written
(below).

**The index** (vault state, §3.3) has one entry per attachment:
`att_id`, `connection_id`, `message_id`, direction, `kind`, the sniffed
`mime`, `size`, the thumbnail's length, `width`, `height`, `name`,
`k_att`, the state and reason; for each of the two objects a flag
**written** and, once written, its store version (so that a delete is
conditional without a read, VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.4); while the
thumbnail is not written, the thumbnail itself; and while a transfer is
due, its blob reference, its expiry, the inner `id` of the
`message.attachment.deliver` that carried it, and its counts.

**Write order.** An object is never written before an entry that names
it is in a flushed state, and an entry is never removed before its
objects are deleted. The entry is created **in the same flush as its
message and the request's or event's inner-`id` record** (§8.2,
§8.3), before the ack, with both objects not written and the thumbnail
held in the entry. A crash before that flush loses nothing: the
message is redelivered (or the request retransmitted) and handled
afresh. After it, the vault writes the thumbnail object and, in a later
flush, marks it written and drops the thumbnail from the entry; the
content object is written when the content is at hand and marked
written in the flush that sets the state. At unlock the vault finishes
what a lock or crash interrupted, from the flags: it writes a thumbnail
object that is not written yet (from the entry), resumes a transfer
whose content is not written, and for an entry that is being erased
deletes its objects (a missing object counting as deleted) before
removing it. Message deletion and vault deletion therefore find every
object (below, §12.5), although the enclave cannot list the store.

**Sending** (D→V, then V↔V):

1. The app prepares the photo (ANDROID-PLAN): it removes EXIF and
   location data and re-encodes and downscales the photo, makes the
   thumbnail, seals the photo as a §5.5 blob under a fresh key, and
   uploads it with `PUT /v1/blob/{vault_mailbox}`, its vault's own
   mailbox, under its standing token (§7.1).
2. It sends `message.send{connection_id, text?, attachment: <device
   send>}`.
3. The vault checks the request: the shape (above); that the
   connection is active (`not_found`, `connection_unavailable` as for
   text); the thumbnail (decoded length, an accepted type by sniffing;
   else `bad_request`); and `limit` for `attachment_storage` (`max` the
   bound, `size` what the store would reach with this `size` and
   thumbnail) or `attachments`. Its declared `size` counts against
   both while the vault takes it in (the `preparing` transfer of step
   5) and is replaced by the stored size, or released if the
   attachment fails.
4. In one flush it stores the message, its entry (direction out, state
   `preparing`, the blob reference to its own mailbox, both objects not
   written, the thumbnail held) and the request's inner-`id` record and
   response, and answers `{message_id, sent_at, att_id}` (§8.3). It
   sends `message.new` (with `thumb`) to its other devices. The
   response is cached as any (§8.2): a retransmission of the request,
   the app's **Retry** included, gets the same answer and starts
   nothing twice.
5. In the background it writes the thumbnail object, fetches the blob
   from its own mailbox (`GET /v1/blob/{id}`, signed by the vault relay
   key) and checks it: at most `max_blob_bytes`, `sha256` in
   constant time, decryption, the framing and padding (§5.5), the
   content's length equal to `size`, and an accepted type by sniffing.
   A failure ends in `failed` (`bad`, or `type`), and the blob is
   deleted at once (`DELETE /v1/blob/{id}`); `blob_unknown` from the
   relay is `bad`. **The message is then not sent at all**: its caption
   is never delivered, the member's devices show it as not sent, and
   the member sends the photo again as a new message. The device
   learns the state from `sync.event` (below).
6. It writes the content object and in one flush marks it written, sets
   the state `sending` and audits `message.attachment_sent`. **Only
   then** does it delete the device's blob from its mailbox: a crash
   before that flush leaves the blob in place for the next unlock to
   fetch again, and the device, which already dropped the photo, loses
   nothing.
7. It uploads a **fresh** blob of the content (a new key) to the peer's
   mailbox with `PUT /v1/blob/{peer_mailbox}` under the standing token
   the peer issued it, records the reference, and queues
   `message.attachment.deliver{message_id, text?, sent_at, attachment:
   <peer view>}` in the outbox (§8.3). It keeps that message's inner
   `id` in the entry: an `unsupported_type` response with that `re`
   (§5.3) is matched to the entry, as a pending request is (§8.1),
   until the entry is `delivered` or `failed` or 14 days have passed.

Every refusal of a `message.send` that names a blob deletes the blob
from the vault's mailbox (best effort): only the vault can delete it.
**`message.attachment.discard{blob_id}`** (D→V, the app only;
`{}`) asks the vault to delete a blob its device uploaded and will not
send: the app's **Cancel** before `message.send`. The vault deletes
only a blob that it can tell this device uploaded: one whose uploader,
in the relay's list of the mailbox's blobs (RELAY-PROTOCOL 0.9.2 §6.8), is that device's relay key, and that no index entry or
pending `message.send` names. It answers `{}` in every case (a blob it
may not delete, an unknown one, or `blob_unknown`), so the answer tells
a device nothing about other depositors' blobs. Without that list the
vault deletes nothing, and the blob expires after the blob TTL.

**Delivery to the peer.** The upload of step 7 can be refused:

- a transient failure (a `429` with `retry_after`, a `5xx`, a transport
  error) is retried with §8.6's backoff, at most once every 10 minutes
  after the first hour, until `attachment_window` ends;
- `quota_exceeded` for the **token** (RELAY-PROTOCOL §7.1 `quota`:
  `token`; before a relay sends `quota`, the first `quota_exceeded`):
  the vault asks for a fresh token (§7.2) and tries once more with it;
- `quota_exceeded` for the **mailbox's blob storage or this sender's
  share of it** (`quota`: `mailbox_blobs` or `sender_blobs`; before a
  relay sends `quota`, a second `quota_exceeded` after a fresh token,
  or one when no fresh token may be asked for): the vault **does not
  retry the upload**. It sends `message.attachment.deliver` without
  `blob` and `expires_at`, and uploads only when the recipient asks for
  it with `message.attachment.status{missing}` (below). A full mailbox
  is not emptied by uploading into it again, and every refused upload
  costs 8 MiB of traffic;
- `token_revoked` and `mailbox_unknown` end the delivery as for any
  deposit (§8.6); the attachment becomes `failed` (`unconfirmed`) at
  the end of the window.

The peer answers with `message.attachment.status`:

- `stored`: state `delivered`; the sender's vault keeps its copy for
  its member's history. A later `missing` is ignored.
- `missing`: "send it now": the peer has no usable upload (none was
  made, or it expired, was deleted or failed its checks). The sender's
  vault, matching by connection and `message_id`, uploads a fresh blob
  and sends `message.attachment.deliver` again with the same
  `message_id`, at most `attachment_reoffers` times per attachment and
  within `peer_reuploads` per connection, at a lower priority than every
  other transfer. It does so while the attachment is `sending` or
  `failed` (`unconfirmed`), up to `missing_window` after its own
  `sent_at`, and as long as it still stores the attachment. This is how
  a recipient that stayed locked longer than the blob's 7 days still
  gets the photo (owner decision 8).
  - **It never ignores a `missing` silently.** When it will not upload,
    it answers `message.attachment.status{withdrawn, reason}`:
    `deleted` (the member deleted the message, or the attachment is
    gone; answered until the attachment's `missing_window` ends, from
    the record that deletion keeps, "Deletion" below; 0.32.1), `limit` (the `attachment_reoffers` are spent; the sender's
    own state becomes `failed` (`missing`)), or `expired` (past
    `missing_window`). The recipient fails the attachment at once
    (`withdrawn:<reason>`). A `missing` for an attachment that is
    `delivered` or `refused` (also one deleted after that), or for a
    `message_id` the vault never sent, is ignored (the recipient has
    its answer, or there is none).
  - **When `peer_reuploads` is used up** the request is kept and served
    when the rolling budget allows, within a day; it is not withdrawn.
    A locked sender serves it after its next unlock. In both cases the
    recipient's round robin (Receiving step 3) keeps the connection's
    other attachments moving meanwhile.
  - **An upload the relay refuses for the recipient's blob storage**
    (`mailbox_blobs` or `sender_blobs`, checked before the body is
    read) is answered with a `message.attachment.deliver` without
    `blob`, as above. It moved no content, so it counts neither as a
    reoffer nor against `peer_reuploads`; the recipient's
    `missing_backoff` is what bounds such rounds.
- `refused`: `failed` (`refused:<reason>`).

If no `stored` arrives within `attachment_window` of `sent_at`, the
attachment is `failed` (`unconfirmed`), audited
`message.attachment_failed` and announced to the member with the feed
item `message.attachment_failed` (`ref` = `message_id`; priority
`normal`). A sender's vault that was locked when the window ended makes
one delivery attempt after its next unlock before it marks the
attachment `failed`. A peer whose release has no attachments answers
`message.attachment.deliver`, an event of a type it does not know, with
`unsupported_type` (§5.3): the attachment is `failed` (`unsupported`)
at once, with the same audit entry and feed item. Each change of state
reaches the owner's devices as `sync.event{kind: "message.attachment",
connection_id, message_id, state, reason?}`.

**Receiving** (V↔V). On `message.attachment.deliver` from an active
connection:

1. **A new `message_id`:** the vault checks, in this order (0.32.1):
   the shape (a malformed one is dropped and audited
   `drop.attachment_malformed`); the `kind` and the thumbnail as in
   sending step 3 (an unaccepted one is `refused` with reason `type`,
   and does **not** count against `peer_attachments`);
   `peer_attachments` (§7.3; `refused` with reason `rate`); then the
   store limits, `peer_storage`, `attachment_storage` and
   `attachments` (`refused`, `full`). The store limits count what is
   stored, this attachment's thumbnail, and the declared `size` of
   every attachment **whose transfer is in progress** (an admitted
   fetch, a minute or two at most), this one's included if it named a
   blob. An attachment that waits for an upload (a deliver without a
   blob, or one waiting for the sender, its backoff or its turn) holds
   only its thumbnail, whose object is stored (owner decision of
   2026-10-15; 0.33.1: the thumbnail counts like any stored object).
   (0.33.1) The limits are checked again when its blob arrives (a
   deliver that names one) and when its fetch starts (step 2). A refusal stores the message (its `text`, if any) with the
   attachment `failed`, answers `message.attachment.status{refused,
   reason?}` (`rate` or `type`; **no reason for `full`**, so that the
   sender learns only that it could not be delivered, not that this
   vault is full: owner decision of 2026-10-15; the member's own app
   sees `failed (full)` and the feed item), deletes the blob from its own
   mailbox if one was named, audits `message.attachment_refused`
   (`full`, `type`) or `drop.attachment_rate` (`rate`), and for `full`
   creates the feed item `message.attachment_refused` (`ref` =
   `message_id`, priority `normal`), so that the member learns that the
   vault is full. Otherwise, in one flush, it stores the message and
   the entry (state `fetching`, the blob reference if one was named,
   both objects not written, the thumbnail held) with the inner-`id`
   record, audits `message.received` as for text, and acks (§8.3). It
   sends `message.new` (with `thumb`) and the delivered receipt as for
   text, then writes the thumbnail object (write order, above).
2. If a blob was named, in the background the vault, when it admits
   the fetch, checks the store limits again with this attachment's
   declared `size` added; a blob that no longer fits is deleted and the
   attachment `refused` (`full`, which the sender sees as a generic
   refusal), as in step 1. The declared size counts only while the
   fetch runs, and is replaced by the stored size when it ends. The
   vault then fetches the blob from
   its own mailbox and checks it as in sending step 5 (with `size`,
   `sha256`, the framing, and an accepted type by sniffing). A blob that
   fails is deleted from the mailbox at once. A blob that passes is
   written as the content object, and in one flush the vault marks it
   written, sets the entry `stored` and audits
   `message.attachment_received`; **only then** does it delete the blob
   from its mailbox (so a crash before the flush fetches it again after
   the unlock) and answer `message.attachment.status{stored}`. Either
   way, every blob it fetched is deleted, good or bad.
3. If no blob was named, or the fetch is answered `blob_unknown`, or
   the blob fails a check, the entry waits for an upload, and the vault
   asks for it with `message.attachment.status{missing}`:
   - for **at most one attachment of a connection at a time**, and only
     when it has no fetch of that connection in progress, so that a
     connection's uploads into its mailbox come one by one;
   - only when its mailbox has room for the attachment: when the relay
     lists the mailbox's blobs (RELAY-PROTOCOL 0.9.2 §6.8), its
     `max_bytes` less `used_bytes` is at least the blob's padded size
     (§5.5). Without the list the vault cannot tell, and only the
     backoff below bounds the rounds. Several connections may pass the
     check at once for the last free room; the relay refuses all but
     one upload before its body, and the others are answered without
     a blob and asked again after the backoff, which is harmless;
   - at most once per `missing_backoff` for the same attachment (10
     minutes, doubling up to 24 hours). The backoff is the
     attachment's own and does not restart when its turn comes round
     again: it starts again at 10 minutes only after an upload of it
     arrives;
   - **in turn**: after `missing_turn` (24 hours) of asking for one
     attachment without an upload, the vault moves to the next waiting
     attachment of that connection, oldest first, and comes back to
     the first in its next turn; so one attachment that cannot come
     (a locked sender, a used-up budget) never holds back the photos
     after it.

   A `withdrawn` from the sender fails the entry at once
   (`withdrawn:<reason>`). A transient failure of the fetch is retried
   as in delivery. A blob that is not one of `photo_types` is `refused`
   with reason `type`. After `attachment_reoffers` + 1 fetches that
   failed their checks the entry is `failed` (`bad`); without a usable
   upload within `missing_window` of **the message's arrival in this
   vault** it is `failed` (`expired`); each is audited
   `message.attachment_failed`.
4. **A known `message_id`** whose entry is `fetching` and that this
   vault asked for with `missing`: a fresh upload; the vault replaces
   the blob reference and fetches it (step 2). For an entry in any
   other state, a blob `id` it already had, or a fresh upload it did
   not ask for, the message is ignored (idempotence, §10), and a named
   blob it will not fetch is deleted from its mailbox.

The peer's `mime` and `name` are kept as claims: the vault records its
sniffed type in their place for `mime`, and serves `name` only as text
(apps sanitize it, ANDROID-PLAN). There is no scanning of the content:
it is end-to-end encrypted, and the checks are the recipient's
(owner decision 6).

**Orphan blobs.** A blob that nobody will fetch fills the mailbox's
blob storage, which every depositor shares (RELAY-PROTOCOL §6.8): a
device's abandoned upload, a peer's upload whose message never came.
A vault deletes a blob in its own mailbox as soon as it has fetched it
or will not fetch it (above). Once a relay lists a mailbox's blobs to
its owner (RELAY-PROTOCOL 0.9.2 §6.8), the vault, after its collect
loop has drained the mailbox once since the unlock and then once a
