- **The first app's handshake.** After `vault.enrolled`, the app sends
  `hs.init` with purpose `app` and `ctx` = `vault_id`, deposited with the
  token from `vault.enrolled`. The vault answers it without approval if,
  and only if, `from.ik` and the collect `sender` equal the keys bound at
  enrollment and the 24 h provisional window has not passed.

### 11.4 Unlock

**The `vault.unlock` request** is sealed to the leased instance's ETK:

```json
{ "user_guid": "...", "vault_id": "...", "request_id": "<ULID>",
  "device_ik": "<b64>", "pin": "<digits>",
  "unlock_secret": "<b64 32 bytes; 0.33.0, release R>",
  "min_state_seq": 1234, "min_header_seq": 1301,
  "token": "<fresh standing token for MB(device), sub = vault relay key>",
  "device_assertion": { },
  "manifest_sha256": "<64 hex>", "manifest_serial": 7,
  "release_update": { "to": "<pcr0 hex>", "to_release": 5, "approval": { } },
  "cancel_recovery": true,
  "sig": "<b64 Ed25519 by device_ik>" }
```

`manifest_sha256` and `manifest_serial` are REQUIRED and name the manifest
the app verified, exactly as in `vault.enroll` (§11.3); the host supplies
the document (§11.5). `release_update` is present only when the member approved a release update
(§11.10.3). The request is padded to exactly 12,288 bytes (§5.4).

`device_assertion` is REQUIRED (§11.7). (0.27.0) On Android it MAY
carry `chain`, which an app sends while the vault has not recorded its
signer (§11.7.1); `chain` is not part of the signing string. `sig`
covers the following string,
where each `\n` is a literal newline:

```
"vettid/vms/2/unlock" \n user_guid \n vault_id \n request_id \n ts \n etk_kid_hex \n
min_state_seq \n min_header_seq \n hex(SHA-256(pin)) \n hex(SHA-256(token)) \n
hex(SHA-256(manifest_bytes)) \n to_pcr0_hex_or_empty
```

`ts` is the request's inner `ts` (§5.3). The line
`hex(SHA-256(manifest_bytes))` is exactly the request's `manifest_sha256`
(the string is unchanged from 0.9.1). Integers are decimal, hex is
lowercase, and there is no trailing newline. No field may contain CR or LF.
When the request carries `cancel_recovery` (present only as `true`,
§11.11.4), the string has a thirteenth line, the literal
`cancel_recovery`. (0.33.0, release R) From release R `unlock_secret`
is REQUIRED (`bad_request` without 32 bytes, before any work on the
PIN), and the string ends with one more line after all of these,
`hex(SHA-256(unlock_secret))`, so that a request cannot be replayed
with another secret.

```
App        Member API                   SQS/Parent                 Enclave
 |--POST /api/vault/unlock{vault_id, request_id, instance_id, etk_kid, envelope}
 |          check lease             |--enqueue--->|--vsock bytes--->|
 |<--202----|                       |             |  replay check; sealed header;
 |          |                       |             |  vault_id/user_guid; unlock key + sig;
 |          |                       |             |  device attestation sig; signer (§11.7.1); backoff; rollback
 |          |                       |             |  (§13.2); derive DEK; load state
 |          |<--response slot{request_id, envelope}----------------|
 |--GET /api/vault/requests/{id} (1 s poll)-->|                    |
 |<--{status: done, envelope}----------------|   on success: §12.2 start order
```

**`vault.unlock.result`** is sealed to the device's `kem` from the sealed
header and padded to 4,096 bytes. Its inner `re` is the request's
`request_id` and its `status` is `ok` (the outcome is in the body), so a
result cannot be presented as the answer to another request. Its body is
one of:

- `{"ok": true, "state_seq": n, "header_seq": m, "token": "<standing token for
  MB(vault)>", "release": "<PCR0 hex>", "release_number": r,
  "release_status": "active|deprecated|retired|removed", "manifest_serial": s,
  "update": {"to": "<pcr0>", "result": "moved|refused|abandoned", "code": "<reason>"},
  "recovery_cancelled": true, "vault_bundle": "<b64>", "credential_backup": true|false}`
  — (0.29.0, release L) `"unlock_id": "<32 hex>"` is present whenever
  the vault resumed (with `token`): the name of this unlock (§10.2
  "Locks"). Its absence tells the app that the release is from before
  L, and that locks are not bound.
  — `update` is present only if the request carried `release_update`, or a
  pending move was completed (§11.10.4). After `moved` the vault is locked
  and sealed to the new release; `header_seq` is the new header's, and
  `token` is absent (the vault did not resume).
  — `recovery_cancelled` is present when the unlock cancelled a recovery
  (§11.11.4); `vault_bundle` and, after it, `credential_backup` (0.10.6) only for the app a recovery registered
  (§11.11.5). Since 0.16.0 `credential_backup` is always `true` there
  (a vault without a backup copy refuses that unlock with `no_backup`);
  apps MUST NOT rely on it and MAY ignore it. (0.33.0, release R)
  Neither member exists from release R: a registered phone does not
  unlock (§11.14.6). (0.34.0; owner decision of 2026-10-16) The one
  exception is `vault_bundle` in the result of the **recovered** phone's
  own unlock before its first handshake, which resumes a lost `ok`
  (§11.14.6, "A lost `ok`"); `credential_backup` stays absent.
- `{"ok": false, "code": "bad_pin|backoff|unknown_device|attestation|signer_refused|state_rollback|vault_missing|manifest|wrong_release|release_key|retry|recovery_pending|no_backup|device_secret|transfer_incomplete",
  "header_seq": m, "retry_after": <s>}` — `signer_refused` (0.27.0):
  the device key's recorded signer is not pinned by this release, or
  the key has no recorded signer and the request brought no valid
  `chain`; decided after `sig` and the assertion verified and before
  the PIN is tried, and not a PIN failure (§11.7.1).
  `recovery_pending`: a recovery
  is in progress and the request did not cancel it (§11.11.4); it is
  answered before the PIN is tried and is not a PIN failure.
  `no_backup` (0.16.0): only to the app a recovery registered, when the
  vault, once opened with the PIN, keeps no backup copy of its
  credential (§11.11.5 step 1). Nothing else is in the body: no token,
  no `vault_bundle`; the vault removes the recovery and the registered
  unlock key and locks again.
  (0.33.0, release R) Two more codes: `device_secret`, the
  `unlock_secret` does not match the vault's `secret_check`, decided
  before the PIN is tried and not a PIN failure (the app tries the next
  epoch once, then shows that this phone no longer holds the vault's
  keys); and `transfer_incomplete`, the requesting app is the new phone
  of a transfer whose state write is not stored (§11.14.2). `no_backup`
  is not used from release R.

**Unlock of a running vault (0.23.3).** An unlock of a vault that is
already unlocked is processed like any other: there is no "already
unlocked" answer, because the PIN, the device assertion, the minimum
sequence numbers and any `release_update` are checked by every unlock,
and its result carries a fresh token. The enclave first locks the
running vault as for an owner request (§12.3: the batch, the flush,
`vault.locking`, the lifecycle `locked`), then opens it with the
request; an unlock that fails leaves the vault locked. The lease the
request took stays across that lock (§11.1). The result's inner `ts` is
set after the lock, so the lock's `vault.locking` is never later than
the result. That notice is relayed and can reach the app after the
result (as can the lock before a release update's confirming unlock,
§11.10.6): an app MUST ignore a `vault.locking` whose `ts` is not later
than that of the latest successful unlock result it received.

On `state_rollback`, the app MUST warn the user that the vault's stored state
is older than state this device has already seen (§13.2). `release_key`
means the running release's own sealing key failed its check (§11.10.7);
`retry` covers state write conflicts (§11.9) and KMS or store failures.

When no unlock key in the header matches `device_ik`, the signature does
not verify, or the release holds no header for `vault_id`, there is no key
to seal to: the enclave answers with random bytes of the result's size
(5,252 bytes), indistinguishable to the API and parent. `unknown_device`
and `vault_missing` therefore reach the app only as an unreadable result.

Every outcome has the same size and the same path, so the response reveals
neither the outcome nor the reason for a failure. VettID can still observe a
success, because the vault then starts collecting and the parent reports its
lifecycle (§11.5).

### 11.5 What the member API stores; queue shape

Nothing secret is stored:

| Store | Contents | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| Vault table | **`app_key`** (0.15.0: `{key, kid, seq}`, the public key of the vault's app key as the enclave last reported it, written by the host; and the API's own `app_key_pending` and recovery claim keys, §11.12; (0.33.0, release R) `app_key_next` `{key, kid, seq}`, the host-written next key of a replacement in progress, §11.14.2), `user_guid`, **`vault_id`** (opaque, 128-bit random, 32 lowercase hex characters, assigned by the API at a member's first enrollment; the routing key for alternate-channel requests), `state` (`enrolling`, `locked`, `unlocked`, `deleted`), **lease** (`instance_id`, `lease_expires_at`), **`sealed_release`** (the PCR0 the vault is sealed to; routing aid, §11.10.5), **`vault_version`** (release that last opened the vault), **`state_version`** (vault-state format version), **`alarm`** (`kind`, `alarm_id`, `at`, `emailed_at`; the last host alarm, below) and `alarm_pending`, **`credential_backup`** (0.16.0: whether the vault keeps a backup copy of its credential, as last reported, below; absent until a release of 0.16.0 reports it), the API's own `deletion` record (§11.11.9), **`deleting_at`** (0.51.0: when the vault reported its deletion's marking flush, the parent's Unix seconds, written by the host, §12.5), **`name_change`** (0.18.0: `{seq, first_name, last_name, at}`, the vault's latest name request, written by the host) and `name_change_pending`, the API's `name_change_result` (§10.8, below), (0.57.0) the cleanup job's `account_deleted_at` (when the account deletion asked the vault to delete itself, MEMBER-API 2.11.0), `created_at`, `updated_at` | account lifetime |
| Instance registry | `instance_id`, **`release`** (PCR0 from its descriptor), queue URL, descriptor, attestation, `heartbeat_at` | while the instance is live |
| Request table (response slots) | `request_id`, `vault_id`, `op`, `status` (`queued`, `done`, `expired`), opaque response `envelope` (≤ 8 KiB) and/or a host `code` | TTL 15 min |
| Request table (0.57.0, the record of a removed deleted vault) | `vdeleted#<vault_id>`: `vault_id`, the vault's app public keys (`key`, `kid`), `deleted_at`, `cause` (MEMBER-API 2.11.0 "Vault deletion") | 90 days (TTL `expires_at`) |
| Audit log | enroll, unlock and lock requests: member, time, `vault_id`, request id, never PINs or envelopes | MEMBER-API audit retention |

- **Not stored:** mailbox ids, relay keys, device identifiers, and request
  envelopes beyond the queue's own retention.
- **Lifecycle reporting.** The enclave emits lifecycle events (`enrolled`,
  `unlocked`, `locked`, `deleted`, `moved` with the target release, carrying
  `vault_version` and `state_version`, a number). Since 0.15.0
  `enrolled`, `unlocked` and `locked` also carry the vault's current app
  key (`app_key`: b64 SPKI DER; `app_key_seq`: the header's count of
  app-key changes, 1 at enrollment), and the event **`app_key`** carries
  the same two values when a transfer (§6.7.1) or a recovery (§11.11.5)
  replaces the app. The enclave hands the `app_key` event to the parent
  together with the header write that made the change, and the parent
  writes it after that store succeeds. (0.33.0, release R) A
  replacement of the app is written in three steps (§11.14.2): the parent
  writes `app_key_next` on the row (conditional on its `seq` being higher
  than `app_key`'s) **before the vault stores the header that names it**,
  in an acknowledged request (0.58.0, VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.7); the event
  **`app_key_next`** (the same two values) goes with the first header
  write and remains as a report (the parent logs it and does not write
  it); `app_key` goes with the third, and the parent then clears
  `app_key_next`. An
  `app_key` event with `next_cleared: true` repeats the current key with
  the same `seq`: the parent skips the `app_key` write and applies the
  clear (§11.14.2).
  `unlocked` and `locked` also carry `next` (bool): whether the header
  has a `next` part (§11.14.2). The parent writes `app_key = {key,
  kid, seq}` on the vault row **whatever the lease**, conditional only on
  `seq` being higher than the row's (a stale instance can only report an
  older one), except that `enrolled` writes it also when the row is still
  `enrolling`, has no key, or already names the same key (0.58.0; a
  replaced provisional vault starts again at 1 by the enroll-mode
  request of VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.7, which replaces the row's key
  whatever it has but only for the instance that holds the vault's
  lease, §11.3); it never takes the key
  from anywhere else. (0.58.0) The writes of `app_key` and
  `app_key_next` are conditional on `seq` and `header_seq`
  (VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §7.2) and are repeated until they are written; a
  failed one is not dropped. `app_key` and the removal of `app_key_next`
  are one write. The enclave tells the parent its app key state again
  after every hello (the event `app_key_assert`: the current key and its
  `seq`; it fills in what the row lacks and never replaces a newer key).
- **The backup bit** (0.16.0, owner decision of 2026-10-06, §15 item
  24). `enrolled`, `unlocked` and `locked` also carry
  `credential_backup` (bool): whether the vault keeps a backup copy of
  its current blob (§3.5.6), the same bit as the sealed header's. When
  it changes on a running vault (the member turns the backup off, or a
  use of the credential stores the copy after it was turned on), the
  vault emits the event **`credential_backup`** with the new value,
  handed to the parent with the header write that recorded it, as for
  `app_key`. The parent writes `credential_backup` on the vault row
  under the lease rule below. It is one bit, about the member's own
  setting, and nothing else: no version, time or device. The member API
  uses it only to refuse a recovery request upfront with a clear answer
  (§11.11.7); the enclave decides from its own header (§11.11.1), so a
  host that misreports the bit can only refuse recoveries it could
  refuse anyway, or forward one the enclave refuses.
- **Name requests** (0.18.0, owner decisions of 2026-10-07, §10.8). After
  a successful `account.name.set` the vault emits the event
  **`account_name`** `{seq, first_name, last_name}`, handed to the parent
  with the flush that stored the request, as for `app_key`. The parent
  writes `name_change = {seq, first_name, last_name, at}` (`at`: its own
  Unix seconds) and `name_change_pending = true` on the vault row
  **whatever the lease**, conditional only on `seq` being higher than the
  row's (absent: 0), so a stale instance can only report an older
  request. **Re-reported on unlock** (0.19.0): an event the parent
  never wrote (lost after the flush, with the instance) is not emitted
  again by that flush, so with every `unlocked` report the vault emits
  `account_name` again for its latest request while that is still
  `pending` (§10.8). The `seq` condition makes this idempotent: a
  request the row already holds fails the condition, which the parent
  treats as done, and a request the member API already processed is
  not reopened. It is the only lifecycle event with member content: the
  member's own instruction about account data VettID already holds. The
  member API processes it (MEMBER-API 2.2.0 "Name changes"), records
  `name_change_result = {seq, status, reason?}` and pushes the snapshot,
  whose `name_change.last` carries that result (§11.13). Only the host
  role writes `name_change` and sets `name_change_pending`.
- **The lease rule.** The parent writes the lifecycle values (other than
  `app_key` and `name_change`, above) to
  the vault table only while it holds the vault's lease or no lease exists
  (a conditional write), so an instance that lost a split brain cannot
  overwrite the holder's values.
- **A stopped vault is locked** (0.10.6). A vault runs only under its
  instance's live lease. When the parent releases a lease because the
  vault stopped (the enclave's "stopped" notice: an owner's
  `vault.lock` over the relay, a lock on lease loss or memory pressure,
  a split brain or an error) it also turns a row's `state = unlocked`
  into `locked` (other states, `enrolling` among them, are left as they
  are), conditional on the lease being its own like the removal itself,
  whether or not a `locked` event arrived first; a `locked` event that
  is lost or late then changes nothing. The member API reports `unlocked` only while the
  row's lease is unexpired; a row that says `unlocked` without one is
  reported `locked` (MEMBER-API "Vault").
- **Host alarms** (0.9.0). The vault reports a clone alarm (§3.5.9) as
  the lifecycle event `alarm.credential_clone`, once per alarm. It
  carries nothing but its kind, the `vault_id` and the usual release
  fields: no device, version or time from the vault. The parent records
  it on the vault row, **whatever the lease** (an alarm is never lost to a
  lease race): `alarm = {kind: "credential_clone", alarm_id, at}`, where
  the parent makes `alarm_id` (a ULID) and `at` (Unix seconds), and
  `alarm_pending = true`. The member API emails the member and clears
  `alarm_pending` (MEMBER-API). Alarm kinds other than those listed here
  are rejected by the parent. A dishonest host can suppress the email but
  not the vault's own alert to the app, its freeze or its audit entry.
- **Deletion mark** (0.51.0, §12.5 "Mark at the host"). Once a
  deletion's marking flush is stored, the vault asks the parent
  (`MarkDeleting`, VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §5.6) to write `deleting_at`
  (the parent's Unix seconds) on the vault row, **whatever the lease**,
  conditional on the row existing, not being `deleted` and having no
  `deleting_at` yet (a mark is never moved); a refused condition counts
  as done. The parent answers only after that write, and the vault tells
  no device before the answer. The row's `state` is not changed by it
  (the `locked` that follows when the process ends is written as
  usual). The parent removes `deleting_at` in the update of an
  `unlocked` event: a vault that runs is not being deleted, so a mark
  there is stale or forged. The member API uses the mark **only** to
  resume the deletion (`delete_resume`, below), with its log and
  metric; it is **never shown to the member** (no status value, no
  account-site text, nothing in the apps). Like the other host-written
  values it is advisory: it never makes anything erase a vault that the
  enclave can read as live.
- **Deletion notice** (0.9.0). On the lifecycle event `deleted` (§12.5)
  the parent also records `alarm = {kind: "vault_deleted", alarm_id, at}`
  and `alarm_pending = true`, whatever the lease: the vault's own audit
  log is gone, so the member API emails the member and then deletes the
  vault rows (MEMBER-API), after which the member enrolls afresh.
- **Lifecycle values are advisory.** `vault_version` should match the
  `release` in the attested descriptor of the reporting instance, but a
  dishonest parent could misreport any of these values. They therefore serve
  the account site and operations only, never security decisions.

**The SQS message** goes to the leased instance's queue. Retention is 5 min,
with a DLQ after 3 receives:

```json
{ "v": 1, "op": "enroll|unlock|lock|delete|delete_resume|recovery|recovery_cancel|recovery_register|recovery_open|account",
  "vault_id": "...", "user_guid": "...", "request_id": "<ULID>",
  "etk_kid": "<16 hex; enroll, unlock, recovery_register and recovery_open only>",
  "envelope": "<b64; enroll, unlock, recovery_register and recovery_open only>",
  "manifest_sha256": "<64 hex; enroll and unlock only>",
  "browser_key": "<b64 65-byte P-256 point; recovery only>",
  "app_key": "<b64 SPKI DER; enroll, recovery_register and recovery_open only>",
  "account": { "...": "the account snapshot, §11.13; enroll, unlock and account only" },
  "signed_at": "<RFC 3339; recovery and recovery_cancel only, 0.33.0, release R>",
  "key_id": "<recovery and recovery_cancel only, 0.33.0, release R>",
  "sig": "<b64 DER; recovery and recovery_cancel only, 0.33.0, release R>",
  "unlock_id": "<32 hex; lock only, optional; 0.29.0, release L>",
  "enqueued_at": "<RFC 3339>" }
```

(0.33.0, release R) `recovery_open` carries `etk_kid`, `envelope` and
`app_key` like `recovery_register` (§11.14.6). `signed_at`, `key_id`
and `sig` are the member API's signature over a `recovery` or
`recovery_cancel` (§11.14.8); they are REQUIRED for both from release
R.

`app_key` (0.15.0) is REQUIRED for `enroll` and `recovery_register`
(0.33.0, release R: and `recovery_open`) and absent otherwise: the key the request was signed with at the API, which
the enclave binds to the sealed `app.api_key` (§11.3, §11.11.3).
`account` (0.15.0) is REQUIRED for `account` and, since 0.18.0, for
`enroll`, and OPTIONAL for `unlock` (the API includes it whenever it can
read the member): the enclave passes it to the vault process after a
successful enrollment or unlock, or, for the op `account`, to the
running vault process; with no running vault it drops it. An `enroll`
without a well-formed `account` (§11.13) is answered `bad_request`
(§11.3), so that every vault holds the account's names from its first
moment (§10.8). `account` takes no lease and has no envelope; the parent answers its
slot `done` (§11.13).

`manifest_sha256` is REQUIRED for `enroll` and `unlock` and absent for
every other op. The member API copies it from the request body (§11.1,
MEMBER-API) after checking only its format (64 lowercase hex); it cannot
check it against the sealed request, and does not need to.

The parent forwards the message to the enclave unchanged, for `enroll`
and `unlock` together with the manifest document it names (below). The
enclave answers the parent with

```json
{ "v": 1, "request_id": "<ULID>", "status": "done|etk_unknown", "envelope": "<b64, 5,252 bytes>",
  "code": "recovery_registered|recovery_unavailable|recovery_attempt|recovery_cancelled|recovery_not_current|locked|not_running|stale" }
```

(0.33.0, release R) The answer to a `recovery` also carries, in the
clear, `not_before`, `expires` and `earliest` (§11.14.5), and a
`recovery_unavailable` also a clear `reason` (`no_backup`,
`no_credential` or `not_offered`, §11.14.13), the one thing the member
API needs from the sealed refusal, and the answer
to a `recovery_open` that was counted carries `code:
"recovery_attempt"` with `retry_at` and `expires` when a wait began
(§11.14.11). The parent copies them into the slot like the other codes,
and `GET /api/vault/requests/{id}` returns `envelope` and `code` for the
slot of a `recovery_open` too. These say that an attempt was counted and
when the next is possible, never whether the guess was right; VettID,
which owns the counter's bucket, sees that already.

(0.49.0) **A recovery cancelled by an unlock.** The answer to an
`unlock` whose sealed result is `{"ok": true, …, "recovery_cancelled":
true}` (§11.11.4) carries the clear marker **`code:
"recovery_cancelled"`** and the clear member **`cancelled_recovery_id`**:
the id of the recovery that this unlock ended, which is the recovery's
own id in the header (the `request_id` of the `recovery` that opened it,
and the member API's `recovery_id`). No other answer carries them: not a
failed unlock, not an unlock without `cancel_recovery`, and no other
operation.

- **Only when the cancel was stored.** The vault process sets
  `recovery_cancelled` in its outcome as soon as the PIN has matched,
  before the release rules, the resume and the write of the header and
  state, and a later failure (for example `retry` after a failed write)
  does not clear it. The enclave therefore sets the marker only when the
  result is `ok: true` **and** carries `recovery_cancelled`, which is
  when the write that ended the recovery is stored. (vettid-vault
  staging release 18: `vault/unlock.go` sets `out.RecoveryCancelled`
  before `releaseRules` and `persist`; `enclave/core.go` `Core.Open`
  returns no marker for an `unlock`, so the unlock job must start
  returning one.)
- **The parent** copies the code and `cancelled_recovery_id`, after
  checking that it is a ULID, into the slot of an `unlock` that carries
  the code, as the slot attributes `code` and `cancelled_recovery_id`,
  and from no other operation's answer. A malformed id drops both.
- **Which recovery.** The member API ends the recovery whose
  `recovery_id` equals `cancelled_recovery_id`, and no other. The queue
  is not ordered (§11.5), so the recovery that was current when the
  member API queued the unlock may not be the one the enclave ended:
  the enclave cancels whatever recovery its header holds when the
  unlock runs.
- **A lost answer, and the backstop.** The marker can be lost between
  the enclave and the slot, and the slot then shows no cancel:
  - if the parent's call times out after the enclave stored the cancel,
    the redelivered message meets the replay set and is answered with
    random bytes and no code (§11.6);
  - if the parent stops after the answer and before it writes the slot,
    the redelivery meets the same.

  So a lifecycle event of that unlock also carries
  `cancelled_recovery_id`: its `unlocked` event whenever it emits one,
  which includes the abandonment of a pending move (which emits
  `unlocked` from the resume and then `moved`, and only the `unlocked`
  carries the id); and its `moved` event only for an unlock that
  completed a release move, which emits no `unlocked` (§11.10.4). The
  id travels from the vault process to the supervisor in the
  `Lifecycle` notification of `internal/vaultipc` (a new field, with a
  channel version step) and from the enclave to the parent in the
  `Lifecycle` frame (VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §7.2). The parent writes it to the vault row as
  `recovery_cancelled: {recovery_id, at}`. (A completed move leaves the
  recovery cancelled under the new release only. An unlock wrongly
  routed to the old release could meet that release's older header, in
  which the recovery still exists; routing by `sealed_release` (§11.1)
  prevents that window. The old release refuses that header as stale
  only after the move is confirmed.) Lifecycle events reach the
  parent before the answer on the same connection and are queued for
  their own table write, so they survive a call that timed out and a
  slot that was never written (vettid-vault `parent/parent.go`
  `onLifecycle`, `parent/consumer.go` `flushEvents` before `writeSlot`).
  The member API ends the matching recovery from either source,
  idempotently. A parent that stops before it has written the event
  loses both; the account site then shows the stale recovery until its
  `expires_at` or until the member cancels it there, as before 0.49.0.

The member API then ends its record of the recovery as `cancelled` and
emails the member (MEMBER-API "A recovery cancelled from the phone").
Without this the API never learned of such a cancel: the account site
kept showing the recovery as pending, and a new request was answered
`409 recovery_active` until the recovery's `expires_at`.

(`envelope` absent for lock, delete and `etk_unknown`; `code` present
only for a `recovery_register` whose sealed result is `{"ok": true}`
(`recovery_registered`, §11.11.3, 0.10.6), or for a `recovery` the
enclave refused (`recovery_unavailable`, §11.11.2, 0.16.0), or (0.49.0)
for an `unlock` that cancelled a recovery (`recovery_cancelled`, above),
or (0.49.0) for a named `recovery_cancel` that cancelled nothing
(`recovery_not_current`, §11.14.8, with no envelope), or, from
release L (0.29.0), for a `lock`: `locked`, `not_running` or `stale`,
below). The parent
writes the response slot: `status: "done"`, the `envelope` if any, and
`code: "etk_unknown"` when the enclave reported it, or the enclave's
`recovery_registered`, `recovery_unavailable` or (0.49.0)
`recovery_cancelled`, the last with `cancelled_recovery_id` (with the
envelope), when its answer carries one, or (0.49.0) the code
`recovery_not_current` of a `recovery_cancel`'s answer, which has no
envelope (the only code copied without one); or `status: "expired"`
for a request it did not forward (lease held elsewhere, §11.1) or that
the enclave could not read (no answer). It writes only slots that are
still `queued`, and no other `code` (the 0.49.0 codes included, each for its own operation only). `GET /api/vault/requests/{id}`
returns `{status, envelope?, code?}`; `code` matches `[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*`
and is a host code. It returns `envelope` and `code` only for the
slot of an `enroll`, `unlock`, `lock` or recovery `register` request;
the slot of any other operation answers `{status}` only. So the
slot of a recovery request never returns the sealed code, which
leaves the member API only through the recovery's status route
(§11.11.7). An operation added later must be added to that list
deliberately, or its result is not returned. A `code` never carries a sealed outcome, with two
exceptions (three from 0.49.0). `recovery_unavailable` (0.16.0) tells the member API that
the enclave refused a recovery request (§11.11.2), so that it ends the
recovery at once; it says no more than the backup bit the host already
has (§11.5), and a forged or suppressed one changes only what the
portal shows. `recovery_registered` tells the member API, in the clear,
that a recovery's code is spent, so that the API stops releasing it
(§11.11.7). That much is no secret from the host, which sees the
registered app unlock next; a host that forges the marker only hides a
code it could withhold anyway, and one that suppresses it leaves a spent
code on the portal, which the enclave refuses (`used`). (0.49.0)
`recovery_cancelled` with `cancelled_recovery_id` tells the member API
that an owner app's unlock ended that recovery, so that the API ends its
own record and tells the member. What it adds for the host is little:
the parent already learns that an unlock succeeded (the clear `unlocked`
event, after which it writes `state: "unlocked"` on the vault row,
vettid-vault `parent/aws.go`), and it already sees every recovery id as
the `request_id` of a queue message. Without the marker, the API could
only infer a cancel from an `unlocked` report while a recovery is
pending. That inference is racy (the queue is not ordered, and the
report and the slot are written separately) and ambiguous (a registered
or recovered app's own unlock is not a cancel), which is why the
enclave says it. A host that **forges** the marker makes the API end
its record, which the host could already stall by holding the queue
messages back, and makes the API send the member a false and alarming
email. The enclave still holds the recovery: the member's app keeps
meeting `recovery_pending` (and can cancel from there), while the
account site shows no recovery until a new request replaces the
enclave's. The vault row's `recovery_cancelled` is a second channel with
the same power: the host writes it, and can forge it without any unlock
at all, with the same effects. A host that **suppresses** the marker
and the event leaves the stale record of before 0.49.0. Apps read
the envelope as usual and ignore the marker. The parent writes the
lifecycle events to the vault table and deletes the queue message when
the enclave reports completion.

- **Lifecycle events:** `enrolled` and `unlocked` at enrollment; `moved`
  with the target release after a move, and back to the earlier release
  after an abandonment (§11.10.4); `alarm.credential_clone`, since
  0.16.0 `credential_backup`, and since 0.18.0 `account_name` (above;
  since 0.19.0 also with `unlocked` while a request is pending).
  (0.49.0) The `unlocked` event of an unlock that cancelled a recovery,
  or its `moved` event after a release move, carries
  `cancelled_recovery_id`, which the parent writes to the vault row as
  `recovery_cancelled: {recovery_id, at}` (above).

**Manifest by hash** (0.10.0, owner decision O10). Enroll and unlock
requests name the manifest by `manifest_sha256` and `manifest_serial`
(§11.3, §11.4) instead of carrying it, so the manifest can outgrow the
12,288-byte request (§11.10.1):

- **Publication.** The step that publishes a manifest first writes the
  exact served document bytes (§11.10.1) to the vault data bucket as
  `manifests/<manifest_sha256>.json`, where `manifest_sha256` is the
  lowercase hex SHA-256 of the manifest bytes (not of the served
  document), and only then lets the site serve it. Objects under
  `manifests/` are never modified; the host role may only read that
  prefix.
- **Parent.** For an `enroll` or `unlock` message, the parent reads
  `manifests/<manifest_sha256>.json`, refusing an object larger than
  90,112 bytes, and forwards the document to the enclave together with
  the message (the vsock queue frame is `[queue message, served document
  or empty]`). It MAY cache a few documents by hash, and MAY skip an
  object whose manifest bytes do not hash to its name (so that a corrupt
  object is not cached). If the object is missing, too large or skipped
  it forwards the message with no document; it never alters the message,
  and there is no host code for this case.
- **Enclave.** Before it uses the manifest (§11.3; §11.10.4 step 1), the
  enclave checks, in this order, and answers the sealed result code
  `manifest` on the first failure: a document is present; it parses as a
  served document (strict format, at most 90,112 bytes); the SHA-256 of
  its manifest bytes equals the request's `manifest_sha256`; the signature
  verifies under a pinned key (`key_id` selects it); the manifest bytes
  parse strictly (§11.10.1); `serial` equals the request's
  `manifest_serial`; for an unlock, `serial` is at least the
  `manifest_serial` recorded in the sealed header (rollback protection is
  unchanged, §13.2); and its own release is listed with its own number,
  PCR1 and PCR2. A `manifest` failure is not a PIN failure and does not
  count toward backoff.
- **What the host can do.** A dishonest host can withhold the document or
  supply another one. Either fails `manifest` (a denial of service it can
  cause anyway); it cannot make the enclave accept a manifest the app did
  not verify, because the hash is inside the sealed, signed request.

**The `lock` operation (0.29.0, release L; approved by the owner
2026-10-12, VAULT-LOCK §3).**

- The message MAY carry `"unlock_id": "<32 hex>"`, copied by the member
  API from the lock request's body (MEMBER-API); a release before L
  ignores it.
- **Bound** (with `unlock_id`): the enclave hands it to the vault's
  process, which locks only if the value names its current unlock.
- **Unconditional** (without): the enclave keeps, with each running
  vault, the `enqueued_at` of the enroll, unlock or (0.56.1)
  `recovery_open` message that opened it, and carries the lock out only if the lock's `enqueued_at` is
  later. An equal or earlier time is stale. Both times are the member
  API's; no clock of the enclave or of a device is compared. (The
  queue is not ordered and a message can be delivered up to 5 minutes
  late, after an unlock queued later.) (0.56.3) A vault whose opening
  has no known `enqueued_at` is locked by an unconditional lock: locking
  only reduces exposure.
  - *Residual (0.56.3).* The rule orders a lock against the unlock that
    opened the vault, not the other way round: an unlock queued
    **before** an unconditional lock (the account site's "Lock my
    vault") but delivered **after** it still opens the vault, because
    the lock, carried out first, found the vault locked or locked it
    under an earlier opening. The opening needs the PIN, and the idle
    lock (§3.6.8) bounds how long a vault opened so stays open; the
    member who wants it closed locks again.
- **The answer is given after the lock**, with a `code`, and the
  status `done`:

  | `code` | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | `locked` | the vault was running on this instance and has been locked (the process has ended, whether or not its final flush succeeded, §12.3) |
  | `not_running` | no process for this vault on this instance |
  | `stale` | the vault runs under a newer unlock (another `unlock_id`, or an unlock queued at or after this lock); nothing was done |

  The parent copies these three codes into the response slot for a
  `lock` and for no other operation. When no instance holds the
  vault's lease the member API writes `done` with `not_running`
  itself, without a queue message.
- A `done` without a `code` comes from a release before L, whose
  enclave answers before it locks; it says only that the message was
  read.
- **The host's word.** The slot is written by the parent, and a lock's
  answer is not sealed: `locked` and `not_running` are as trustworthy
  as the host (§13.3). The vault's own word reaches the member's
  devices over the relay (§10.2 "Locks").

`lock`, `delete`, `delete_resume` and `account` carry no envelope. Locking is harmless, and deletion
through the API is an operator power the host has anyway (§13.5).
(0.51.0) `delete_resume` finishes a deletion that the vault itself
marked and that stopped before its `deleted` report (§12.5 "Without
the app: the resume"); it erases nothing that the enclave can read as
live, and the member API sends it only for rows with `deleting_at`. A
release before 0.51.0 does not know it: its parent drops the message
as it drops any unknown operation. The API
sends `delete` for an account cancellation (MEMBER-API) and, since
0.16.0, for a member's "delete my vault and start over" once its 24 h
have passed (§11.11.9). The
recovery operations are in §11.11; `recovery_register` carries a
12,288-byte padded request like enroll and unlock, and the response to
`recovery` is the sealed code (5,252 bytes, §11.11.2). None of them takes
the lease: the vault is not left open.

### 11.6 Replay protection

- **Replayed requests.** The enclave remembers every `request_id` it has seen
  for as long as the ETK that request was sealed to is live, and rejects
  repeats. Destroying an ETK (≤ 25 h after creation, or at restart) makes
  every request sealed to it undecryptable. Requests whose `ts` is more than
  5 minutes from enclave time are rejected.
- **Redirected requests.** `user_guid`, `vault_id` and `request_id` appear
  inside the ciphertext as well as in the queue message, and a mismatch is
  rejected. A request therefore cannot be redirected to another vault.
- **Session-only attackers.** Unlock requires both a registered unlock key
  and passing device attestation (§11.7). A member session alone, which
  VettID could obtain, cannot attempt a PIN. Since 0.15.0 a member session
  cannot even submit an unlock: the route takes only app-key-signed
  requests (§11.12).
- **Replayed API requests** (0.15.0). App requests carry a timestamp and a
  single-use nonce under the app key's signature (§11.12.2); the sealed
  request inside keeps its own replay protection above.

### 11.7 Device attestation (REQUIRED for enroll and unlock)

(0.33.0, release R) From release R the app also holds a **phone key**,
an HMAC key with the same properties as the device attestation key (on
an iPhone a Secure Enclave key-agreement key, 0.35.0, §11.14.1), and
sends the unlock secret it computes with every enrollment, unlock,
recovery open and transfer `hs.init` (§11.14.1); and the release
constant `android_min_version_code` is checked against the attestation's
version code at enrollment, a transfer's `hs.init` and a recovery's
register (§11.14.14). The recovery open carries `device_assertion` like
an unlock.

Enroll and unlock MUST carry platform device attestation: **Android hardware
key attestation** or **iOS App Attest**. Only role `app` can produce it,
which is why only apps unlock (§3.1). Both are verified **inside the
enclave**; the attestation data travels inside the sealed envelope, and the
member API sees none of it. The challenge is bound to the request:

```
challenge = SHA-256("vettid/vms/2/devatt" || request_id || vault_id_or_empty || ts)   # inside the envelope
```

`request_id` and `vault_id` are the ASCII strings exactly as carried in
JSON (`vault_id` is empty at enrollment), and `ts` is the request's inner
`ts` (§5.3). Both have fixed lengths, so the concatenation is unambiguous.
Android and iOS use the same challenge.

**Wire fields.** Enrollment (§11.3) and app pairing (§6.7) carry
`device_attest`; unlock (§11.4) carries `device_assertion`:

```json
device_attest:    {"platform": "android", "chain": ["<b64 DER cert, leaf first>", "..."]}
                | {"platform": "ios", "key_id": "<b64>", "attestation": "<b64 CBOR attestation object>"}
device_assertion: {"platform": "android", "sig": "<b64 DER ECDSA P-256 signature over challenge>",
                   "chain": ["<b64 DER cert, leaf first>", "..."]}   # chain: optional (0.27.0, §11.7.1)
                | {"platform": "ios", "assertion": "<b64 CBOR assertion>"}
```

**What the device key signs.** Android signs with ECDSA P-256 and SHA-256
(SHA256withECDSA, DER): for `device_assertion` the message is the 32
challenge bytes; for an approval (§11.10.3) it is the approval string's
bytes. iOS asserts with `clientDataHash` = the challenge for
`device_assertion`, and SHA-256(approval string) for an approval; the
signature is checked as ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 over `nonce` =
SHA-256(authenticatorData || clientDataHash).

`chain` has 1–10 certificates. Unknown members are ignored; a missing or
mistyped member, or another `platform`, is rejected.

Each platform has a **device attestation key**: a hardware-held signing key
that is attested once, when the app enrolls (§11.3), is transferred to
(§6.7.1) or registers for a recovery (§11.11.3), and then signs the
challenge at every unlock.

- **Android (hardware key attestation).**
  - At enrollment or pairing, the app generates a non-exportable EC P-256
    signing key in Android Keystore with `setAttestationChallenge(challenge)`,
    in StrongBox if the device has it and in the TEE otherwise, and sends the
    key's certificate chain.
  - The enclave verifies the chain up to a Google hardware attestation root
    pinned in the image (0.27.1: under the **chain rules** below), then
    checks the attestation extension of the leaf: the
    challenge; attestation and key security level `TrustedEnvironment` or
    `StrongBox` (never `Software`); `RootOfTrust` with `deviceLocked` true and
    `verifiedBootState` `Verified`, or `SelfSigned` with an allowlisted
    `verifiedBootKey` (GrapheneOS, below); the `attestationApplicationId` package
    name and signing-certificate digest of the VettID app (0.27.0:
    exactly one digest, pinned by the release, §11.7.1); a signing-only,
    non-exportable key.
  - **Chain rules** (0.27.1; enforced from staging release S10,
    vettid-vault #64). "Verifies the chain" means all of these, the
    same wherever a chain is verified: at an attestation (enrollment, a
    transfer's `hs.init`, a recovery's register) and at a bind by chain
    (§11.7.1).
    1. The chain has 1–10 certificates, leaf first. Each is signed by
       the next; the last is self-signed and carries the public key of
       a pinned root (roots are compared by public key).
    2. **Only the leaf (`chain[0]`) carries the attestation extension**
       (KeyDescription, OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.1.17). A chain in which
       any other certificate carries it is refused. A certificate with
       that extension is an app's own Keystore key, and what such a key
       signs says nothing about a device. (The VettID app generates its
       key without an attest key, so its chain never holds a second
       one.)
    3. Every certificate above the device's attestation certificate
       (`chain[2]` and up, the root included) is a CA: basicConstraints
       with cA, and keyCertSign where the certificate has a keyUsage.
    4. Path-length constraints are honoured, the root's included: a CA
       certificate has no more certificates between it and the leaf
       than its pathLenConstraint allows.
    5. `chain[1]`, the device's attestation certificate, is **not**
       required to be a CA. The factory-provisioned attestation
       certificates of older devices say cA FALSE with digitalSignature
       only and sign their leaves all the same; the chains Google
       publishes as test data for its own verifier include them. Rules
       2 and 4 apply to it as to any certificate.
    6. No other extension is examined. In particular the provisioning-
       information extension of a remotely provisioned attestation
       certificate (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11129.2.1.30) on `chain[1]` is
       accepted.
    7. **At an attestation, every certificate is within its validity
       period** at the enclave's time. A bind by chain does not check
       validity (§11.7.1 says why).

    A chain that breaks a rule is a failed attestation, answered as
    any other: `attestation` at enrollment, at a recovery's register
    and at a bind by chain, and a dropped `hs.init` at a transfer
    (§6.7.1 step 2).
  - **A phone whose attestation certificates have expired cannot
    attach a vault** (0.27.1; owner decision of 2026-10-11: "those
    older devices will likely no longer get security updates and os
    updates so i don't want to support them"). Rule 7 refuses it at
    enrollment, as a transfer's new phone and at a recovery's register;
    the app shows what it shows for any failed attestation. The phones
    concerned are old ones whose factory-provisioned attestation
    certificate has run out; a remotely provisioned phone gets fresh
    certificates. An unlock verifies no chain, so a vault attached
    while the certificates were valid keeps unlocking after they
    expire (kept: owner decision, 2026-10-11; refusing at unlock
    would lock members out of vaults they already have).
  - **Chains seen on real phones** (0.27.1; recorded without device
    identifiers). The chains of the app's own key generation on the two
    test phones on 2026-10-11, a Pixel 10 Pro on GrapheneOS and a
    Pixel 7 on stock Android, each had 5 certificates, a StrongBox key
    and remotely provisioned certificates, 3,145 and 3,290 bytes of DER
    in all, the attestation extension on the leaf only and every issuer
    a CA. Both pass the rules.
  - Certificate revocation uses Google's attestation status list. The
    enclave fetches it over TLS it terminates itself, like relay traffic
    (§12.2; the parent forwards only TCP bytes to an allowlisted host), and
    caches it. Enrollment and pairing need a list fetched in the last 24 h;
    unlock rechecks the stored chain against the cached list and fails if
    the list is more than 7 days old. A parent that blocks the fetch can only
    deny service, which it can do anyway. Every serial the list names counts
    as revoked, whatever its `status` (`SUSPENDED` included); freshness is
    the time the enclave fetched the list. The enclave accepts
    `attestationVersion` 3 or later, and requires the key properties to be
    hardware-enforced: purposes within {SIGN, VERIFY} and including SIGN,
    EC P-256, origin GENERATED.
  - The enclave stores the attested public key and (0.27.0) the signing-
    certificate digest with that app's unlock key in the sealed header.
    Each unlock carries a signature over `challenge` by that key, and the
    recorded digest must still be pinned (§11.7.1).
  - (0.26.0) The package name is the channel's `android_package`
    (§11.10.8): `com.vettid.app` in production, `com.vettid.app.staging`
    in staging. It is checked where an attestation is verified
    (enrollment, a transfer, a recovery's register). An unlock and a
    release approval check the stored key's signature and the stored
    chain's revocation status, not the package again; (0.27.0) they do
    check that the key's recorded signer is still pinned (§11.7.1).
- **GrapheneOS** (owner decision, 2026-10-03; 0.9.0). GrapheneOS runs
  with the device's bootloader locked to its own signing key, so the
  attestation reports `verifiedBootState` `SelfSigned`. The enclave
  accepts `SelfSigned` **only** when `verifiedBootKey` (32 bytes) equals
  one of the GrapheneOS verified boot key fingerprints pinned in the
  release (vettid-vault `vms/pins`); `deviceLocked` true is still
  required, and every other check is unchanged. `Verified` is accepted as
  before; `Unverified` and `Failed` are refused, and so is `SelfSigned`
  with any other key (another custom OS, or a self-built one).
  - Source: the GrapheneOS Attestation Compatibility Guide,
    <https://grapheneos.org/articles/attestation-compatibility-guide>, which
    tells apps to "enforce that `verifiedBootState` is either `Verified`
    or `SelfSigned`" and, for `SelfSigned`, to "check that
    `verifiedBootKey` matches one of the official GrapheneOS verified boot
    keys".
  - The allowlist is part of the release: adding a device family or
    changing a key is a release update (§11.10). Fingerprints as of
    2026-10-03 (SHA-256, lowercase hex):

    | Device | `verifiedBootKey` |

  - OWNER DECISION (recommended: GrapheneOS only). Other hardened OSes
    (for example CalyxOS) would each be an allowlist entry in a release;
    none is added until requested.
- **iOS (App Attest).**
  - At enrollment or pairing, the app sends an attestation object with
    `clientDataHash` = `challenge`. The enclave verifies it against Apple's
    App Attest root, which is pinned in the image, and checks the App ID and
    the production environment. It then stores the attested public key and
    counter with that app's unlock key in the sealed header.
  - Each unlock carries an assertion over `challenge`. The enclave checks the
    signature, the App ID and that the counter increases.
  - (0.37.0) The App ID is the release constant `ios_app_id`
    (§11.10.8, "iOS App ID"): the channel's one value,
    `<team id>.<bundle id>`, compared with the authenticator data's
    `rpIdHash` at the attestation and at every assertion. A build
    without complete channel constants accepts none (iOS fails closed,
    as Android does without a package). The development environment
    (aaguid `appattestdevelop`) is refused by every release image.
  - (0.37.0) The development enclave's device policy file (devenclave
    builds only) may add `apple_app_attest_root` (the pinned Apple root
    beside the TEST CA), `ios_app_ids` (App IDs accepted besides the
    TEST App ID, for the debug and dev-stack builds) and
    `ios_development_environment` (accept `appattestdevelop`), so that
    a development build on a real iPhone can enroll against a local
    stack. Release images cannot load the file.

**Rationale.** Both checks are local cryptography against pinned vendor
roots, so they need no VettID credentials and no third-party API call (Play
Integrity was rejected for that reason). Attestation keys and certificate
chains are stable device identifiers, so they stay inside the enclave and
never reach the API. The gate is enforced by the attested enclave, not by
VettID's servers; it is an anti-abuse control, and confidentiality never
depends on it.

Desktops and agents have no platform attestation and do not unlock.

#### 11.7.1 Signer binding (Android, 0.27.0)

(Owner decision of 2026-10-11, ANDROID-PLAN 0.1.36 §7 "Signing and the
two distributions"; §15 item 35. Approved by the owner 2026-10-11.)

A release may pin more than one Android signing certificate: VettID's
own, which signs the F-Droid and direct builds, and, once the app is
on Google Play, the Play app-signing certificate, whose key Google
holds. Until 0.27.0 the vault treated them as one set: an attestation
was accepted if its signing digest was any pinned one, the digest was
not kept, and nothing told the member which signer their vault's app
has. From 0.27.0 **each vault is bound to the signer of its app**.

**What an unlock proves, and what it does not.** An unlock carries no
fresh attestation. It carries a signature by the device key that was
attested when the app enrolled, was transferred to or registered for a
recovery (above). That key cannot leave the installation that
generated it, and Android replaces an installation only with one
signed by the same key, so the signer of whatever unlocks is the
signer recorded at attestation. The binding therefore adds no check
that a correct phone could fail by itself. It adds what the vault did
not have:

- the signer is **recorded**, and shown to the member (below);
- a signer that a release **stops pinning** stops unlocking (before
  0.27.0, a key attested under a signer kept unlocking on a release
  that no longer listed it);
- a **change of signer** happens only where the owner proves the PIN
  and the credential password, is confirmed explicitly in a transfer,
  and is audited;
- any present or future operation that presents an attestation for a
  bound vault outside those flows is refused.

It does not protect a member who installs from Google Play against a
build signed by Google: that build has the bound signer (ANDROID-PLAN
§7).

**The signer of an attestation.** The attestation's
`attestationApplicationId` MUST contain exactly one signing-certificate
digest, and it MUST be pinned by the running release. (Before 0.27.0:
one or more, all pinned. VettID's builds have one signer; an
attestation that reports several is refused with the code of a failed
attestation. 0.27.1: the entries are counted, not the distinct values,
so an attestation that lists the same pinned digest twice is refused
too.) That digest is the app's **signer**. Each pinned signer
has a **class**, set in the release configuration (§11.10.8):

| Class | Meaning | The app's text (ANDROID-PLAN §7) |
|---|---|---|
| `vettid` | Signed with a key only VettID holds: the F-Droid and direct builds | "F-Droid or direct (signed by VettID)" |
| `google_play` | Signed with the Play app-signing key, which Google holds | "Google Play (signed by Google)" |
| `development` | A development or automation key; refused in a production release's configuration | "Development build" |

The class is an identifier from this table, not free text: the vault
never supplies member-facing wording.

**Recording.** The enclave stores the signer digest in the device
binding, beside the attested public key and the chain's serial numbers,
in the sealed header, for every Android key it attests: at enrollment
(§11.3), at a transfer's `hs.init` (§6.7.1) and at a recovery's
register (§11.11.3). The vault has one app (§6.7), and **the vault's
signer binding is the signer recorded for that app's key, or the kept
Android signer while the app has none** (an iOS app; "Across an iOS
app" below). (0.55.9) **The kept signer is stored in the vault's
DEK-encrypted state** (`kept_signer`: the digest and the class), as
`recovered_signer` is, **not in the sealed header's device bindings**.
Its freshness is `recovered_signer`'s: the enclave refuses a
state whose `state_seq` is below the header's (§13.2), and every flush
that sets or clears it also rewrites the header (the app's unlock key
changes in that flush); a host that serves an older header and state
together is the header rollback the unlock refuses, and such a pair
has the old Android app as the vault's app. A state without the member loads
unchanged; no format change.

- **Enrollment** binds the vault to the enrolling app's signer; audit
  `device.signer_bound` (`ref` = the class). (0.27.1) The entry
  carries no `device_id` at enrollment and at a bind by chain (below);
  at a transfer or a recovery that binds a vault with no recorded
  signer, its `device_id` is the new app.
- **Unlock** (§11.4) and a **release-update approval** (§11.10.3), the
  two operations that verify a device-key signature, additionally
  require, after the signature has verified, that the key's recorded
  signer is pinned by the running release. If it is not, the result is
  `signer_refused` (below).
- **Nothing else changes the binding** except the two flows that
  replace the app, both of which prove the owner's PIN and credential
  password:
  - **Direct transfer** (§6.7.1). The new app's attestation gives its
    signer. `device.transfer.pending` carries `signer` (the new app's
    class) and `signer_changed` (whether its digest differs from the
    binding, the kept Android signer counting as recorded (0.55.9);
    `false` when the vault has no recorded signer and none kept: an
    unbound vault, the staging case below, or an iOS-first vault, where
    the transfer simply binds and is audited `device.signer_bound`).
    When it differs, `device.transfer.approve` MUST carry
    `signer` equal to the new app's class; without it the vault
    answers `signer_unconfirmed`, after it has spent the UTK (0.52.0,
    §3.5.4) and before it tries the PIN (the backoff untouched), and
    the transfer stays open. The binding moves to the new
    app's signer in the flush that completes the transfer.
    As implemented (0.27.1):
    - **A `signer` that is not the new app's class is
      `signer_unconfirmed` in every case**, also when nothing changed
      and when the new app has no signer (iOS): the holder confirmed
      something the vault is not about to do. An approval without
      `signer` is refused only when the signer changed.
    - **Changed is decided by digest, confirmed by class.**
      `signer_changed` compares digests; the confirmation names a
      class. The two are equivalent while each class has one pinned
      certificate, which every channel file has today. If a release
      ever pinned two certificates of one class, a transfer between
      them would say `signer_changed: true` with the class the vault
      already has, be confirmed by that same class and be audited
      `<class>:<class>`: the holder could not tell which certificate.
      A release that does so needs the confirmation to name the digest
      first (a wire change, then). Owner decision, 2026-10-11: keep
      the confirmation by class, on that condition.
    - **Across platforms.** When the new app has no signer (Android to
      iOS), `device.transfer.pending` carries neither `signer` nor
      `signer_changed`, no confirmation is asked, and the transfer is
      unaudited as a signer event; (0.55.9) the vault keeps the Android
      signer it had ("Across an iOS app" below), and keeps it across
      a move from one iOS app to another. When the old app has none
      (iOS) and the new one is an Android app, the kept signer decides:
      another signer is `signer_changed: true`, confirmed and audited
      `device.signer_changed`; the same signer is `signer_changed:
      false` and binds, audited `device.signer_bound`; with nothing
      kept (an iOS-first or unbound vault), `signer_changed` is `false`
      and the transfer binds, audited `device.signer_bound`.
  - **Recovery** (§11.11). The registered key records its own signer
    at register; the vault's binding does not move then. In release R it
    moves at the recovered phone's first handshake (§11.14.6); the open
    only records the binding as `recovered_signer`. A recovery that is cancelled, expires or is voided
    leaves the binding as it was. (0.55.9) The same rules as for a
    transfer apply, with the kept signer, in release R's recovery open
    and in the recovered phone's pairing, and in a recovery open that
    is resumed after a state write failed.
  - In both, when the digest changed, the vault audits
    `device.signer_changed` (`device_id` = the new app, `ref` =
    `<old class>:<new class>`, for example `vettid:google_play`) and
    creates a feed item `device.signer_changed` of priority `high`
    with the same two classes. The audit entry and the feed item carry
    classes, not digests. (0.27.1) A pinned signer's class is the
    running release's. For an old signer the running release no longer
    pins, the old class is the one recorded with the binding when it
    was made, and `unknown` if none was recorded (so `ref` may read
    `unknown:vettid`).
- A fresh attestation for a vault's app in any other operation (none
  exists in 0.27.0; a later one that re-attests the device key would
  be) MUST show the bound digest and is otherwise refused with
  `signer_refused`, without changing the binding.
- An enrollment never rebinds an existing vault: it is answered
  `vault_exists`, or it replaces an unconfirmed provisional vault with
  a new one (§11.3), which binds as any enrollment.

**The refusal.** `signer_refused` is a code of `vault.unlock.result`
(§11.4):

- It is returned only inside the uniform sealed result, to a request
  whose `sig` and `device_assertion` both verified, that is, to the
  bound app itself. The member API and the parent see the same size
  and path as for every other outcome (§11.4). Any other requester
  gets what it got before: random bytes, or `attestation`.
- It is decided before the PIN is tried and is not a PIN failure: it
  neither counts toward nor resets the backoff (§11.8).
- (0.27.1) **Order.** It is decided right after the device assertion
  verifies: before `recovery_pending`, before `backoff` (a refused app
  is answered `signer_refused` even while a backoff runs) and before
  the header rollback check. Two consequences, stated plainly:
  - **A refused app cannot cancel a recovery.** `cancel_recovery`
    (§11.11.4) takes effect only after the PIN, which a refused unlock
    never reaches. A member whose app is refused cancels a recovery
    someone else started from the account site or the email's link.
  - **The ways out of a refusal** are a recovery (§11.11), or an
    unlock on a release that still accepts the key, for as long as
    that release lives; a direct transfer needs an open vault, so an
    unlock first. A vault whose **credential backup is off** has no
    recovery (§11.11.1): once every release that accepts its key is
    removed, that vault is lost. This is what removing a signer costs
    ("A release that stops pinning a signer" below).

  Both are **accepted as built** (owner decision, 2026-10-11):
  another order would let a refused installation act on the vault.
  Removing a signer therefore needs the same care and notice as
  retiring a release, and a member whose vault is bound to it with
  the backup off is told before it happens.
- It is recorded in the sealed header's log, as the steps of a
  recovery are (§11.11.6), at most once per 24 hours, and written to
  the audit log at the next unlock that succeeds as
  `device.signer_refused` (`ref` = `unpinned`, or `unbound` for the
  case below). (0.27.1) The entry shares the recovery log's 64
  entries, the oldest dropped first. It is **not written when the
  stored header's `header_seq` is below the request's
  `min_header_seq`** (a host serving an older header): the answer is
  still `signer_refused`, but writing the entry would store the
  rolled-back header one sequence number further on.
- **It raises no clone alarm and no host alarm** (§3.5.9). The alarm
  is for a second copy of the credential; it freezes the credential,
  emails the member and forces a rotation. A signer refusal can only
  reach the vault from the owner's own installed app, on a release
  that does not pin its signer: a release that dropped a signer would
  alarm every vault bound to it at once, each alarm false. A member
  who deliberately changes store never meets the refusal at all: that
  change goes through a transfer or a recovery, which rebind. And an
  app the owner did not install but which carries the bound signer is
  not something the vault can tell from the owner's. The owner learns
  of a refusal from the app's message and the audit entry. OWNER
  DECISION (2026-10-11): refuse and audit, no alarm.
- The app's message: "This vault no longer accepts this installation
  of VettID. Update the app, or recover your vault with a current
  version."

A transferred-to or recovering app whose signer is not pinned is
refused as before 0.27.0: its attestation fails (§6.7.1 step 2,
§11.11.3 check 6).

**A release that stops pinning a signer** strands the vaults bound to
it: they are refused at the release, including at the confirming
unlock of a move into it (§11.10.4), until the member transfers or
recovers to an app with a pinned signer (a release that still pins the
old signer accepts the unlock as long as it lives). A **kept** signer
(0.55.9) that the running release no longer pins strands nothing: it
is never checked at unlock, so an iOS app is not refused because of
it, and a later return to Android is `signer_changed` with the kept
class (the new app's digest must be pinned, so it cannot equal the
unpinned kept one). Removing a signer
is therefore a decision of the same weight as retiring a release, with
the same notice (VAULT-RELEASES §3.4 C6); adding one changes nothing for
existing vaults.

**Vaults enrolled before 0.27.0.** Their bindings hold no signer, and
an unlock presents none. They are bound from the attestation they
already made:

- The Android `device_assertion` gains an optional member `chain`: the
  certificate chain of the bound device key, the same certificates the
  app sent at attestation (Android Keystore keeps them with the key).
  An app of 0.27.0 or later sends it at every unlock while its
  `device.list` entry shows no `signer`. Releases before 0.27.0 ignore
  it (unknown members are ignored, above).
- For a key with no recorded signer, the enclave verifies the chain as
  at attestation (pinned root, the attestation extension's package and
  exactly one pinned digest) with two differences: the leaf's public
  key MUST equal the bound key and the chain's serial numbers MUST
  equal the stored ones, and the challenge and the certificates'
  validity periods are not checked again (both were when the chain was
  first accepted, and the equal serials tie this chain to that one).
  It then records the digest; audit `device.signer_bound`. A chain
  that fails is answered `attestation`.
  - (0.27.1) "As at attestation" is every check of §11.7 except those
    two: the chain rules 1–6, the attestation version and security
    levels, the key properties, the root of trust, the package and the
    one pinned digest. **A chain the chain rules refuse leaves the key
    unbound and is answered `attestation`**, including a chain that a
    release before S10 accepted at attestation (one extended below an
    attested key, changelog 0.27.1). Such a vault is attached again
    with a genuine attestation, by a transfer or a recovery.
  - (0.27.1) **Why validity is left out.** The certificates above the
    leaf of a remotely provisioned key live about a week (on the test
    phones on 2026-10-11 they ran to 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-21), so a
    chain that was valid at enrollment has usually expired by the time
    it is sent again. Checking validity here would refuse nearly every
    vault this path exists for.
  - (0.27.1) **When the binding is stored.** The binding and its
    `device.signer_bound` entry are written with the unlock's next
    header write. That is a successful unlock, **and also a wrong
    PIN**, whose backoff count is a header write: a bind is kept even
    when that same unlock then fails on the PIN. This is safe, because
    the result does not depend on who sent the chain or on the PIN: it
    is fixed by the certificates of the key that enrolled. An unlock
    that ends with no header write (`recovery_pending`, `backoff`, a
    rollback, `manifest`) leaves the key unbound, and the app sends
    the chain again.
  - (0.27.1) **Size.** The unlock request (12,288 bytes padded, §11.4)
    has room for about 8,100 bytes of chain together with a
    `release_update` and `cancel_recovery`, more than enrollment or a
    recovery's register have, so every chain that was attested over
    the alternate channel fits the unlock that re-sends it (real
    chains are 3,100 to 3,300 bytes, §11.7). **Known limit:** a chain
    attested in a transfer's `hs.init` travelled in a handshake
    envelope, which is larger; such a chain above about 8,100 bytes
    could not be sent again at unlock, and that vault would bind only
    by a new transfer or a recovery. None is known.
- A key with a recorded signer ignores `chain`.
- **A key with no recorded signer and no valid `chain` is answered
  `signer_refused`**, except on the staging channel, where it unlocks
  unbound (staging vaults are disposable, and staging apps older than
  0.27.0 exist). Staging accepts them from S10, the first staging
  release with the rule, and refuses them from the staging release
  after it (owner decision, 2026-10-11). No production vault is in
  this case: 0.27.0 is in production release 1 (owner decision,
  2026-10-11; VAULT-RELEASES 0.1.12 §5.2).
  (0.27.1) **The exception is not a release constant.** No member of
  the channel file turns it on: the image derives it from its
  measured channel and release number (`staging` and release 10 or
  lower), so a production file cannot express it and a later staging
  file cannot bring it back. "No valid `chain`" means no chain at
  all: a request that brings a chain which fails is answered
  `attestation`, on staging too.

**With the staging application id (0.26.0, §11.10.8 "Android
package").** S10 carries both changes, and they compose: a staging
vault enrolled under `com.vettid.app` is unbound, so its old build
keeps unlocking it on S10 without a chain, exactly as "Moving the
existing staging vaults" needs; it cannot bind by `chain`, because the
chain's package is checked against S10's `android_package` and is the
old one; and the transfer, recovery or new enrollment that attaches it
to the `com.vettid.app.staging` build is a fresh attestation, which
records the signer and binds it (no confirmation is asked, there being
no earlier signer). A staging vault still unbound at the release after
S10 has not been moved to the new build and is refused there.
(0.27.1) So on staging **no vault ever binds by `chain`**: every vault
from before S10 belongs to the old package, whose chain S10 answers
`attestation`. The chain path is exercised by the vault's own tests
on its test PKI, not by a staging phone.

This is acceptable because the digest is not taken on trust from
whatever unlocks first. It is read from the certificate that Google's
attestation root signed for the very key that enrolled, so it is the
signer of the app that enrolled, whoever presents it and whenever.

**What the member sees.** The app's own entry in `device.list` (§10.3)
carries `signer: {class, digest}` for an Android app with a recorded
signer: `class` from the table above, `digest` the 64 lowercase hex
digits of the certificate's SHA-256 (public: it is in every APK). The
app shows the class in its vault status as "Installed from: …"
(ANDROID-PLAN §7); the digest is for a details view and for support,
not for the status line. Desktops reading `device.list` see the same
member. The recovering app's reduced answers (§11.11.5) carry nothing
of it.

**iOS.** The rule is Android-only for now. An iOS release pins one App
ID (team and bundle), there is one distribution path, and App Attest
reports no signing certificate; an iOS binding has no `signer` and
`device.list` carries none (the kept Android signer, below, is not
shown either). If a second iOS path were ever pinned (a
second App ID), the release configuration would list the App IDs with
classes as it lists Android signers, the binding would record the App
ID attested, and every rule above would apply with "App ID" for
"signer digest".

(0.27.1) **Across an iOS app.** (Owner decision, 2026-10-11; built
in vettid-vault #142, 0.55.9; (q1) and (q2) approved 2026-10-23.) The
vault keeps the last recorded Android signer (digest and class) while
its app has none, also across a move from one iOS app to another, and
clears it when the binding moves to an Android app. The vault's
signer binding is the app's recorded signer, or the kept signer while
the app has none, and the kept signer counts as recorded for
`signer_changed`.

- Android S1, iOS, Android S2 is `signer_changed: true`: an approval
  without `signer`, or with the wrong class, is `signer_unconfirmed`
  (the UTK spent first, the PIN backoff untouched, 0.52.0 §3.5.4);
  confirmed, it is audited `device.signer_changed` and creates the
  high-priority feed item, as between two Android apps.
- **The same signer as the kept one** (q1): `device.signer_bound`,
  with no confirmation and no `signer_changed`.
- An iOS-first or unbound vault: its first Android app is
  `device.signer_bound`, as before.
- A recovery follows the same rules: release R's open records the
  binding (the old app's signer, or the kept one) as
  `recovered_signer` before it removes the apps, also when the open is
  resumed after a state write failed, and the binding moves at the
  recovered phone's first handshake. (`credential.recover`, removed in
  release R, did the same.)
- A kept signer the running release no longer pins is never checked
  at unlock; see "A release that stops pinning a signer".
- `device.list` does not show the kept signer; the audit entry and
  the feed item carry classes, never digests.
- A kept signer of no known class is stored with the class `unknown`.

**Tests required.**

- Attestation: one pinned digest accepted and recorded; two digests,
  both pinned, refused; an unpinned digest refused; the class of each
  configured signer.
- Enrollment binds and audits `device.signer_bound`; `device.list`
  shows `signer` on the app's entry only.
- Unlock and a release-update approval with a bound signer the running
  release pins: unchanged. With a bound signer the release does not
  pin (the same vault moved to an image whose configuration omits it):
  `signer_refused`, sealed and sized as any result; the backoff
  counters unchanged; no alarm opened, nothing reported to the host;
  one header-log entry per 24 hours; `device.signer_refused` in the
  audit log after a later successful unlock.
- A wrong `device_ik` signature or a wrong assertion never yields
  `signer_refused`.
- Transfer to the same signer: no `signer` needed in the approval, no
  `device.signer_changed`. To another pinned signer:
  `device.transfer.pending` shows `signer_changed: true`; an approval
  without `signer`, or with the wrong class, is `signer_unconfirmed`
  with the PIN backoff untouched (0.52.0: the UTK spent, §3.5.4); with it, the
  transfer completes, the binding is the new signer, and
  `device.signer_changed` is audited with both classes and in the
  feed. To an unpinned signer: dropped as today.
- (0.55.9) VA4: Android, then iOS: the signer is kept, nothing is
  audited, `device.list` shows no `signer` on the iOS entry. Back to
  another pinned signer: `signer_changed: true`, `signer_unconfirmed`
  without `signer` and with the wrong class (UTK spent, PIN backoff
  untouched), then `device.signer_changed` and the feed item. Back to
  the same signer: `device.signer_bound`, no confirmation, no
  `signer_changed`. iOS to iOS keeps it. An iOS-first vault: the first
  Android app is `device.signer_bound`. A kept signer the release does
  not pin: unlock still succeeds for the iOS app, and the later
  return is `signer_changed` with the kept class. The same through a
  recovery (release R's open and the recovered phone's pairing),
  including a resumed recovery open for Android to another signer,
  Android to iOS and iOS (kept) to another signer. A state without
  `kept_signer` loads unchanged; an empty value is not written.
- Recovery to another pinned signer: the binding is unchanged after
  register, after a cancel and after an expiry; changed, audited and
  in the feed after `credential.recover`; the old app's key no longer
  unlocks. (0.27.1) "After an expiry" is an expiry **before** the
  register: the vault removes a recovery by time only when a register
  arrives too late. A registered recovery's record and unlock key stay
  in the header until it completes, is cancelled or is replaced by a
  new request (existing behaviour, §11.11); only the registered app's
  first handshake stops being accepted at the expiry.
- A header written before 0.27.0: with a valid `chain`, bound and
  audited; with a chain naming another package than the channel's
  `android_package`, `attestation`; a transfer from an unbound vault
  shows `signer_changed: false`, needs no `signer` and binds; with a chain for another key, with other serials, with two
  digests or with an unpinned digest, `attestation`; without a chain,
  `signer_refused` on a production-channel build and an unbound unlock
  on a staging-channel build; a bound key ignores `chain`.
- Release configuration (§11.10.8): entries without a class, an
  unknown class, a duplicate digest, `development` in the production
  file, and the bare-string form are each refused by the release
  build.
- On real phones (staging): a Pixel on stock Android and one on
  GrapheneOS enroll and show the expected class; ~~a vault enrolled on
  the previous staging release binds by `chain` at its first unlock~~
  (0.27.1: cannot be run on S10, "With the staging application id"
  above; replaced by the next item);
  the attestation of the app as built reports exactly one digest
  (to confirm, also for an app whose signing key was rotated, which no
  VettID build is).
- (0.27.1) On real phones at S10, as run on 2026-10-11: a vault of the
  old package (`com.vettid.app`) moved to S10 keeps unlocking there,
  unbound; a direct transfer to the `com.vettid.app.staging` app binds
  it (`device.signer_bound`), with no confirmation asked; a transfer
  between apps of staging's two signers (`vettid` and `development`)
  shows the change and is refused without the confirmation; the app's
  vault status shows the class. The app as built on both test phones
  reported exactly one digest.

### 11.8 Rate limits and backoff

**Member API limits:**

- enroll: 3 per member per day;
- unlock: 10 per member per 15 min; per source network, 10 per 15 min per
  IPv6 /64 and 60 per 15 min per IPv4 address (carrier NAT puts many
  members behind one address);
- polling: 2 per second;
- setup codes (0.15.0, §11.12.1): issue 5 per member per hour and 20 per
  day, one live issuance per member; redeem 10 per 5 min per IPv6 /64
  and 30 per IPv4 address; typed redeems 5 per 5 min per (email, source
  network) and 800 per issuance. No limit is global.

Enroll, unlock and lock requests are audited (§11.5), without PINs or
envelopes.

**Enclave backoff**, kept in the sealed header and counted in `header_seq`:

- after 3 consecutive failures, the delays are 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 15 min,
  60 min, then 60 min for every further failure;
- a successful unlock resets the backoff;
- failures never wipe the vault.

### 11.9 Failure handling

| Failure | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Instance gone or lease moved | The API answers `409 instance_moved`, or the request expires (queue retention, or the parent found the lease held elsewhere and marked the slot `expired`). The app refetches `/api/vault/enclave` and re-seals. |
| Unknown or expired `etk_kid` | The enclave reports `etk_unknown`; the response slot carries `code: "etk_unknown"` and no envelope (§11.5). The app refetches and retries. |
