  modules on a light background. The version is whatever fits (the
  account site uses the smallest one at level M). For a 32-hex
  `vault_id` the payload is 181 bytes with 0.15.0's `api`, which needs
  **version 10** (57 × 57 modules) at level M; before `api` it was 146
  bytes, version 8 (49 × 49). The app
  MUST accept any version and any level from M up.
- **Typed form** (0.25.0). For a phone that cannot scan, the portal
  also shows the code as text: 48 characters in 12 groups of four,
  made of a 12-character locator from the member API, the code, and
  4 check characters (§11.11.10). 0.10.6–0.24.1 showed the bare code
  "in groups of four, for typing"; since 0.15.0 no app could use it
  (it names neither the vault nor the recovery), and it is no longer
  shown.
- **Why the vault mints the code.** VettID's servers never hold the code
  in a usable form: the API stores only the ciphertext sealed to the
  member's browser. The 24 h delay and the expiry are enforced inside the
  enclave. So a copy of the API's tables, or an operator reading them,
  cannot register a device, and neither can an API that releases the
  ciphertext early.
- **A recovery started by the host** (0.27.4, disclosure; nothing
  changes). The operation `recovery` carries no envelope and no
  signature (§11.5), so the host can queue one itself, for any vault,
  with a browser key of its own, without the member's session and
  without the member API's email to the member (§11.11.7).
  - *What it gives:* a running vault is locked (§11.11.1 step 2); the
    recovery record is written into the sealed header; and the host can
    open the code once the enclave's 24 h have passed.
  - *What it does not give by itself:* anything of the vault. A register
    still needs an app that passes device attestation (§11.11.3), and
    the recovery still needs the PIN and then the credential password,
    online (§11.11.5). **Neither backoff holds against a host that
    replays stored objects** (§13.2): the PIN backoff is in the sealed
    header and the password backoff in the state, the host stores both,
    a newly registered app has no minimums, and an app raises its
    minimums only from a result the host delivers. Such a host can
    register its own attested phone against a pending header it kept,
    and then try PINs, and after the PIN passwords, at the speed of the
    app. With the credential backup off, and never on in any copy the
    host still holds, there is no recovery at all (§11.11.1).
  - *What the member sees:* the owner's devices are sent
    `vault.locking{reason: "recovery"}` when a running vault locks, and
    from then on the member's app is refused `recovery_pending` at
    every unlock (§11.4, §11.11.4) until the recovery ends. The member
    is told by the vault, not by the host. That is a protection only
    against a host that serves the current header: a host that keeps the
    header with the pending record aside and serves the member's app the
    one from before it shows the member nothing, and can undo a cancel
    by serving the earlier header again. Against a host that does not
    replay, the member's app can cancel with `cancel_recovery` and the
    PIN (§11.11.4). The `recovery` entry of `GET /api/vault/status` and
    the member API's email come from the API and would be missing.
  - So "an operator reading them cannot register a device" above stands
    for an operator who only reads. A host that starts a recovery and
    replays stored objects is a larger exposure than §13.5's row
    "Member's email and account session (24 h, unnoticed)": no email, no
    notice to the member's devices, and no working backoff.
    `recovery_cancel` has no envelope either: the host can end a
    member's own recovery (availability).
  - **Open design question** (not a requirement; the owner has not
    decided): whether a later vault release should require a `recovery`
    and a `recovery_cancel` to carry a signature of the member API,
    under a key the release pins, which the enclave verifies. It would
    take the power to start a recovery from the host process and leave
    it with the member API, which VettID also runs. (0.33.0: decided;
    release R requires it, §11.14.8. From release R the host that starts
    a recovery and replays stored objects gets at most the attempts of
    §11.14.6, counted outside what it stores.)
- **Residual: the portal's code.** A VettID that serves malicious portal
  code to the member's browser can read the code; the browser key protects
  data at rest, not against the page's own author. Such an attacker still
  needs the PIN and the password, guessed online under the enclave's
  backoffs. The same holds for an attacker who controls the member's email
  and account session for 24 h without being noticed. The backoffs do not
  hold if the attacker is also a host that replays stored objects ("A
  recovery started by the host" above).
- **PQC exception.** The browser seal uses P-256 ECDH, the only key
  agreement in WebCrypto. A recorded ciphertext is worthless to a future
  quantum attacker, because the code expires within 48 h and is
  single-use. This is the one place where §1.1 item 7 does not apply.

#### 11.11.3 Register

The new app scans the QR, or takes the typed form (0.25.0, §11.11.10:
the identifiers then come from the claim, §11.11.7), and sends
`vault.recovery.register` over the alternate channel. The request is
the same either way: the enclave cannot tell how the app read the code.
Like `vault.unlock`, the request is sealed to the ETK
of the instance named by `GET /api/vault/enclave` and padded to 12,288
bytes:

```json
{ "user_guid": "...", "vault_id": "...", "request_id": "<ULID>",
  "recovery_id": "<ULID>", "code": "<32 chars>",
  "app": { "ik": "<b64>", "kem": "<b64 ek>",
           "relay": {"url": "<base>", "mailbox": "<id>", "pk": "<b64>"},
           "name": "<device name>", "device_attest": { },
           "api_key": "<b64 SPKI DER, P-256>" } }
```

`app.api_key` (0.15.0) is REQUIRED: the new app's app key (§11.12),
which the enclave binds to the queue message's `app_key` like
`user_guid`. The app takes `user_guid` from the claim (§11.11.7).

The enclave applies the binding and replay rules of §11.3 and §11.6. It
then checks, in this order:

1. the recovery exists and `recovery_id` matches;
2. the recovery is still `pending`, and the header records a credential
   and a backup copy of it (`has_credential`, `credential_backup`;
   0.16.0). The backup cannot change while a recovery locks the vault,
   so this only catches a header written before 0.16.0 or a damaged
   one; on failure the recovery record is removed and the answer is
   `no_backup`;
3. the code has not expired;
4. `not_before` has passed;
5. the code matches the hash, compared in constant time;
6. the device attestation is valid (§11.7), over the challenge with this
   request's `request_id`, the `vault_id` and the inner `ts`. It is checked
   only after the code matched, so a failure leaves the code usable.
   (0.27.0) Its signer may be any the release pins and need not be the
   one the vault is bound to; it is recorded with the registered key and
   becomes the vault's binding only when the recovery completes
   (§11.7.1, §11.11.5).

On success it adds the app to the header's unlock keys, with its app key,
and sets the state to `registered`; the code is spent. (0.33.0, release
R: it records the phone's keys, app key and attestation binding in the
recovery record only; a registered phone can send nothing but
`vault.recovery.open`, §11.14.6.) Its answer to the host then also
carries the clear marker `code: "recovery_registered"` (§11.5, 0.10.6),
which the host copies into the response slot, so that the member API
stops releasing the spent code (§11.11.7). Any other answer, `ok: false`
or random bytes, carries no marker.

The answer is `vault.recovery.result`, sealed to `app.kem` and padded like
unlock results:

- `{"ok": true}`, or
- `{"ok": false, "code": "no_recovery|used|expired|too_early|bad_code|attestation|bad_request|retry|no_backup"}`.

A request the enclave cannot read or bind is answered with random bytes.

#### 11.11.4 Cancel

A recovery is cancelled by any of:

- the portal or the email link: `POST /api/vault/recovery/cancel` and
  `/cancel-link`, which enqueue `recovery_cancel`. (0.49.0) From the
  release that implements it, the cancel names the recovery it means
  (§11.14.8), and the enclave cancels only that one;
- an owner app's `vault.unlock` with `cancel_recovery: true`. It cancels
  only if the unlock succeeds (PIN, device assertion), and the result says
  `recovery_cancelled: true`. (0.49.0) Its answer carries the clear
  marker `recovery_cancelled` with `cancelled_recovery_id`, and its
  `unlocked` event the same id (§11.5). The member API ends the
  recovery with that id as `cancelled` and emails the member. It does
  not enqueue a `recovery_cancel` for it, since the vault has already
  ended the recovery;
- expiry, or the fifth wrong code.

Cancelling removes the record and any registered unlock key. A recovered
app that was already paired but has not finished `credential.recover` is
unlinked at the next unlock (§7.4).

While a recovery is in progress, an unlock by any app other than the
registered one is refused with `recovery_pending`, without trying the
PIN. That keeps a thief who holds a lost phone and its PIN out of the
vault for the 24 h, unless they cancel. Cancelling is always allowed,
because it only reduces exposure. Owner apps learn of the recovery from
`vault.locking{reason}`, from `recovery` in `GET /api/vault/status`
(§11.11.7), or from `recovery_pending`, and can cancel from there.

#### 11.11.5 Unlock, password and handover

(0.33.0, release R) Replaced from release R by the recovery open
(§11.14.6); this section describes the releases before R.

Only a vault with a backup copy of its credential gets here (§11.11.1,
§11.11.3). Until the password has been proved against that copy, the
recovering app learns nothing of the vault's contents (0.16.0): not its
devices, connections, items, messages, profile, audit log or feed, and
not its owner check's state.

1. **PIN.** The registered app unlocks with `vault.unlock` and the PIN,
   under the normal enclave backoff (§11.8).
   - The app does not know the vault's relay key yet, so its `token` is an
     open token for its own mailbox. The vault ignores the token of a
     device it has no record of.
   - **No backup copy: refused** (0.16.0). If the vault, once opened with
     the PIN, keeps no backup copy of its credential (§3.5.6; possible
     only for a header written before 0.16.0, §11.11.1), it answers
     `{"ok": false, "code": "no_backup"}` with no token and no bundle,
     removes the recovery record and the registered unlock key (as a
     cancel does, §11.11.4), and locks again in the same step, before it
     collects or serves anything. The app tells the member that the
     vault cannot be recovered and points to §11.11.9.
   - Otherwise the result carries `token` (a standing token for the
     vault's mailbox) and `vault_bundle` (`{v, suite, ik, kem, relay}`,
     as in `vault.enrolled`): the vault's public keys and relay address,
     which the app needs for the handshake, and nothing of the vault's
     contents. The bundle is authenticated by being sealed to `app.kem`,
     which only the attested enclave received, inside the register
     request.
   - The result also carries `credential_backup` (bool, 0.10.6), which
     since 0.16.0 is always `true` (above).
2. **Handshake.** The app sends `hs.init` with purpose `app` and `ctx` =
   `recovery_id`. It is accepted without approval, exactly as the first
   app's handshake (§11.3), because its keys were bound at registration.
   The resulting device record is **recovering**:
   - it may send only `credential.utk.get`, `credential.recover`,
     `vault.status` and the token and address types (`relay.token.*`,
     `relay.address.update`); anything else is `forbidden` (0.16.0
     removed `credential.reset` and `vault.delete`);
   - `vault.status` answers it only `{vault_id, state_seq, header_seq}`
     (§10.2, 0.16.0);
   - it receives no fan-out, `sync.event`, feed item, alarm or held
     notice (`vault.held`), and its `relay.token.*` and address messages
     carry only its own tokens;
   - it is not announced to the other devices;
   - the owner-check hold (§3.6.3) does not apply to it: a vault held
     when the recovery began (the usual case after 24 h) still lets the
     recovering app send these types.
3. **Password.** The app first gets UTKs with `credential.utk.get`, which a
   recovering app may send. It then sends `credential.recover{utk_id,
   sealed{password}}`.
   - The vault opens its own backup copy of the latest blob (§3.5.6) with
     the current CEK and the password, under the credential's password
     backoff (§3.5.3). 0.9.0 removed the member-supplied blob: there is
     no off-device copy to supply (§3.5.6).
   - As with every use, the vault then rotates the CEK, re-keys every
     critical item (§10.7) and returns the new blob (`{credential,
     version, utks}`). The copy on the lost phone becomes undecryptable.
   - **The new app replaces the old one,** in the same flush:
     - the device becomes the vault's app and the credential's holder
       (§3.5.9), and the recovery record is removed;
     - (0.27.0) the vault's signer binding becomes the signer recorded
       for its key at register (§11.7.1); if that differs from the old
       app's, audit and feed item `device.signer_changed`;
     - its app key becomes the vault's app key (`app_key_seq` + 1), and
       the vault reports it to the host (`app_key`, §11.5; 0.15.0): the
       old app's key is refused by the member API from then on;
     - every other device of role `app` is removed as by `device.unlink`
       (§7.4): `device.unlinked{reason: "replaced"}` best effort, its
       relay key denylisted, its unlock key and UTK pool removed, audit
       `device.replaced` and a feed item, `sync.event{kind:
       "device.unlinked"}`;
     - **desktops and agents are kept**, with their access sessions and
       LEASH grants;
     - the other devices receive `sync.event{kind: "device.paired"}`;
     - the owner check's clock starts (§3.6.1): the registered app's
       unlock verified the PIN and this step the password, and a hold
       ends.
   - Only from here is the app an owner device with the holder's rights;
     everything it learns about the vault, it learns now.
   - A clone alarm that is open (§3.5.9) moves to `rotation_required`:
     the recovered app must rotate before using the credential.
   - A member who recovers in order to delete the vault does so as the
     holder after this step (`vault.delete`, §12.5).
4. **Backup off: no recovery** (0.16.0, owner decisions of 2026-10-06,
   §15 item 24, replacing 0.9.0's "access only" path). With
   `credential.backup` off there is no recovery flow at all: the API
   refuses the request (§11.11.7), the enclave refuses it (§11.11.1),
   a register (§11.11.3) and the registered app's unlock (step 1), so no
   recovering device record is ever created and nothing of the vault is
   released. 0.9.0–0.15.2 let the recovering app reset the credential
   (keeping the rest of the vault: messages, connections, profile,
   `data` and `secret` items, the audit log, the feed, the location log)
   or delete the vault with the PIN alone; both are removed, with
   `credential_lost`. The member's only path is to delete the vault and
   enroll a new one (§11.11.9).
5. **No credential, no recovery.** A vault without a credential is refused
   at the request (§11.11.1). It cannot exist past enrollment (§3.5.7).
   There is no completion on the PIN alone.

#### 11.11.6 Limits and audit

- **Enclave limits:**
  - 5 wrong codes per recovery;
  - the PIN backoff (§11.8);
  - the credential password backoff (§3.5.3);
  - one recovery per vault (a new request replaces the old).
  - (0.33.0, release R) In place of the two backoffs: ten attempts at
    the PIN and password together for the life of the pair, with the
    waits of §11.14.6, and the 72-hour quiet period (§11.14.5), counted
    outside everything the host stores (§11.14.4).

  These limits are kept in the sealed header and in the state, which the
  host stores. They hold against everyone except a host that replays stored
  objects (§13.2). Such a host can serve a copy in which the wrong codes,
  wrong PINs and wrong passwords were never counted, and in which a recovery
  that was used, cancelled or replaced is still pending.
- **Member API limits** (§11.11.7): requests, claims, registrations,
  cancels and status polls are rate-limited. A claim, scanned or by locator,
  is limited per source network before the lookup and per
  vault after it, on a hit only; none of these limits is global (§11.11.10).
- **Audit in the vault.** Every step is recorded (`recovery.*` kinds,
  §10.9). Steps taken while the vault was locked are written from the
  header's log at the next unlock.
- **Audit in the API.** The API audits the request, every cancel, the
  release of the sealed code and every register request. It never
  records the code, the browser key or envelopes.

#### 11.11.7 Member API routes

All routes follow MEMBER-API conventions. The first three are the
portal's. The request and the status require a session of an active
member with the current terms. The cancel requires only a session of
the account holder, whatever the account's status or terms (0.29.5, as
built; MEMBER-API 2.6.2). The last two are the new app's (0.15.0),
signed by its app key (§11.12.2) and needing no session:

| Route | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/vault/recovery` | `{browser_key}` (b64 of 65 bytes) | `202 {recovery_id, available_at, expires_at}` |
| `GET /api/vault/recovery` | — | `{recovery: {recovery_id, vault_id, state, requested_at, available_at, expires_at, sealed_code?, locator?} \| null}` |
| `POST /api/vault/recovery/cancel` | `{recovery_id}` | `200 {cancelled}`; `404` when `recovery_id` is not the vault's current recovery (0.29.4, as built) |
| `POST /api/vault/recovery/claim` | `{vault_id, recovery_id, app_key}` (scanned), or `{locator, app_key}` (typed, 0.25.0) | `200 {user_guid, email_hint, vault_id, recovery_id}` (0.15.0; the two identifiers since 0.25.0) |
| `POST /api/vault/recovery/register` | `{vault_id, request_id, instance_id, etk_kid, envelope}` | `202 {vault_id, request_id}`; the result is polled like unlock (`GET /api/vault/requests/{id}`) |
| `POST /api/vault/recovery/open` (0.33.0, release R) | `{vault_id, request_id, instance_id, etk_kid, envelope}`, signed by the recovering key | `202 {vault_id, request_id}`; polled likewise; forwarded only while the recovery is `registered` (`409 recovery_not_available`) (MEMBER-API "Vault recovery") |

- **Claim** (0.15.0). The new app, which has no session and no vault
  key at the API yet, presents the QR's `vault_id` and `recovery_id` with
  its app key. The API accepts it only while that recovery is
  `available` (`409 recovery_not_available`; `404` for an unknown pair),
  records the key as one of the recovery's **claim keys** (at most 10, the
  register limit; the oldest is dropped), and answers the member's
  `user_guid` (for the sealed register and unlock bodies) and
  `email_hint` (§11.13), which the app shows. A claim key may call
  `enclave`, `register` and poll its own requests. The API forwards a
  register only if it is signed by a claim key, and puts that key in the
  queue message's `app_key`. When a register's slot carries
  `recovery_registered`, that register's key becomes the recovery's
  **recovering key**, which may also read `status` (and, from release R,
  `open`; `unlock` and `lock` are refused, §11.14.6) until the recovery
  ends or the vault reports the key as its app key (§11.11.5 step 3).
  After a recovery that ended without adopting it, the key is told `410
  recovery_ended` (0.60.0, §11.14.6 "A recovery that ended without the
  phone"). Knowing `vault_id` and `recovery_id` (both in the
  QR) lets a stranger claim, which gains nothing: the enclave still
  needs the code and an attestation.
- **Claim by locator** (0.25.0, §11.11.10). The app that was given
  the typed form presents `{locator, app_key}`, signed by that key
  with an empty `vault` (as a setup code's redeem, §11.12.2), because
  it does not know the vault yet. The API looks the locator up. A
  locator it does not hold, or one whose recovery is no longer the
  vault's current one, is `404`, with the body and timing of an
  unknown pair. Otherwise the API proceeds **exactly as for the pair
  the locator names**: the same account checks, `409
  recovery_not_available` unless the recovery is `available`, the key
  recorded as a claim key, the same answer. The answer of either form
  carries `vault_id` and `recovery_id` (0.25.0), which the typed app
  needs for every later request and the sealed register body. Either form of the
  claim is limited per source network before the lookup (so misses
  count) and per vault after it; a miss is charged to no recovery and to no vault.
- **`locator`** (0.25.0): 12 Crockford base32 characters (60 random
  bits), minted by the API with the request, unique among the
  recoveries it holds, kept with the recovery and dropped when the
  recovery expires. `GET /api/vault/recovery` returns it only
  together with `sealed_code`. It is not derived from the code, which
  the API cannot read, and the enclave never sees it.

The email link uses its own route, `POST /api/vault/recovery/cancel-link`
with body `{token}`, answered `200 {cancelled}` like the session's
cancel, and `404` for a token the API does not hold, one past the
recovery's `expires_at` or one of a recovery that a newer one has
replaced (0.29.4, as built). It needs no session: the token stands in
for it.

- **No vault.** Without an enrolled vault (none, `enrolling` or
  deleted), `GET /api/vault/recovery` answers `{recovery: null}`, not
  `404` (0.10.6, as the API always did).
- **`vault_id`** (0.10.6): the vault being recovered, which the portal
  needs for the seal's HKDF `info` (§11.11.2) and the QR payload.
- **State.** `state` is `pending`, `available` (from `available_at`, when
  `sealed_code` is returned), `registered` (0.10.6), `cancelled`,
  `expired` or `unavailable` (0.16.0: the enclave refused it, below). `sealed_code` is the slot's 5,252 bytes; the API returns it
  only between `available_at` and `expires_at`, and only while the state
  is `available`.
- **Registered** (0.10.6). Once a `recovery_register` request for this
  recovery has been answered with the marker `recovery_registered`
  (§11.11.3; the API sees it in that request's slot, whether through the
  app's poll of `GET /api/vault/requests/{id}` or its own check), the
  API records the recovery as `registered`: the code is spent and
  `sealed_code` is no longer returned, so the portal says the code was
  used. A registered recovery stays active (it blocks a new request
  with `409 recovery_active`, it is shown in `GET /api/vault/status` and
  it can still be cancelled, §11.11.4) until the host reports the
  registered app's key as the vault's `app_key` (§11.5), when the API
  records it as `completed`, an ended state (0.27.0; MEMBER-API 2.4.1,
  owner decision of 2026-10-11), or until `expires_at`, after which it
  keeps reading `registered`. The API sees nothing else of the rest of
  the recovery (unlock, `credential.recover`): the vault makes that key
  its app key only in the flush of a successful `credential.recover`
  (§11.11.5 step 3), and removes its own record then.
- **Cancelled.** `{cancelled: true}` when this call ended an active
  recovery (`pending`, `available` or `registered`), `{cancelled: false}`
  when the recovery named is the vault's current one and there was
  nothing to cancel (it had ended already, by a cancel or
  its expiry). The cancel link stays usable until
  the recovery's `expires_at`, so a second use answers `false`, and
  after `expires_at` the link answers `404`. A `recovery_id` that is
  not the vault's current recovery (no vault, no recovery, or a
  recovery that a newer one has replaced) is `404`, not `false`
  (0.29.4, as built; MEMBER-API 2.6.3 lists every answer).
- **Request.** The API accepts a request only for a vault in a state other
  than `enrolling`, and only when no recovery is `pending`, `available`
  or `registered` before its `expires_at`
  (`409 recovery_active`; 0.29.5, as built). **Backup off** (0.16.0): when the vault row's
  `credential_backup` (§11.5) is `false`, the API answers `409
  recovery_unavailable` with `reason: "no_backup"`, enqueues nothing,
  locks nothing and sends no email; the portal says that the vault
  cannot be recovered because its credential backup is off, and offers
  §11.11.9. When the bit is absent (a vault not yet reported by a 0.16.0
  release) the API forwards the request and the enclave decides
  (§11.11.1). The API also answers `409 deletion_pending` while a
  start-over deletion is pending (§11.11.9). It records the recovery on the vault row and
  sends the member an email with a cancel link (a random
  256-bit token; the API stores its SHA-256). The link is not used up
  by a cancel: it stays usable until the recovery's `expires_at`, and a
  second use answers `{cancelled: false}` (Cancelled, above; 0.29.5, as
  built).
- **Refused by the enclave** (0.16.0). When the request's slot comes
  back with `code: "recovery_unavailable"` (§11.11.2), the API records
  the recovery as `unavailable` (an ended state), returns the slot's
  envelope as `sealed_code` at once, for the portal to decrypt and
  show the reason, and emails nothing further. Claim and register are
  refused for it (`409 recovery_not_available`).
- **Register.** The API forwards a register only while the recovery is
  `available` (`409 recovery_not_available` otherwise). The enclave
  re-checks everything; the API's gate only saves work.
- **Cancel.** A cancel marks the recovery `cancelled`, enqueues
  `recovery_cancel` and emails the member.
- **Status.** `GET /api/vault/status` adds `recovery: {state,
  available_at} | null`, so that owner apps can show the recovery and
  offer to cancel it.

#### 11.11.8 Decisions

- **The recovered app replaces the old app; desktops and agents are
  kept** (owner decision, 2026-10-03, replacing 0.4.1's "old owner devices
  are kept"). The old app is removed at `credential.recover`, its unlock
  key and device keys revoked, and the credential copy it held is under
  a destroyed CEK. A stolen phone:
  - cannot use the vault during the 24 h (`recovery_pending`), though it
    can cancel the recovery;
  - after the recovery, is no longer a device of the vault.
- **No recovery without the credential** (owner decision, 2026-10-03).
  A recovery always ends with the member's credential password against
  the vault's backup copy of the latest blob.
- **No recovery with the backup off** (owner decisions of 2026-10-06,
  §15 item 24, replacing 0.9.0's "access only" recovery): "if you lose a
  credential and have backups disabled you should not have a path back
  besides re-enrolling. we don't want to leak anything to someone
  without the credential", and "THERE IS NO RECOVERY IF BACKUP IS
  DISABLED". The member API refuses the request upfront, from the one
  content-free bit the vault reports (§11.5); the enclave refuses it
  too. The only path is to delete the vault and enroll a new one
  (§11.11.9).
- A vault without a credential is not recoverable. It cannot exist past
  enrollment anyway (§3.5.7).
- **The code can be typed** (owner decision, 2026-10-11: "we should
  allow a typed recovery code"; §15 item 33). A locator from the
  member API stands for the QR's identifiers, and check characters
  catch typing mistakes on the phone; the enclave, the code and every
  limit are as they were (§11.11.10).

#### 11.11.9 Starting over: deleting a vault without the app

(0.16.0; owner decision of 2026-10-06, §15 item 24.) A member who has
lost the phone with the backup off, or who does not want to recover,
deletes the vault from the account portal ("Delete my vault and start
over") and then enrolls a new, empty vault with a setup code (§11.12.1).
The deletion needs no app, PIN or credential, because it **reveals
nothing**: it never opens the vault and returns nothing from it; it only
destroys (§12.5). Because it destroys, it has a recovery's delay, emails
and cancel, so that someone holding the member's account session cannot
destroy a vault at once.

| Route | Caller | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/vault/deletion` | portal (session) | `{confirm: "delete my vault"}` | `202 {deletion_id, requested_at, deletes_at}` |
| `GET /api/vault/deletion` | portal (session) | — | `{deletion: {deletion_id, state, requested_at, deletes_at} \| null}` |
| `POST /api/vault/deletion/cancel` | portal (session), or the vault's app (signed by its app key, §11.12.2) | `{deletion_id}` | `200 {cancelled}` |
| `POST /api/vault/deletion/cancel-link` | the email's token, no session | `{token}` | `200 {cancelled}` |

- **Request.** A session of an active member with the current terms, as
  for a recovery request. `bad_request` without the exact phrase; `404`
  without a confirmed vault (none, `enrolling` or deleted; a provisional
  vault is replaced by the next setup code anyway, §11.3); `409
  recovery_active` while a recovery is `pending`, `available` or
  `registered`; `409 deletion_pending` while a deletion is pending. A
  recovery request is likewise refused `409 deletion_pending` while one
  is (§11.11.7). The portal offers it whatever the backup bit, and
  first when the API reports the backup off or a recovery was refused;
  with the backup on it says that a recovery would keep the vault.
- **24 hours, emails, cancel.** `deletes_at` = request + 24 h. The API
  emails the member at once (what will be deleted, when, that nothing
  can be restored, and a cancel link,
  `https://account.vettid.org/vault/deletion/cancel#t=<token>`, stored
  as its SHA-256 only), and again on a cancel. The link is not used up
  by a cancel: it stays usable until `deletes_at`, and a second use
  answers `{cancelled: false}` (0.29.5, as built). A deletion is cancelled
  from the portal, the email link or the vault's app (its app key); the
  app learns of it from `deletion: {deletion_id, state, deletes_at}`
  in `GET /api/vault/status` (0.16.1: the id its cancel names), which it reads after every unlock and whenever
  it shows vault status, and offers to cancel. The vault is not locked
  and not told during the wait: it has nothing to decide.
- **Execution.** At `deletes_at` the API's scheduled job marks the
  deletion `executing` and enqueues the queue operation `delete` (§11.5)
  as for an account cancellation: a running vault deletes itself with
  the full semantics of §12.5, and a locked one has its stored objects
  erased by the instance. Retries follow MEMBER-API until the vault
  reports `deleted`, whose notice emails the member and removes the
  vault rows (§11.5). A cancel after `executing` answers `{cancelled:
  false}`.
- **Then.** With no confirmed vault, the portal issues a setup code
  (§11.12.1) and the member enrolls a new vault with a new `vault_id`.
  Nothing carries over: the new vault has none of the old one's items,
  connections, messages, profile, grants, audit log or feed, and the old
  connections are told only what §12.5 sends (`connection.removed`
  from a running vault; otherwise nothing, and their deposits fail once
  the mailbox is gone or its tokens expire).
- **Who enforces the delay.** The member API. An enclave-enforced delay
  would add nothing: deleting stored state is an operator power VettID
  has anyway (§13.5), and the deletion discloses nothing.
- **Limits and audit.** Requests 3 per member per day; cancels and the
  cancel link as for a recovery (§11.11.7). The API audits
  `vault.deletion_request`, `vault.deletion_cancel` (`via: session |
  link | app`) and `vault.deletion_executed`; never the token.

#### 11.11.10 Typed entry (0.25.0)

(Owner decision of 2026-10-11: "we should allow a typed recovery code";
§15 item 33. Approved by the owner 2026-10-11.) Enrollment already has
"Type the code instead" (§11.12.1); recovery was camera-only, so a
member whose new phone has a broken camera could not recover. Typed
entry is a second way to **read** the same code. It changes nothing in
the enclave and nothing after the claim: no vault release is needed.

**The problem.** The QR carries four things: `api`, `vault_id`,
`recovery_id` and the code (§11.11.2). The code alone (32 characters)
does not say which vault and which recovery it belongs to; the claim
(§11.11.7) and the enclave's hash (§11.11.2) need both, and the app has
no account session to ask with (§11.12). Typing the two identifiers as
well would mean 84 characters (26 for the 128-bit `vault_id`, 26 for
the ULID, 32 for the code).

**The typed form.** 48 characters of the code's alphabet
(`0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z`), shown in 12 groups of four:

```
typed   = locator (12) || code (32) || check (4)
locator = 60 random bits from the member API's CSPRNG, as 12 Crockford
          base32 characters (most significant 5 bits first)
check   = the first 20 bits of
          SHA-256("vettid/vms/2/recovery-typed-check" || 0x00 || api || 0x00 || locator || code),
          as 4 Crockford base32 characters (most significant 5 bits first)
```

- **`locator`** is minted by the member API with the recovery request
  and stands for the pair (`vault_id`, `recovery_id`) at the claim
  (§11.11.7). It is **not derived from the code** and is no secret that
  opens anything: whoever holds it can do exactly what the holder of
  the QR's two identifiers can do (claim; §11.11.7), and nothing more.
  The API returns it to the portal only together with `sealed_code`,
  so nobody outside the API has it before the code can be read. The
  enclave never sees it.
- **`code`** is the enclave's code, unchanged.
- **`check`** is computed by the portal, in the browser, after it has
  opened the code. `api` is the same exact string as the QR's `api`
  (the portal's own origin, no trailing slash; ASCII), `locator` and
  `code` in canonical form (upper case). The check characters are
  never sent anywhere: the app verifies them and drops them. They hold
  no secret an attacker lacks (anyone can compute them for a guess), so
  they change nothing about guessing.

**What the portal shows** (MEMBER-API 2.4.0). Under the QR, "Can't scan?
Type this code in the app", and the 48 characters as twelve groups of
four, in three rows of four groups. The bare 32-character text of
0.10.6–0.24.1 is no longer shown: since 0.15.0 no app could use it.
A recovery requested before the API mints locators has none: its page
shows only the QR and says that typing needs a new recovery. The typed
form is shown and removed with the QR (on **Show the code**, **Hide**,
re-render and `pagehide`) and is never sent, logged or stored. There is
no copy button: the code does not go to a clipboard.

**What the app does.** The recover screen offers **Type the code
instead** wherever it offers the scan (ANDROID-PLAN 0.1.33). The app:

1. normalizes what is typed or pasted: spaces, hyphens and line breaks
   are dropped; letters are upper-cased; `I` and `L` are read as `1`
   and `O` as `0` (Crockford's look-alikes, which the canonical form
   never contains). **`U` is not in the alphabet and is not mapped**:
   it is refused in the field with "The code has no letter U. Check
   whether it is a V." Any other character is refused the same way. A
   silent guess would turn a visible mistake into a counted wrong code;
2. at 48 characters, recomputes `check` with **its own built-in member
   API origin** (the one it compares a QR's `api` with). On a mismatch
   it sends nothing and says: "That code doesn't match. Compare it
   with the account site group by group, and check that the site is
   <the app's account host>." This is input validation, as for a QR
   that is not a recovery QR: it is not a wrong code, reaches neither
   the API nor the enclave, and is not counted. A typing mistake
   passes the check with probability 2⁻²⁰;
3. claims with the locator (§11.11.7), signed by its app key with an
   empty `vault`, and takes `user_guid`, `email_hint`, `vault_id` and
   `recovery_id` from the answer;
4. continues **exactly as after a scan** with the `vault_id`,
   `recovery_id` and `code` it now holds: the same sealed
   `vault.recovery.register` (§11.11.3), the same result codes and the
   same texts for them, the same count of wrong codes, then the PIN
   and the credential password (§11.11.5).

**The environment check without a QR.** The scanned `api` exists so that
an app never acts on another environment's code. Typed entry keeps that
in three ways: the check characters are bound to the portal's origin,
so a staging code typed into the production app fails on the phone
(step 2); the app only ever talks to its own built-in origin, as with a
scan; and locators, vaults and recoveries of another environment do not
exist at that origin, so a claim there is `404`. The typed setup code
of §11.12.1 has always relied on the last two alone.

**Wrong codes are counted as before.** The enclave decides
(§11.11.3 check 5) and cannot tell a typed code from a scanned one. A
typed string that names a live recovery and carries a wrong code is
`bad_code`, counted, and the fifth voids the recovery; a typed string
whose locator names no recovery is the claim's `404`, exactly as a QR
whose identifiers name none, and there is no recovery to count it
against in either case. No answer exists for a typed code that a
scanned one does not get, and none is missing.

**Why this is no cheaper path for an attacker.**

- *Guessing the code.* Unchanged: 160 bits, 5 tries, inside the
  enclave. The locator and the check characters carry nothing of the
  code. The API learns nothing derived from the code.
- *Enumerating recoveries.* A claim by locator is a guess at 60 bits
  against the few recoveries that are `available` at that moment; with
  *n* of them a guess hits with probability *n* / 2⁶⁰, under the
  claim's per-network limit (§11.11.7). A scan's claim needs the
  128-bit `vault_id` and the ULID, so the typed claim is weaker in
  bits; neither is reachable online (10⁹ guesses a day against 100
  live recoveries: 10⁻⁷ a day). A miss is `404`, identical in body and
  timing for every miss, and cannot be charged to a recovery: there is
  none to charge. No limit is global, as for setup codes (§11.12.1), so
  nobody can stop other members' recoveries by guessing.
- *What a hit would give.* What the QR's two identifiers give: a claim
  key, the member's `user_guid` and masked `email_hint`, and the means
  to send five wrong codes and void that one recovery (the member
  requests again and waits 24 hours). Never the code, the PIN or the
  password, and never a registered device.
- *The 24 hours, the expiry and single use* are the enclave's
  (§11.11.2) and are not touched.

**Accessibility.**

- Portal: each group is its own element and each row its own line; the
  text is selectable and scales with the page; a font with a slashed
  or dotted zero; a screen reader gets the groups one at a time
  ("group 3 of 12"), spelled character by character, never read as
  words. The page says the code has no I, L, O or U.
- App: one text field, shown in groups of four as it fills, with
  "*n* of 12 groups" beside it; paste is accepted; no autocorrect,
  suggestions or keyboard learning; lower case is accepted; the
  refusals of steps 1 and 2 are announced to screen readers and name
  the group to look at when one character is refused; the entry is
  kept across a rotation, never written to disk, and excluded from
  screenshots and the recent-apps preview.

**Tests required** (follow-up implementations).

- Portal: the check characters against §16's vector for the production
  and staging origins; the grouping; the typed form removed with the
  QR; no bare 32-character text.
- Member API: a locator minted per request and unique; `locator` only
  with `sealed_code`; claim by locator: hit, miss (`404`, same body as
  an unknown pair), stale locator of a replaced or cancelled recovery
  (`404`), not available (`409`), paused service, both limits, the
  answer's `vault_id` and `recovery_id`, the key recorded as a claim
  key; the QR form unchanged.
- App: normalization (case, spaces, hyphens, `I`/`L`/`O`, `U` and other
  characters refused); the check against §16's vector, and a staging
  string refused by a production build; a failed check sends no
  request; a typed code registers with the same request bytes as the
  scanned one for the same recovery; `bad_code` shows the same text
  and count either way.
- End to end on staging: a recovery completed by typing; a wrong typed
  code counted by the vault (`recovery.bad_code` in the audit log after
  the next unlock) and the fifth voiding the recovery.

### 11.12 Enrollment codes and app keys

(0.15.0; owner decision of 2026-10-05: the app and the account portal are
separate. Design and rationale: ENROLLMENT-CODES.md.)

The app never signs in to the member API. The portal, where the member is
signed in, issues a **setup code** (a QR secret, and a short code typed
with the member's email); the app redeems it with its **app key**, which
then signs every app request to the API.

#### 11.12.1 The setup code

(Revised before approval, owner review of 2026-10-05: 5 minutes; a long
QR secret as the primary path; the typed code only with the member's
email; no global limit that one attacker could exhaust for everyone.)

- **Issue.** The portal's "Set up your vault" calls `POST
  /api/vault/enroll-code` with the member session (MEMBER-API). The API
  requires an active account in state `member` with the current terms
  (`403 terms_required` otherwise), revokes the member's live issuance
  if any, and makes one **issuance** with two secrets, both returned
  once:
  - the **QR secret**: 16 bytes from a CSPRNG, written as 22 characters
    base64url without padding (128 bits);
  - the **typed code**: 8 symbols from `23456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTUVWXYZ`
    (31 symbols: no 0, 1, I, L or O), each chosen uniformly by rejection
    sampling: 31^8 ≈ 8.5 × 10^11, about 39.6 bits; shown as `XXXX-XXXX`.
- **Validity.** 5 minutes from issue, single use, at most one live
  issuance per member. Redeeming either secret spends the issuance, so
  both end together; a new issuance, the portal's cancel or expiry ends
  both too.
- **At rest.** With `k_code`, a secret key held by the API (never in the
  tables):
  - the issuance is stored under `HMAC-SHA-256(k_code, "qr" || 0x00 ||
    secret)`, its lookup key;
  - it holds `user_guid`, `code_mac = HMAC-SHA-256(k_code, "code" || 0x00
    || user_guid || 0x00 || code)`, `expires_at`, `state` and a count of
    typed attempts;
  - the member's pointer names the live issuance.
  Neither secret is stored, logged or audited.
- **QR.** The portal shows the QR secret as the QR payload

  ```json
  {"v":1,"t":"e","api":"<member API origin>","s":"<22 chars base64url>"}
  ```

  encoded as the recovery QR is (§11.11.2: byte mode, level M or higher,
  4-module quiet zone, any version), and the typed code beneath it as
  text. The QR does not carry the typed code. `api` is the portal's
  origin (production `https://account.vettid.org`): an identifier that
  the app compares exactly with its own built-in member API origin,
  refusing a mismatch with a message naming the other environment. An app
  MUST NOT send anything to an origin taken from a QR. On a phone the
  portal also offers the App Link `https://<account host>/vault/enroll/#s=<QR
  secret>`; it never puts the typed code in a link.
- **Redeem.** `POST /api/vault/enroll/redeem`, signed (§11.12.2) by the
  key in `app_key` with an empty `vault`, with exactly one of:
  - `{secret, app_key}` (scanned QR or App Link): the API looks the
    issuance up by `HMAC(k_code, "qr" || 0x00 || secret)`;
  - `{email, code, app_key}` (typed): the API normalises both (email
    trimmed and lower-cased; code without spaces or hyphens, upper case),
    finds the member by email and the member's live issuance through the
    pointer, and compares `code_mac` in constant time. The code is
    compared with that one member's issuance only: there is no space of
    codes shared between members.

  Either way the issuance must be live, unexpired, the member's current
  one, and its member an active `member`; for the typed form also not
  `typed_blocked` (below). Any failure, of either form, is `404
  invalid_code`. Then the API:
  1. marks the issuance used with a conditional write (single use, both
     secrets);
  2. finds the member's vault, or assigns a new `vault_id` (§11.3,
     "Re-enrollment"), and records `app_key` as the vault's **pending app
     key** for 1 hour;
  3. emails the member that a phone used their setup code, with the time;
  4. answers `{vault_id, user_guid, email_hint}`.

  The app shows `email_hint` ("Setting up a vault for m***@example.com")
  before it asks for a PIN, then enrolls (§11.3) with `user_guid` in the
  sealed request and every call signed by the app key. The pending key
  may call `GET /api/vault/enclave`, `POST /api/vault/enroll` and poll its
  own requests, nothing else. The enclave binds the vault to `user_guid`
  as before: the API, which issued the code, remains the authority on
  which member a vault belongs to.
  As for every enrollment, the vault's first `credential.create` starts
  the daily owner check's clock (§3.6.1); redeeming a code does not.
- **Vault service pause.** While the operator has paused the vault
  service (MEMBER-API 1.2.0, "Vault service pause"), issue, redeem and
  recovery `claim` (§11.11) are refused with `503 vault_unavailable` like
  `enroll`, before anything is spent, counted or written; reading and
  revoking the member's code are still served.
- **Limits** (§11.8), none of them global:
  - per source network, both forms: 30 redeems per 5 minutes per IPv4
    address, 10 per IPv6 /64;
  - typed, per (email, source network): 5 per 5 minutes;
  - typed, **per issuance: 800 attempts** across all sources. The chance
    that they find the code is at most 800 / 31^8 ≈ 9.4 × 10^-10 per
    issuance, and with at most 20 issuances a day at most 1.9 × 10^-8 per
    member and day. On reaching it the issuance becomes `typed_blocked`:
    typed redeems of it fail, a QR redeem of it still works, the member
    is emailed and operations are alerted. Flooding therefore costs at
    most one member the typed entry of one issuance;
  - the QR secret (2^128) needs no other limit.
- **No account oracle.** The typed form answers a wrong email, an email
  without a live issuance, a wrong code, and an expired, used, revoked or
  blocked issuance identically (`404 invalid_code`), after the same work
  (a member lookup and a MAC compared against the stored or a dummy
  `code_mac`) and no sooner than 250 ms after receipt. Its limits count
  attempts for every email, existing or not.
- **An existing vault.** A code can be issued and redeemed whatever the
  member's vault; the enclave decides (§11.3: a confirmed vault is never
  replaced, `vault_exists`). A pending key never replaces the vault's
  `app_key` at the API; only the enclave's report does (§11.5).

#### 11.12.2 The app key and signed requests

- **The key.** Each app makes, per vault, a P-256 signing key that never
  leaves its hardware: Android Keystore (StrongBox if present, else the
  TEE; non-exportable; purpose SIGN; no user authentication, so that lock
  and polling work in the background) or an iOS Secure Enclave key. It is
  distinct from the device attestation key (§11.7), whose certificate
  chain stays inside the enclave. Its public form is the b64 of its SPKI
  DER, and its id `akid` the first 16 bytes of SHA-256(SPKI DER), 32
  lowercase hex.
- **The header.** Every app request to `/api/vault/*` carries

  ```
  X-VettID-App: v=1; vault=<vault_id or empty>; kid=<akid>; ts=<Unix s>; nonce=<b64url, 16 bytes>; sig=<b64url DER ECDSA>
  ```

  where `nonce` and `sig` are base64url (RFC 4648 §5) **without
  padding**, canonical (0.17.0, editorial: as the apps send and the
  member API accepts; a padded value fails the header's syntax), and
  `sig` is ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 over (each `\n` a literal
  newline, no trailing newline):

  ```
  "vettid/member-api/app/1" \n METHOD \n path \n query \n vault_id \n akid \n ts \n nonce \n hex(SHA-256(body))
  ```

  `path` is the request path as sent, `query` the raw query string
  without `?` (or empty), `body` the exact body bytes (empty for a GET).
  (Not `Authorization`, which the account site's CloudFront cannot forward
  through an origin request policy.)
- **Verification** (the member API). `ts` within 300 s of the API's
  clock; `nonce` not seen for this `akid` in the last 600 s (recorded
  with a conditional write); the key is one the vault row allows for the
  route (below); the signature verifies. Otherwise `401 unauthorized`,
  one answer for all. A request with this header is authenticated by it
  alone: cookies are ignored and the CSRF header is not required.
- **Which key may call what:**

  | Key | Recorded by | Routes |
  |---|---|---|
  | The vault's `app_key` | the host, from the enclave's reports (§11.5) | `enclave`, `unlock`, `lock`, `status`, its own `requests/{id}` |
  | The pending key | the API, at redeem; 1 hour | `enclave`, `enroll`, its own `requests/{id}` |
  | A recovery's claim keys | the API, at claim (§11.11.7) | `enclave`, `recovery/register`, their own `requests/{id}` |
  | A recovery's recovering key | the API, from `recovery_registered` | as a claim key, and `unlock`, `lock`, `status` |

  "Its own" requests: the API records the signing `akid` on each response
  slot, and answers a poll signed by another key `404`.
- **What the key cannot do.** The member API holds only public keys, and
  the enclave does not check app-key signatures: they authorize routing,
  rate limits and account checks, not anything in the vault. Every
  operation that matters still needs what only the app has (PIN, unlock
  key signature, device assertion, release approval, recovery code,
  attestation). A dishonest API can therefore do with app keys only what
  it could do already: refuse, misroute, lock.
- **Rotation and revocation.** The vault's app key changes only when the
  app does: a transfer (the new app's `api_key` in its `hs.init`, §6.2,
  §6.7.1) or a recovery (the key of the registered app, §11.11.5). Each
  change increments the header's `app_key_seq` and is reported to the
  host (`app_key`, §11.5); the old app's key is refused from then on.
  There is no other rotation in 0.15.0. A phone that lost its Keystore
  lost its attestation key too, and recovers.

### 11.13 Account status through the vault

(0.15.0.) Apps show the member's membership, terms and subscription
state, read-only, and get it only from their vault; changes are made on
the portal. Since 0.18.0 the snapshot also carries the account's first
and last name, which the vault puts in the core of its shared profile
(§10.8) and which the member changes only from the app
(`account.name.set`, §10.8), never on the portal. Since 0.20.0 it carries the member's full
email address, which the vault shows to the member's own app and
desktops only (owner decision of 2026-10-07, §15 item 28).

- **The snapshot** the member API builds from the member's account:

  ```json
  { "v": 1, "as_of": "<RFC 3339>", "email": "member@example.com",
    "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace",
    "name_change": { "allowed_after": "<RFC 3339>|null",
                     "last": { "seq": 3, "status": "applied|refused",
                               "reason": "too_soon|invalid|account" } | null },
    "state": "member", "account_status": "active|canceled", "deletes_at": "<RFC 3339>|null",
    "terms": { "needs_acceptance": false },
    "subscription": { "type_name": "...", "status": "trial|active|expired|canceled",
                      "paid": false, "expires_at": "<RFC 3339>" } | null,
    "voting_rights": false }
  ```

  `email` (0.20.0, owner decision of 2026-10-07) is the member row's
  address, the one the member verified at registration, as the member
  API stores it (trimmed and lower-cased; at most 254 characters, the
  registration rule, so at most 1,016 bytes of UTF-8 and in practice
  ASCII). It replaces 0.15.0's `email_hint` (the first character of the
  local part, `***`, `@` and the domain), which the snapshot no longer
  carries; the masked `email_hint` remains only in the code-redeem and
  recovery-claim answers (§11.11.7, §11.12.1), which reach an app before
  it has proved anything. `first_name` and `last_name` (0.18.0, owner
  decision of 2026-10-07) are the member row's names, as registered
  (MEMBER-API `/api/public/request`) or last changed from the app
  (§10.8): letters, spaces and `'’.-`, at most 40 characters each, so at
  most 160 bytes each. Every member has them from registration, and
  every snapshot carries them. `name_change` (0.18.0) is the member API's
  state of the name changes: `allowed_after`, when the next change may
  be applied (30 days after the last applied one; `null` when a change
  may be applied now, as before any change: the registration names do
  not count), and `last`, the outcome of this vault's latest
  `account.name.set` request that the API processed (`seq` as the vault
  sent it), or `null`. `last.status` is `"applied"` or `"refused"`
  (0.19.0); `reason` is present only with `"refused"`, as `"too_soon"`,
  `"invalid"` or `"account"` (§10.8), and is absent with `"applied"` (a
  vault ignores one there). Nothing else about the member is sent (no
  `user_guid`). At most 2 KiB, names and email included: the names
  take at most 320 bytes and the email at most 1,016, the rest about
  530 bytes (with a 64-byte subscription `type_name`), so the largest
  snapshot is about 1.9 KiB and a realistic one well under 1 KiB; the
  member API still sends none over 2 KiB (MEMBER-API).
- **The email stays with the member (0.20.0).** The vault returns the
  `email` only in `account.get`, to the member's app and to desktops
  (the member's own devices, a desktop within its access session as
  for every desktop request; §6.8). It MUST NOT put it, or anything
  derived from it (a hash, a hint, its domain), in a `profile.update`,
  an `hs.init` profile, an invitation bundle or its `hint`, a feed
  item, an audit entry, a LEASH statement or any other message to a
  connection or an agent, or in an event to its host, unless a future
  version of this specification says so. Agents never receive it:
  `account.get` is not an agent type and no LEASH grant reaches the
  snapshot (§10.11). Apps and desktops show it only to the member
  (the avatar sheet, Settings) and never include it in anything they
  send.
- **Version (0.18.0).** The snapshot keeps `"v": 1`, with `first_name`,
  `last_name` and `name_change` **required**: VettID has no members'
  vaults to stay compatible with (owner decision of 2026-10-07), so no
  older form is accepted. The vault refuses a snapshot without them, or
  with a name that is not a string of 1–160 bytes without control
  characters (C0, DEL, C1, U+2028, U+2029; DEL since 0.21.0, owner
  decision of 2026-10-08: the member API's names never contain it,
  MEMBER-API 2.3.1), or with a `name_change.last.status` other than
  `"applied"` or `"refused"` (0.19.0), as it refuses a wrong type, and
  keeps the one it had. Since 0.20.0 `email` is **required** too, still
  with `"v": 1`: a string of 3–1,016 bytes of UTF-8, with an `@`,
  without control characters, which for the email are (0.21.0) C0
  (U+0000–U+001F), DEL (U+007F), C1 (U+0080–U+009F), U+2028 and
  U+2029, the names' set (0.20.0 named no set; its reference refuses
  the first three and admits the line and paragraph separators, which
  a 0.21.0 vault refuses too). The member API refuses the same
  characters at registration (MEMBER-API 2.3.1, owner decision of
  2026-10-08), so that a vault never refuses a snapshot built from a
  registered member. A 0.20.0 vault refuses a snapshot without it, and
  ignores an `email_hint` if one is present (an unknown member). Older
  releases need no change to accept the new form: 0.15.0–0.19.0 vaults
  (staging release S4, and vettid-vault #45) check `email_hint` only
  when it is present and ignore unknown members, so they accept a
  snapshot with `email` and without `email_hint`, store it as received
  and return it in `account.get` unchanged; S3 predates the snapshot
  (0.15.0) and never parses one. The member API therefore sends
  `email` only, from MEMBER-API 2.3.0.
- **Delivery.** The API puts the snapshot in every `enroll` (0.18.0) and
  `unlock` queue message (`account`, §11.5) and, when the member's
  account changes (terms accepted, subscription started, cancelled or
  changed, account cancelled, and since 0.18.0 a name change processed,
  applied or refused), sends the op `account` to the vault's live
  leaseholder; with no live lease it sends nothing (the next unlock carries it). A new terms
  version is not fanned out: each vault learns it at its next unlock. A
  trial's expiry needs no message: apps show `expired` once `expires_at`
  has passed.
  A **suspended** account gets no snapshot (0.15.2; `account_status` is
  `active` or `canceled` only): the API sends none, in an unlock or as
  an op, and the vault keeps the last one it stored (MEMBER-API 2.0.1).
- **In the vault.** After a successful enrollment (0.18.0) or unlock, or
  on the op `account` for a running vault, the vault parses the snapshot strictly (unknown members
  ignored, wrong types refused, over 2 KiB refused), ignores it unless its
  `as_of` is later than the stored one, stores it in DEK state with a
  `version` (+1 per change) and its own `received_at`, and sends
  `sync.event{kind: "account.changed", version}` to the app and desktops.
  They read it with `account.get` (§10.2). Agents and connections never
  receive it (§13.7), and never its `email` (above), except its
  `first_name` and `last_name`, which every
  connection receives in the shared profile's core (§10.8, 0.18.0) and an
  agent delegated `profile.get` reads there. A stored snapshot whose names
  differ from the last ones sent triggers the `profile.update` of §10.8,
  and its `name_change.last` settles a pending name request (§10.8).
- **While held** (§3.6.3). The op `account` is still stored (it comes
  from the host, not an owner device), but `account.get` is not on the
  hold's allow list (`owner_check_required`), and
  `sync.event{account.changed}` waits for the check like any other
  fan-out; devices catch up with `sync.since` after it.
- **Display only.** Nothing in the vault depends on the snapshot except
  the profile's core names (0.18.0), and it is not authenticated beyond
  the host path: it is VettID's own data about the member, which VettID
  could equally withhold or change. That is why apps present the names
  as the account's, never as verified (§10.8). Membership and terms are
  enforced by the member API (§11.1).

### 11.14 Recovery and unlock from release R (0.33.0, release R)

*Owner decisions of 2026-10-13 to 2026-10-15; wording for the owner's
approval. It applies from **release R**, which is not built: the first
staging vault release that carries this section ("R" for recovery). It
binds nothing before. Every rule elsewhere in this document marked
"0.33.0, release R" points here. The old phone's keys after a transfer
(§11.14.10) were decided by the owner on 2026-10-15.*

**Why.** Until release R the limits on guessing a PIN and a credential
password during a recovery are kept in the sealed header and the vault
state (§11.11.6), which the host stores. They hold against everyone but
a host that replays stored objects, and VettID runs the host. A host
can start a recovery for any vault, register its own attested phone,
and then guess the PIN and after it the password at the speed of the
app (§11.11.2 "A recovery started by the host", §13.2). Release R moves
the count of attempts out of everything the host stores, tests the PIN
and the password only together, and adds a secret that only the
member's phone can produce to every unlock.

**What changes for a member.**

- Recovery still starts on the account site, still shows a one-time
  code after at least 24 hours, and still needs a new phone, the PIN
  and the credential password. The member keeps nothing new.
- On the new phone the PIN and the password are entered on **one
  screen** and tested **together**. The answer is "right" or "PIN or
  password is wrong", never which one.
- There are **ten attempts in total** for one PIN and password, for the
  life of that pair, not ten a day. The first two can be made at once;
  after that each wrong attempt is followed by a **wait** of 1, 2, 4, 8
  and 16 days, then 30 days each. Typing the same wrong pair again on
  the same phone is not counted again, and the app shows what was
  typed before it is sent.
- A recovery cannot succeed until **72 hours** after the member last
  proved both secrets to a running vault (an owner check, §3.6). A
  member who passed an owner check within the last three days cannot be
  recovered; a member who has just lost the phone waits up to three
  days instead of one. VettID can prevent owner checks by not running
  the service; if it does so for three days, only the ten attempts,
  their waits and the member's password protect the vault.
- Every attempt is counted before it is tested, recorded where the host
  cannot remove it, shown in the app's History and sent by email.
- Changing the PIN or the password ends every attempt against the old
  pair and gives ten new ones. After ten used attempts recovery is off
  until one of the two changes.
- A new credential password needs at least 12 characters, must not be a
  common password and must pass an estimate of how hard it is to guess.
- **Unlocking also needs a secret that only the phone's hardware can
  produce.** Someone who holds everything VettID stores can no longer
  test PINs against it without the member's phone.
- A transfer to a new phone needs the password as well as the PIN
  (as before release R), takes a few seconds longer and can be answered
  "busy, try again".
- On an iPhone the phone-held secret comes from a Secure Enclave key
  agreement instead of an HMAC key (0.35.0, §11.14.1).

**What this rests on, said once.** The count of attempts is kept in
Amazon S3 under Object Lock in compliance mode (§11.14.4,
VAULT-HOST-PROTOCOL §8.1). AWS documents that such a lock cannot be
shortened or removed by any user, including the account's root user.
VettID owns that AWS account, and this design assumes that AWS could
act for the account's owner if it chose to. Until a second record
outside AWS exists (§11.14.13), read "ten attempts" as "ten attempts,
unless AWS were to act for VettID".

**Which path the app takes** (0.34.0): the app learns whether a vault
implements release R from the release capabilities of §11.10.9, in the
attested descriptor or a transfer's bundle, before it sends anything.

**Staging vaults from before release R** cannot move into it: the
sealed header and the DEK change shape. They are deleted and enrolled
again (§11.14.14). Production has no vault.

#### 11.14.1 The phone-held unlock secret and the random DEK

From release R this replaces §3.3.1's derivation of the DEK. The
state's at-rest format gains the DEK's version in the clear (authenticated
as part of the AAD), so that the enclave can read it before it holds any
DEK:

```
state = 0x02 || state_seq (8, big-endian) || dek_version (8, big-endian) || nonce (24)
        || XChaCha20-Poly1305(DEK, nonce, aad, state_json)
aad   = "vettid/vms/2/state" || 0x00 || vault_id || 0x00 || state[0:17]
```

**The DEK** is 32 random bytes made by the enclave. It has a version,
`dek_version` (1 at enrollment), and is **replaced** at every event
meant to take power away from an old secret or an old phone
(§11.14.2). It is never stored in the clear. The state names the
`dek_version` it is encrypted under (above). The sealed header holds the
current DEK wrapped:

```
x            = Argon2id(PIN, salt, t = 3, m = 64 MiB, p = 1, 32)
unlock_key   = HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = x || unlock_secret, salt = pepper,
                            info = "vettid/vms/2/unlock-key" || 0x00 || vault_id, L = 32)
dek_wrap     = nonce (24) || XChaCha20-Poly1305(unlock_key, nonce, aad, DEK)
aad          = "vettid/vms/2/dek-wrap" || 0x00 || vault_id || 0x00 || dek_version (8, big-endian)
secret_check = HMAC-SHA-256(key = pepper,
                            msg = "vettid/vms/2/unlock-secret-check" || 0x00 || vault_id || 0x00 || unlock_secret)
```

- `unlock_secret` is exactly 32 bytes, supplied by the vault's app
  with `vault.enroll` (§11.3), every `vault.unlock` (§11.4), a recovery
  open (§11.14.6), a transfer's `hs.init` (§11.14.10), `pin.change` and
  `vault.secret.renew` (§11.14.9). The enclave uses it for the
  derivation above, keeps it and `unlock_key` in the vault process's
  memory while the vault is unlocked, and never writes either anywhere.
- A request that carries no `unlock_secret`, or one that is not 32
  bytes, is `bad_request` before any work on the PIN. **There is no
  PIN-only path in release R.**
- If the secret sent matches neither `secret_check` nor, while a `next`
  part exists, `secret_check_next` (§11.14.2), the answer is
  `device_secret`: decided before the PIN is tried and not counted as a
  PIN failure. `secret_check` does not depend on the PIN, so it cannot
  test one; guessing the secret through it means guessing 256 bits.
- A wrong PIN gives an `unlock_key` under which `dek_wrap` does not
  open: `bad_pin`, counted in the backoff of §11.8 as before. The
  everyday parameters stay `t = 3`, `m = 64 MiB`, `p = 1`, so an unlock
  costs what it cost before.
- **The PIN check in a running vault** (an owner check, §3.6.1 step 5;
  a transfer's approval; `vault.delete`; `credential.reset`; a name
  change; a History export) derives `unlock_key` from the PIN sent, the
  pepper and the secret held in memory since the unlock, and compares it
  in constant time with the `unlock_key` in memory. Nothing is stored
  for it, and nothing on the wire changes.
- The enclave cannot judge the secret's quality and accepts any 32
  bytes. An app that sent a constant would have a vault without this
  protection, and nobody could tell; that is the same trust in the
  published app as the rest of §11.7.
- `opener` (§11.14.3) holds the same DEK under the recovery key. It is
  the only way to the DEK without the phone's secret, and it needs the
  PIN and the password together at the heavy parameters.

**What the enclave stores, against the rule "nothing that lets the PIN
be tested without the phone's secret".**

| Stored | Where | Can the PIN be tested with it, without the secret |
|---|---|---|
| `dek_wrap`, `dek_wrap_next` | header | No: `unlock_key` needs the secret |
| `secret_check`, the KDF parameters, the pepper, the §11.8 backoff counters | header | No: none depends on the PIN |
| The recovery wrap and its `opener`s (§11.14.3) | header | Only the PIN and the password together, at the heavy parameters |
| `last_wrong` (§11.14.6) | header | Only a wrong pair, at the heavy parameters |
| The state | store | No: the DEK is random. (Before release R the state itself was the test: it decrypts under a DEK derived from the PIN) |
| The credential's backup copy, the owner-check record, the audit log | state | No: they are inside the state, and none holds the PIN |
| A request in transit (`vault.enroll`, `vault.unlock`, the recovery open) | the queue, briefly | It holds the PIN and the secret themselves, sealed to the ETK (§13.5, row "ETK") |

**On the phone** (§11.7; ANDROID-PLAN §4 "Recovery and unlock from
release R"). At enrollment, at a transfer and at a recovery the app
creates a new non-exportable HMAC-SHA-256 key in the Android Keystore,
the **phone key**, in StrongBox where the phone has it and in the
trusted execution environment otherwise, with exactly the properties of
its device attestation key and its app key. `key_vault` is the vault id
the key was made for, or the empty string for a key made at a transfer
to this phone (the new phone does not know the vault id when it sends
`hs.init`), and is fixed for the key's life. (0.36.0) For each **epoch**
the app makes 32 fresh random bytes `r` and the secret is

```
unlock_secret = HMAC-SHA-256(phone key, "vettid/vms/2/unlock-secret-2" || 0x00 || key_vault || 0x00
                             || epoch (8, big-endian) || r (32))
```

computed by the phone's hardware each time it is needed and held in the
app's memory only while a request is built. Nothing changes for the
vault, which accepts any 32 bytes (above), and the phone key is the same
HMAC key as before.

- `epoch` is a counter the app keeps: 1 at enrollment, at a transfer and
  at a recovery (each makes a new phone key), and one higher at each
  `pin.change` and `vault.secret.renew`. Each epoch has its own `r`,
  never derived from anything else: a value computed from stored or
  public inputs could be computed in advance by code that ran as the
  app.
- **The record.** The app keeps `(key_vault, epoch, r)` as one record in
  its encrypted account record, in storage excluded from backups, and
  writes the epoch and its `r` in the **same atomic write**. `r` is not
  secret without the phone key; the account record's authenticated
  encryption makes a damaged record fail to load instead of giving a
  wrong secret. A lost record is a lost secret.

**Records and lost answers** (0.36.0). The record the app believes the
vault holds is **current**; a record made for a change whose answer has
not arrived is a **candidate**; a record that a confirmed later one
replaced is **replaced**.

1. **Store before send.** The app writes a candidate, and builds the
   first request that carries its secret only once that write is known
   to be durable. A write that fails or is dropped (a record that is
   stale, closed or unreadable) stops the operation: nothing is sent and
   the member is told to try again. At epoch 1 the order is: create the
   phone key, then write the record with `key_vault`, epoch 1 and `r`,
   then send the enrollment, the transfer's `hs.init` or the recovery's
   register. A phone key that no record names, found at start-up or at
   the next attempt, was never sent, and the app makes a new key and a
   new record.
2. **Reuse on automatic retries.** A retry of the same request (a network
   retry, the UTK-sealed resend, the app restarting into the same flow)
   reuses its candidate. At epoch 1 a retry reuses the phone key and `r`
   when they exist for the same `key_vault`; a new attempt with another
   `key_vault` makes new ones.
3. **A new change makes a new candidate and keeps the unconfirmed ones.**
   A `pin.change` or `vault.secret.renew` the member starts again makes a
   fresh candidate, so that one made while unwanted code ran is not
   reused after a clean-up. Earlier unconfirmed candidates stay, **at
   most four**. While four are unconfirmed the app refuses a new
   `pin.change` or `vault.secret.renew` before sending anything and asks
   the member to unlock first (below); it never drops a candidate to make
   room, since the vault may hold any of them.
4. **Confirmation.** A candidate becomes current when its operation's
   answer arrives (`pin.change` `epoch_advanced: true`;
   `vault.secret.renew` `{credential, version, utks}`), (0.44.0) when
   the check of §11.14.9 "A lost answer" finds that its `pin.change`
   applied, or during an
   unlock: after `device_secret` with the current record the app tries
   the candidates, newest first, each at most once, and the first that
   gets an answer the vault gives only after the secret matched (`ok`,
   `bad_pin`, `transfer_incomplete`) becomes current. Each try is one
   more sealed `vault.unlock`; `device_secret` is decided before the PIN
   and is not a PIN failure. An answer decided before the secret check
   (`backoff`, `retry`, a refusal) proves nothing and ends the tries with
   the records unchanged. An unlock answered `ok` with the **current**
   record shows that the vault holds that record's secret and no
   candidate's (the vault drops a `next` part at that unlock, §11.14.2),
   so the candidates are then replaced records. (0.44.0) While a PIN
   change is unresolved, the app asks for the previous PIN for the
   current record and for the new PIN before it tries the candidate,
   instead of reusing the PIN typed (§11.14.9 "A lost answer" step 5).
   (0.45.0) The new PIN goes only with that change's own candidate, and
   only once no other candidate is left untried; other candidates are
   tried with the previous PIN (step 5 there).
5. **Never drop the current record on any other answer.** A change
   answered `retry`, `busy`, `bad_pin`, `bad_password`, `backoff`,
   `counter_unavailable`, refused, or not answered leaves the current
   record current; its candidate stays a candidate.
6. **Deletion.** When a candidate is confirmed, the record it replaces
   and every other candidate are replaced records. They are deleted
   **7 days** after that confirmation, the longest an operator restore of
   §11.14.2 can come back to the earlier state, or at a wipe, whichever is
   first. The 7 days count from the confirmation, or from the moment the
   app notices that its clock is behind it; a clock set back never
   extends them. After that a replaced epoch's secret cannot be computed
   on the phone again.
7. **The earlier secret, only when the member asks.** While a replaced
   record exists, the "this phone no longer holds the keys" screen
   offers an explicit step to try it. The app tries the replaced
   records, newest first, each once, only from that step and never on
   its own: an automatic try would let a host that serves an old header
   make the phone open an older state without the member knowing. Only
   `ok`, or `transfer_incomplete` for a transfer that did not finish,
   makes that record current again; the record it displaces becomes a
   replaced record under rule 6. **`bad_pin` moves nothing**: it shows
   only that the secret matched a header the host served, and nothing
   opened, so accepting it would let one served old header and a typed
   PIN make the old record current and get the real one deleted 7 days
   later. On `bad_pin` the records stay as they are and the member may
   type the PIN again. After an `ok` the app records it in History (on the phone for
   now; a vault History event may follow in a later release) and
   asks the member for a new phone secret (`vault.secret.renew`) at once:
   the vault is back on an older secret, which unwanted code may have
   computed. This is the case of §11.14.2 where an operator restored the
   state from before a PIN change or a new phone secret.
8. **A failing Keystore.** Only a definite loss counts as "this phone no
   longer holds the keys": the phone key missing, or reported
   permanently invalidated; for the account record, the file missing,
   or a decryption that fails while its Keystore key works. A refusal
   that may be temporary (a busy Keystore or StrongBox, the record's
   Keystore key refusing for a moment, any other error) is shown as "try
   again", sends nothing and changes no record.
9. **An older app.** The account record carries its format. An app that
   meets a record whose format it does not know refuses to start on it
   rather than compute a secret by another rule, which would only give
   `device_secret`. That refusal writes nothing, wipes nothing and makes
   no key.

**Form 1 records (staging only).** A record made before 0.36.0 has no
`r` and uses
`HMAC-SHA-256(phone key, "vettid/vms/2/unlock-secret" || 0x00 || key_vault || 0x00 || epoch (8, big-endian))`.
Phones that hold one keep it, with no prompt, and the app computes each
record with its own rule; the phone's next `pin.change` or
`vault.secret.renew`, or a new phone key, makes a record of the form
above. Until then such a phone stays exposed as described under "What
the secret protects against" below. Production has no vault, so no
production phone holds a form 1 record.

- The key's security level, as the Keystore reports it, MUST be
  `TrustedEnvironment` or `StrongBox`. The app refuses to enroll, to
  receive a transfer or to recover where it would be `Software`. A phone
  whose StrongBox does not offer the key falls back to the trusted
  execution environment, as for the other two keys.
- The phone key MUST NOT be bound to user authentication or to an
  unlocked screen. Android destroys such keys when certain phone
  settings change; the three keys are lost together or not at all.
- The secret is sent only inside a request sealed to the ETK, a
  transfer's `hs.init` sealed to the vault, or a UTK-sealed payload;
  never over the relay in the clear, never to the member API.
- The enclave cannot see how the phone holds the secret and relies on
  the app being the published one, which device attestation shows.
- **Clearing the app's data, or restoring the phone from a backup,**
  loses the phone key with the device key and the app key, as before
  (Keystore keys are not backed up, and the app's data is excluded from
  backups). With the credential backup on the member recovers; with it
  off the vault cannot be brought back (§3.5.6). The app cannot ask the
  vault which applies; the account site shows the backup bit.

**On an iPhone** (0.35.0; IOS-PLAN §6.3). The Secure Enclave holds
elliptic-curve keys, not HMAC keys, so the iPhone app makes the secret
from a key agreement. Nothing changes for the vault, which accepts any
32 bytes (above). At enrollment, at a transfer and at a recovery the
app creates a new Secure Enclave P-256 key-agreement key
(`SecureEnclave.P256.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey`), the **phone key** `P`:

- its access control is `privateKeyUsage` only, with the protection
  class `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`: the Secure
  Enclave uses the key only while the iPhone is unlocked. Every request
  that carries the secret is started in the app in the foreground (most
  of them by typing the PIN; a transfer's `hs.init` and the candidate
  retry below carry it without a new PIN entry), so the iPhone is
  unlocked whenever the key is needed, and code that runs on a locked
  iPhone, even after its first unlock, cannot make the Secure Enclave
  compute the secret (§11.14.12: a broken sealing plus the phone's
  secret takes the PIN offline);
- it is not bound to biometry or to the passcode (`biometryCurrentSet`
  is invalidated when a fingerprint or face is added; `userPresence`
  would add a prompt to every unlock);
- its key blob (`dataRepresentation`, usable only by this iPhone's
  Secure Enclave) is kept in the keychain with the same class,
  `kSecAttrSynchronizable` false, under a label that names `key_vault`.

**The protection class is stricter than Android's rule, as decided by
the owner on 2026-10-17.** Android forbids binding the phone key to an unlocked
screen (above) because Android destroys such keys when certain settings
change; the reason recorded with that choice (§15 item 39, decision 6)
is that the three keys are lost together or not at all. iOS deletes
neither `WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly` nor `AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`
items when the passcode is changed or turned off, so the stricter class
