  answer is a free test and a member's wrong pair is usually one slip
  from the right one. A host that drops or replays the header write
  makes the same wrong pair count twice, which costs the member an
  attempt and gains the host nothing. A pair typed again on another
  phone or in a later recovery is counted.
- **The recovery stays open across waits.** When a wait begins, the
  enclave moves the recovery record's `expires` to the wait's end plus
  24 hours and says so in the clear (`retry_at`, `expires`, with the
  marker of §11.14.11). The phone stays registered. If that header write
  is lost, the member requests a new recovery, whose `not_before`
  respects the wait (§11.14.5).
- While a recovery is open the member's old app is refused
  `recovery_pending` (§11.11.4); a member who still has it cancels.
  After a cancel by unlock (`cancel_recovery`), the app sends an owner
  check at once, which marks the member present (§11.14.5) and restarts
  the quiet period. (0.49.0) The member API learns of the cancel from
  the unlock's clear marker `recovery_cancelled` (§11.5, §11.11.4).

**Why a held-back answer gains nothing.** Every byte between the
enclave and the counter passes through the host, which can hold any
request or answer back. The rule above is: **a guess is tested only if
its own attempt was spent at a counter time `at` at which the generation
was open, the member had been absent for 72 hours, and every earlier
wait had run out**, and only if the read after the spend was made within
10 minutes of `at`. Holding back the status makes the enclave spend
later, at a true later `at` that the read after it judges. Holding back
the spend's answer for more than 10 minutes makes step 4b refuse.
Holding back the read after the spend tests late an attempt that was
spent rightly; it gains no attempt, which carries `at`, is counted and
shown, and starts its wait. Many enclaves at once all name the same next
attempt, and only one gets it. So within one absence VettID can test at
most the attempts the schedule allows in that absence, and cannot carry
an unspent guess out of it.

**A host can turn a member's own attempts into untested ones**, in three
ways: by holding back the counter's answers (`attempt_lost`), by holding
the spend's answer past 10 minutes, or by writing a present record
between the spend and the read after it (`quiet` with an attempt used).
A slow service with nobody at fault can do the first two. Ten times ends
the vault's recovery without a guess tested. Such a host can also delete
the vault (§13.5); it is stated because it needs no phone and no guess.
A host that drops step 1 of the order of writes after a right guess
every time can likewise use up all ten attempts with the member's
correct entries.

**What is removed in release R.** The device state "recovering"
(§11.11.5 step 2), `credential.recover` (§10.6), a registered phone's
entry among the header's unlock keys (§11.11.3), `vault_bundle` and
`credential_backup` in `vault.unlock.result` (§11.4), the recovering
app's row in the hold's allow list (§3.6.3), and the member API's
permission for a recovering key to call `unlock` and `lock`
(§11.11.7). Release R's image cannot perform the recovery of §11.11.5.
§11.8's PIN backoff and §3.5.3's password backoff stay for the everyday
unlock and for credential operations; recovery does not use them.
Until both secrets are proved together a registered phone has nothing:
no running vault, no token, no public keys of the vault.

**Someone with the member's account session or email who is not
VettID.** Against a present member the quiet period stops them. Against
a member who has just lost the phone, they can request a recovery, read
the code, register their own phone, use the two immediate attempts and
then one at the end of each wait, and cancel the member's own requests
from the same session. Ten wrong pairs end the vault's recovery for
good. The power to destroy is not new (the same session can delete the
vault through "start over", §11.11.9, after a delay and with a cancel
link); what is new is that wrong guesses use up the member's attempts
and start waits. The member is told by email at each attempt, unless
the attacker also reads and deletes the mail. A rule that the first
phone to make a counted attempt keeps the recovery would let this
attacker hold it against the member for months, and is not adopted.

**Other cases.** A desktop cannot pass an owner check and is no help in
a recovery, and does not delay one. A recovery that completes on a phone
the member did not mean removes every other app, and with the phone-held
secret a removed phone comes back only through a transfer or another
recovery. A member API that lies about time or account status can still
delete a vault through the unsigned `account` and `delete` operations
(§13.3); none of that is new.

#### 11.14.7 Passwords

From release R this replaces §3.5.1's "A UTF-8 string of 8–1,024
bytes".

- **One form.** The enclave normalizes every password to Unicode form
  NFC before any use: before the checks below, before the recovery wrap
  and before the credential's password key. The app does the same. (A
  new phone whose keyboard produces another encoding of the same letters
  would otherwise spend the member's attempts on a right password.)
- **Every password** is valid UTF-8 of at most 1,024 bytes. **A password
  that is set** (`credential.create`, the `new_password` of
  `credential.password.change` and `credential.reset`) must also:
  1. have at least **12 characters**, counted as Unicode scalar values;
  2. not be one character repeated;
  3. not be on the release's **common-password list**, compared after
     lowering ASCII letters;
  4. not equal the PIN;
  5. have an **estimated guessability** of at least **10^10 guesses**
     by the release's estimator.

  A password that breaks a rule is refused with `weak_password` and a
  `reason` (`short`, `repeated`, `common`, `same_as_pin`, `guessable`),
  after the UTK is opened and before anything else changes.
- **The estimator** is in the manner of zxcvbn: it looks for dictionary
  words, names, keyboard runs, repeats, sequences and dates and estimates
  how many guesses a well-informed attacker needs. It runs in the enclave,
  which decides, and in the app, which tells the member while typing;
  both with no network, the word lists being part of the release image
  and of the app. No online service is asked. The enclave's verdict is
  final. Both are tested against one shared file of passwords with
  expected verdicts, and the app's threshold is set a little higher than
  the vault's, so that a password the app accepts is rarely refused.
  **The 10^10 figure is tried with real people on phones on staging
  before production**; a different figure is a change to this section.
  The estimate is a model and can be wrong in both directions.
- **The list** is one file in vettid-vault, one password per line, lower
  case, sorted: a published list of the 100,000 most common passwords
  cut to the entries of 12 or more characters, with VettID's own obvious
  words added. It is compiled into the image, so it is part of what
  members approve, and its SHA-256 is printed in the release notes.
- **Licences.** The estimator's code and word lists, and the list's
  source, are used only after their licences have been read and allow
  it; nothing ships before.
- **Passwords that already exist** are checked only when set, but
  **recovery is armed only for a password that meets rules 1, 2 and 5**
  (§11.14.3): at an owner check the vault holds the password and checks
  them. A vault whose password does not meet them stays disarmed,
  reports `recovery.state: "change_required"`, and the app asks for a
  new password.

Twelve characters and a list do not make a password strong; they remove
the passwords an attacker would try first. The PIN adds little against
a guesser with ten tries (ten guesses find a measurable share of chosen
6-digit PINs); the password carries the weight.

#### 11.14.8 Signed recovery requests

From release R the operations `recovery` and `recovery_cancel`
(§11.5) carry a signature of the member API, and the enclave verifies
it. This settles §11.11.2's open design question.

- **Who signs.** The member API, with the **recovery request key**: an
  ECDSA P-256 key that exists only in AWS KMS, in the account that runs
  the member API, usable for signing by the member API's vault function
  and nothing else (MEMBER-API "Vault recovery").
- **What is signed**, with literal newlines and no trailing newline:

  ```
  "vettid/vms/2/recovery-request" \n op \n vault_id \n user_guid \n request_id \n signed_at \n hex(SHA-256(browser_key))
  ```

  `op` is `recovery` or `recovery_cancel`; `signed_at` is RFC 3339 in
  UTC to the second; for a cancel the last line is empty. The queue
  message carries `signed_at`, `key_id` and `sig` (base64 of the DER
  signature) in the clear.
- (0.49.0; approved by the owner (2026-10-19)) **A
  cancel names its recovery.** A `recovery_cancel` may carry the clear
  member `recovery_id` (a ULID): the recovery it means, which is the
  member API's `recovery_id`. When it does, the signed string has an
  eighth line, that `recovery_id`, after the empty seventh:

  ```
  … \n signed_at \n "" \n recovery_id
  ```

  The enclave verifies the signature over the string that matches the
  message: seven lines without the member, eight with it. A host that
  adds, removes or changes the member breaks the signature, and the
  cancel is ignored like any that fails. With the member, the enclave
  cancels only when its header holds a recovery with that id
  (`vault.RecoveryCancel` with the id, which already compares it). It
  answers `done` with no envelope, as for every cancel, and, when it
  cancelled nothing (another recovery, or none), the clear code
  `recovery_not_current`. That is the only host code on an answer
  without an envelope: the enclave's answer check (`enclave/wire.go`
  `ParseResponse`, which today refuses any code without an envelope)
  and the parent (`parent/consumer.go`, which today copies codes only
  from an answer with an envelope) both take it for a `recovery_cancel`
  only, and the parent copies it into that cancel's slot and nowhere
  else. Nothing reads a cancel's slot: the member API never polls it
  (`recovery_cancel` is not among its polled operations) and already
  ended its own record of the recovery it meant. The code is there for
  the operator's logs and tests. Without the member, the enclave
  keeps the earlier rule and cancels whatever recovery is in progress.
  **Why.** A cancel from the account site that reaches the enclave
  after a newer `recovery` (the queue is not ordered) would otherwise
  end the newer recovery in the enclave while the API still shows it
  pending.
  **Compatibility.** Releases up to staging 18 ignore the member but
  verify the seven-line string, so a named cancel fails there and is
  ignored. The member API therefore names the recovery only when the
  instance the cancel goes to runs a release at least
  `RECOVERY_CANCEL_ID_FROM_RELEASE` (a stack setting, unset until the
  release exists, as `TIME_SCALE_FROM_RELEASE`), and sends the
  seven-line form otherwise. Cancels already queued in the old form are
  valid for at most 5 minutes (`signed_at`) and keep the old rule.
  **A named cancel sent to a release that is too old** (a wrong setting,
  or an instance that reports another release than it runs) fails the
  signature and is ignored without an answer code. The enclave then
  keeps the recovery while the API shows it cancelled: safe, since a
  pending recovery only keeps the old app out until it cancels or the
  recovery expires, but silent. So the setting is changed only after a
  staging test that sends both forms to the boundary release and to the
  one before it. The member API's signer (`lambda/shared/recovery-sign.ts`
  `recoveryRequestSigningString`) gains the optional `recovery_id`, and
  §16 gains the eight-line vector.
- **What the release pins.** `recovery_request_keys` (§11.10.8): one or
  two public keys with their `key_id`, so that a key can be replaced by
  a release that still accepts the old one.
- **What the enclave verifies**, before it locks a running vault and
  before it reads or writes the header: the signature under a pinned
  key; that `op`, `vault_id`, `user_guid`, `request_id` and the browser
  key are those of the queue message; that `signed_at` is within 5
  minutes of its clock; and that `request_id` has not been seen (§11.6).
  A `recovery` that fails is answered with random bytes of the sealed
  code's size and nothing is locked or recorded; a `recovery_cancel`
  that fails is ignored. (Before release R the instance asked a running
  vault whether to refuse and then locked it, with no signature checked
  first; the signature now comes first.)
- The replay set is per instance (§11.6), so a signed request can be
  sent again to another instance within the five minutes. That gains
  nothing: a second `recovery` with the same `request_id` writes the
  same record or is refused by the header's state, and a cancel is
  harmless to repeat.

**What it protects against, and what it does not.** It takes the power
to start or cancel a recovery from someone who controls the host and
the vault's AWS account but not the member API's signing key. It does
**nothing** against VettID as a whole, which holds that key, and nothing
about the other operations without an envelope (`lock`, `delete`,
`account`), which the host can still forge (§13.3). In production the
member API and the vault run in two AWS accounts with one owner and one
sign-in, and the management account administers the vault account's
organization: the signature helps against an intruder inside the vault
account only. On staging both run in one account, and the signature
separates two roles there and no more; staging proves nothing about this
separation.

#### 11.14.9 Changes of PIN, password and phone secret

From release R:

| Type | Request body | Response body |
|---|---|---|
| `credential.create` | `{utk_id, sealed{pin, password}}` | as before; also arms (§11.14.3), waiting up to 60 s inside the request for the heavy-derivation permit and otherwise leaving arming to the next owner check (`recovery.state: "needs_check"`), never answering `busy`; a counter that cannot be reached likewise leaves it at `needs_check`, not an error. `pin` is verified against the vault's unlock key as in an owner check; `weak_password` (§11.14.7) |
| `pin.change` (the holder; a credential operation) | `{credential, utk_id, sealed{pin, new_pin, password, new_unlock_secret}}` | `{credential, version, utks, epoch_advanced: true}`; `bad_pin`, `bad_password`, `backoff`, `busy`, `counter_unavailable`, `retry`, `bad_request` (a `new_pin` that is not 6–32 digits, or a `new_unlock_secret` that is not 32 bytes) |
| `credential.password.change` | `{credential, utk_id, sealed{pin, password, new_password}}` | as before; `bad_pin`, `weak_password`, `busy`, `counter_unavailable`, `retry` |
| `credential.reset` | unchanged | as before; `weak_password`, `busy`, `counter_unavailable`, `retry` |
| `vault.secret.renew` (the holder; a credential operation) | `{credential, utk_id, sealed{pin, password, new_unlock_secret}}` | `{credential, version, utks}`; `bad_pin`, `bad_password`, `backoff`, `busy`, `retry` |

- **`pin.change`** verifies the PIN and the password as an owner check
  does (§3.6.1 steps 1–7, its `bad_pin` and `bad_password` counting as
  failed checks), takes the permit and computes the new generation's wrap
  for the new pair, closes the old generation, derives a new
  `unlock_key` from `new_pin`, a fresh salt, the pepper and
  `new_unlock_secret` (the phone's next epoch, §11.14.1), and replaces
  the DEK in the order of writes of §11.14.2. It is refused while the
  vault is held (§3.6.3), as before. It replaces 0.32.1's "re-derives
  the DEK from `new_pin` … and re-encrypts", whose write order was left
  open (§15).
- **`credential.password.change`** carries the PIN, which is verified;
  it closes the generation and arms the next in the same change, and
  replaces the DEK; the PIN and the secret do not change. (0.45.0) **The
  order of checks** is that of `pin.change` and the owner check: the
  blob first (the holder, the version and the clone rule of §3.5.9, so
  that an old blob is answered `stale_credential` and a clone raises its
  alarm before any secret is tested), then the PIN under the §11.8
  backoff, then the password under its backoff. vettid-vault releases up
  to staging 17 (and main at eb72d82) test the PIN first. There a
  request with an old blob and a wrong PIN is answered `bad_pin` and
  counted, and a clone's PIN guesses are answered before the alarm is
  raised. A vault release corrects this; an app that follows "A lost
  answer" below never sends such a request. (0.46.0) Its `bad_pin` and
  its `bad_password` **each count as a failed owner check** (§3.6.4),
  as in the owner check itself and in `pin.change`; a request refused
  before any secret is tested (`stale_credential`, a clone) counts
  nothing (§3.6.1).
- **`vault.secret.renew`** gives the phone a new secret with the PIN
  unchanged: it opens the current wrap with the pair, wraps a replaced
  DEK for the PIN and `new_unlock_secret`, and makes a new `opener`. The
  generation does not change. The app offers it in Settings, and after a
  member reports a phone that ran code it should not have, to be made
  after that code is gone (§11.14.1). (0.36.0) It ends exposure to such
  code only for the secret: it does not undo what else the code reached
  as the app, which a recovery or a transfer to another phone followed
  by a rotation does. On Android before 0.36.0, and while the phone's
  current record is of form 1, the next secret could be computed in
  advance by code that ran as the app, so there only a new phone key (a
  transfer or a recovery) ends that exposure.
- **Turning the credential backup off** closes the generation
  (§11.14.3); with the counter unreachable the setting is refused
  `counter_unavailable`.
- None of these marks the member present (§11.14.5). The app sends an
  owner check right after a change only where the change did not arm.

**A lost answer** (0.44.0; corrected and completed in 0.45.0). When
the app gets no answer to `pin.change` or `credential.password.change`
(a timeout after the automatic resends of §8.6, the network gone, the
app suspended or stopped), the change may have applied. The vault then
holds the new PIN or password, and a second request with the old one is
answered `bad_pin` or `bad_password`, which counts as a failed owner
check (§3.6.4) or under the password backoff (§3.5.3). A second request
is a new one with the old blob. The vault answers it `stale_credential`
before it tests any secret (§3.5.9; for `credential.password.change`
from the release that checks the blob first, see the bullet above), and
it is the apps' generic retry (fetch the blob, resend with the same
typed secrets) that spends the attempt. So the app **decides** the
change instead of repeating it.

1. **Before the send.**
   - (0.45.0) **Nothing else in flight.** A change is sent only when no
     other credential operation (§3.5.9's types, the owner check and
     `vault.secret.renew` included) is waiting in the app's outbox or
     waiting for its answer. Otherwise the app first waits for those
     answers, for at most 30 s, and if they do not come it refuses the
     change with nothing sent. This is what makes "version + 1" in step
     3 mean this change and no other.
   - (0.46.0) **Settled on answers only.** A credential request the app
     sent is settled by its answer, or by the `ts` of an answer from the
     vault (to any request) that is more than 1 minute after the
     request's `exp`, as in step 3. Other messages from the vault
     (events, notices) settle nothing. When every pending request
     should have expired by the phone's estimate, the app may send one
     `credential.version` to obtain a vault time.
   - (0.46.0) **A renew is settled before a PIN change.** The app records
     an unresolved `vault.secret.renew` before sending it, as in the
     next bullet. (0.47.0) An answer to the renew's own request decides
     it: success is applied, and any refusal, `stale_credential`
     included, is **not applied**, as step 4 says for a change. Only a
     renew whose own answer never arrived is decided by
     `credential.version` with step 3's table. A PIN change is sent only once every renew is
     decided. While a renew could still apply, the PIN change is refused
     with the "earlier request" text. When the version cannot decide it
     (step 3's "ends without a decision"), the PIN change is refused and
     the app offers to lock and unlock the vault: the PIN has not
     changed, so the unlock costs nothing, and it confirms the renew's
     candidate or the current record (§11.14.1 rule 4).
   - (0.47.0) **Sent with the vault's current blob.** Right before it
     sends a change or a renew, inside the same serialization that sends
     its credential operations and once every earlier credential request
     is settled (above), the app asks `credential.version`. When
     `version` equals the version of the blob the request would carry,
     it sends. Otherwise an earlier operation applied without its answer
     reaching the phone: every operation that rotates the CEK moves the
     version (§3.5.3), an owner check, a name change,
     `credential.unlock`, `credential.rotate` and a transfer's approval
     included. The app then fetches the latest blob (`credential.get`)
     and keeps it, and sends the request with that blob when the fetched
     version equals the vault's. A fetch that fails or gives another
     version refuses the request with nothing sent, with the "earlier
     request" text; no answer to `credential.version` refuses it as the
     second sub-bullet below says. This is what makes step 3's "version + 1" mean
     this request: it carries the vault's current version, and no earlier
     request can still apply. It rests on the vault handling one batch at
     a time, the messages of a batch in mailbox order, and nothing while
     it is locked (vettid-vault `vault/inbound.go` `ProcessBatch`, main
     07bf770). Since every earlier request is settled, any of them
     applied before the answer to `credential.version` was produced, or
     never will, whatever the order of delivery.
     - (0.47.1) **An answer that shows no version counts as "differs".**
       An error answer to `credential.version`, an answer without a
       `version`, or `exists: false` is handled as a version that
       differs: the app fetches, and sends only when the fetched blob is
       the vault's current one. When the answer gave a version, that is
       a fetched version equal to it. When it gave none, it is a blob
       that `credential.get` returned: the vault answers `credential.get`
       with its latest blob or `not_found`, never with an older one
       (vettid-vault `features/credential/credential.go`, staging release
       18). Otherwise the request is refused with nothing sent, with the
       "earlier request" text.
     - (0.47.1) **No answer** to `credential.version` refuses the request
       with nothing sent, with the app's plain "can't reach the service"
       text (ANDROID-PLAN names it). It is not a "change pending" text
       such as step 2's "can't reach your vault" or ANDROID-PLAN's
       "unreachable" text: nothing was sent, so nothing is pending.
       (0.47.0 named the "can't reach" text here.)
   - Besides the candidate record of a PIN change (§11.14.1 rule 1), the
     app durably stores an **unresolved change**: the type, the inner
     `id`, the blob version the request carries, and the request's
     `exp`. It holds no PIN, password or secret. The store refuses when
     an unresolved change with another `id` exists (0.45.0), so two
     changes started together cannot overwrite each other. A write that
     fails stops the operation before anything is sent, as rule 1 does.
   - The request carries `exp` (§5.3): **10 minutes after the vault's
     clock as the app last saw it**. That is the `ts` of the newest
     answer from the vault plus the time elapsed since on the phone's
     monotonic clock, or the phone's clock when it has no answer yet.
     The vault drops a request whose `exp` has passed before its dedupe
     and before any handler, unanswered, so a copy that has not reached
     the vault by then never applies (the assumptions are listed after
     step 6).
   - The app keeps the request it sent (the same inner `id` and body) in
     memory only, never on disk, until the change is decided.
2. **No answer is not a failure.** The app does not report a failure
   and keeps the member's new entries. While the change is unresolved it
   sends **no** new `pin.change`, `credential.password.change`,
   `vault.secret.renew`, owner check or other credential operation: each
   of them would carry a PIN or password that may be the old one, or a
   blob that may be stale. (0.45.0) It also refuses a **release update**
   (§11.10.3: the update locks the vault and carries its approval in an
   unlock) and any other flow that locks and unlocks the vault with a
   PIN typed outside the unlock of step 5, "Finish the move" of a
   transfer (§11.14.10) included (0.46.0); the same holds while a PIN is
   uncertain (step 3). Only the unlock's two-step prompts of step 5 send
   a PIN with a candidate. The member may still lock the
   vault (§3.6.8, §10.2); the next unlock follows step 5. The app
   decides the change first: at once, and again whenever it reconnects
   or starts.
   - (0.45.0) **The gate.** An operation refused under this step is
     refused at once, with nothing sent and without waiting for the
     decision. The text says why: "still checking" while the vault can
     be reached, and "can't reach your vault" while it cannot
     (ANDROID-PLAN has the texts).
3. **Deciding.** While `exp` has not passed by the vault's clock as in
   step 1, the app may **resend the same request** (the same inner `id`
   and body, in a new envelope). The vault answers it from its response
   cache if it handled it (§8.2, 24 hours), or handles it once if it
   never arrived. Either way no secret is tested twice and no attempt is
   counted twice. This is an exception to §8.6's "at most twice". The
   app also asks **`credential.version`** (§10.6; no secret, any owner
   device, allowed during a hold):
   - `version` equal to the stored version **+ 1**: the change
     **applied**. Credential operations come only from the holder, and
     this app had none other in flight when it sent the change (step 1)
     and sent none while the change was unresolved (step 2), so no other
     operation moved it. The app fetches the latest blob
     (`credential.get`, §3.5.3) and keeps it (after a password change it
     opens with the new password), tops up its UTKs, makes the PIN
     change's candidate current (§11.14.1 rule 4), clears the unresolved
     change and tells the member that the change succeeded.
   - `version` equal to the stored version, in an answer whose `ts` is
     **more than 1 minute after the request's `exp`**: the change **did
     not apply and never will**. The app clears the unresolved change
     and tells the member that nothing was changed. The member's next
     attempt is a new request with the PIN or password that is still
     current. The candidate stays as rules 3–5 of §11.14.1 say.
   - `version` equal to the stored version in an earlier answer: not
     decided yet. The app resends the same request if it still holds
     it, or asks again after a pause (30 s, doubling up to 5 minutes).
   - Anything else (no credential, another version, a clone alarm):
     the check **ends without a decision**. The app clears the
     unresolved change, leaves the candidate to the next unlock
     (§11.14.1 rule 4) and follows that answer's own path (§3.5.9).
     (0.51.1) A `forbidden` answer is not this case: it ends the change
     as "Another phone became the holder" (below) says.
     (0.45.0) It offers no retry that would send the PIN or password
     again. After a PIN change, the PIN stays **uncertain**: until an
     unlock under step 5 settles it, the app refuses the owner check and
     every other operation that carries the PIN, and offers to lock and
     unlock the vault with step 5's prompts, which spend no attempt when
     the member types the PIN each prompt asks for. After a password
     change, the app says that either password may be the current one.
   - No answer at all: the change stays unresolved, and the app tells
     the member that it will check when it can reach the vault.
4. **An answer that arrives** to the request (to the first send or a
   resend) decides the change by itself:
   - `epoch_advanced` or the new blob is success. It is shown as success
     even when the app's own write of the confirmation fails; the
     unresolved change and the candidate then stay, and the next check
     or unlock confirms them.
   - `bad_pin`, `bad_password`, `weak_password` and the other refusals
     are shown as they are, with the entry that was wrong cleared, and
     the change did not apply. (0.51.1) `forbidden` ends the change as
     "Another phone became the holder" (below) says.
   - (0.45.0) **`stale_credential`** means that **this change did not
     apply**: the vault answers it before running the change and caches
     that answer under the request's `id` (§8.2), so no copy of the
     request can apply later. The app clears the unresolved change,
     fetches the blob (`credential.get`), and does **not** retry with
     the typed secrets. It does **not** decide by `credential.version`
     here: the version moved because of the earlier operation that made
     the blob stale, not because of this change. (0.44.0 said "decides
     as in step 3", which would read that earlier operation as this
     change.)
5. **A locked vault.** `credential.version` needs a running vault.
   While a PIN change is unresolved, or its PIN is uncertain (step 3),
   and the vault is locked, the unlock asks for the **previous PIN** and
   sends it with the current record (§11.14.1 rule 4).
   - (0.45.0) **`ok` does not decide the change.** A copy of the request
     may still wait in the vault's mailbox and apply after this unlock,
     until its `exp`. The unresolved change stays, and the app decides
     it as in step 3 once the vault runs. (0.44.0 said that `ok` decides
     "not applied".) An uncertain PIN is settled by `ok`: the vault held
     the previous one.
   - `device_secret` shows that the vault holds another epoch than the
     current record, decided before any PIN is tested. (0.45.0) The app
     asks for the **new PIN** only when the change's candidate is the
     only unconfirmed candidate left. (0.46.0) Since a renew is settled
     before a PIN change is sent (step 1), this arises only as a
     fallback, for a renew candidate left from before that rule.
     Otherwise, for example after an
     unanswered `vault.secret.renew`, whose candidate goes with the
     previous PIN, it first tries the other candidates with the previous
     PIN already typed, newest first, each once. `device_secret` from
     every one of them leaves the change's candidate, and only then does
     the app ask for the new PIN. Any other answer the vault gives after
     the secret matched (`ok`, `bad_pin`, `transfer_incomplete`) confirms
     that candidate (rule 4); the vault then holds the previous PIN, and
     the change stays undecided until step 3 decides it, as in the first
     bullet of this step. The new PIN is never reused for a candidate
     that goes with the previous one, and the reverse is also true.
   - An unresolved password change does not change the unlock (it needs
     only the PIN); the app decides it once the vault runs.
6. **The member is never sent to lock and unlock** to find out, except
   to settle an uncertain PIN with step 5's prompts (step 3). Unlocking
   with the wrong one of the two PINs costs an attempt, and the check
   above costs none.
7. (0.45.0) **Telling the member.** The decision often comes after the
   member has left the change screen, or after a restart. The app shows
   the decision once, wherever the member is: a notice on the main
   screen until the member dismisses it, and a notification when the app
   is in the background. A change screen opened later starts afresh and
   ignores a decision it did not start.

**What the vault must do for this** (0.45.0). The 1-minute margin of
step 3 and the "never applies" of step 1 rest on four properties of the
vault, each of which a release must keep or this section must change:

- it checks `exp` **before** its dedupe and before any handler, with
  **no tolerance** (a message is dropped when the vault's clock is after
  `exp`), and it answers nothing for a dropped message;
- it reads its clock **once for each batch** it processes, uses that
  reading both for the `exp` check of every message in the batch and as
  the `ts` of every answer from that batch, and processes **one batch at
  a time**. An answer stamped after `exp` therefore comes from a later
  batch than any copy that passed the check, and shows that copy's
  effect, however long its handler ran (a wait for the heavy-derivation
  permit included);
- its clock does not step back by more than **1 minute** (the margin);
- it caches every answer of a request (errors included, §8.2) under the
  request's `id`, so that a resend before `exp` meets the same answer.

vettid-vault staging releases 15 and 17 (the releases in service on
2026-10-18) and main at eb72d82 have all four (`vault/inbound.go`
`ProcessBatch` and `dispatch`; `vms/envelope/inner.go` `CheckTime`).

What it reveals, and to whom: `credential.version` tells an owner
device, over its own session, the blob's version number, which the
holder learns at every operation anyway. A resend of the same request
is answered from the cache or handled once, and an expired copy is
dropped unanswered. None of them tests a PIN or a password, so none lets
anyone learn whether a guess was right or spend fewer attempts per
guess. No step drops a record or a key: the candidate is kept until an
answer or an unlock decides it, as before.

`vault.secret.renew` has the same shape, but a retry with the same PIN
and password spends nothing. (0.46.0) Its lost answer is recorded and
decided as step 1 says, before any PIN change; step 5's fallback covers
a renew candidate left unconfirmed from before that rule.
(0.48.0) `credential.reset` follows below.

**A lost answer to `credential.reset`** (0.48.0; owner decision of
2026-10-19; vettid.org #358 part 1). Up to 0.47.x a reset was not
covered here. But a reset that applied without its answer reaching the
phone leaves the vault at version 1 of a new credential, under a new
credential key, while the phone still holds blob N of the old one
(§3.5.5). The phone's next credential operation presents that dead
blob, for example a reset sent again after "can't reach", or the daily
owner check. The blob is neither the current one nor the holder's
version current − 1, so the vault takes it for a **clone**: it answers
`credential_frozen`, opens an alarm with presenter `holder`, and the
member gets the alarm email (§3.5.9). A reset waits for the
heavy-derivation permit (the table above: `busy`), so a lost answer is
realistic. The app therefore sends and decides a reset as it does a
change:

1. **Before the send**, as step 1:
   - nothing else in flight, and every earlier credential request
     settled on answers only;
   - the `credential.version` pre-check ("Sent with the vault's current
     blob"). The app records the `key` of that answer with the blob it
     sends, as the **held key**. When the answer gives no `key`, the
     request is refused with nothing sent, with the "earlier request"
     text;
   - an unresolved change of type `credential.reset`, stored durably
     before the send: the inner `id`, the blob version the request
     carries, the held key and the request's `exp`. It holds no PIN or
     password;
   - the request carries `exp`, 10 minutes after the vault's clock as
     the app last saw it, and the app keeps the request (the same inner
     `id` and body) in memory only until the reset is decided.
2. **While it is unresolved**, the gate of step 2 refuses **every other
   credential operation** (§3.5.9's types, the owner check,
   `vault.secret.renew`, the changes, critical items, wallet signing and
   (0.56.0) `wallet.caps.raise` included) at once, with the same texts. A reset changes neither the
   PIN nor the phone's secret, so the unlock is not affected, as for a
   password change (step 5, last bullet).
3. **Deciding.** While `exp` has not passed, the app may resend the same
   request (the same inner `id` and body, in a new envelope): the vault
   answers it from its response cache, or handles it once if it never
   arrived (step 3). It also asks `credential.version`:
   - a **`key` that differs from the held key, or a `version` lower than
     the stored version**: the reset **applied**. Of the requests this
     app could have sent, only a reset or a `credential.rotate` changes
     the key, and the gate refused the rotation. The app fetches the
     latest blob (`credential.get`), keeps it (it opens with the new
     password), acknowledges it (`credential.ack`), tops up its UTKs
     (`credential.utk.get`; the holder kept the rest of its pool across
     the reset), treats its critical items as destroyed, as on the
     reset's own answer, clears the unresolved change and tells the
     member that the new credential was made;
   - the **same `key` and `version`**, in an answer whose `ts` is more
     than 1 minute after the request's `exp`: the reset **did not apply
     and never will**. The app clears the unresolved change and tells
     the member that nothing was changed;
   - the same `key` and `version` in an earlier answer: not decided yet.
     The app resends the request while it holds it, or asks again after
     a pause (30 s, doubling up to 5 minutes);
   - anything else (no credential, the same `key` with another
     `version`, an answer that shows an alarm): the check **ends without
     a decision**. The app clears the unresolved change, offers no retry
     that would send the PIN or a password again, and says that either
     password may be the current one. An alarm follows its own path
     (§3.5.9), whose fetch brings the latest blob either way. (0.51.1)
     A `forbidden` answer is not this case: it ends the reset as
     "Another phone became the holder" (below) says;
   - no answer at all: the reset stays unresolved, and the app tells the
     member that it will check when it can reach the vault.
4. **An answer that arrives** to the request (the first send or a
   resend) decides it by itself, as step 4 says: the new blob (with its
   `key`, version 1) is success; `bad_pin`, `bad_password`,
   `weak_password`, `backoff`, `busy`, `counter_unavailable`, `retry`
   and the other refusals mean **not applied**; `stale_credential`
   means not applied, and the app fetches the blob and does not retry
   with the typed secrets. (0.51.1) `forbidden` ends the reset as
   "Another phone became the holder" (below) says.
5. **Telling the member** is step 7's.

The vault needs no change for this. vettid-vault staging release 18
(`release/staging/18`) has the four properties listed above for
`credential.reset` as for any other request that is not volatile
(`vault/inbound.go` `dispatch`: `CheckTime` before the dedupe, and every
answer, errors included, cached under the request's `id`;
`credential.reset` is not a volatile type). `credential.version`
answers `{exists, version, key, updated_at, alarm?}`, and the reset's
own answer is `{credential, version, key, utks}`
(`features/credential/credential.go` `Handle`, `holderReset`,
`create`).

**Another phone became the holder** (0.51.1; owner decision of
2026-10-20, approved by the owner (2026-10-20); found while
implementing the reset's lost answer on iOS). Deciding an unresolved
change or reset ("A lost answer", "A lost answer to
`credential.reset`") uses requests that only the holder may make
(§3.5.9): the resend of the request itself, and `credential.get`,
`credential.ack` and `credential.utk.get` after "applied"; and
`credential.version`, which needs an owner device. If another phone has meanwhile become the holder
(a recovery completed elsewhere, §11.14.6, or a transfer, §11.14.10),
the vault answers them `forbidden`. Up to 0.51.0 nothing here covered
that answer: the change stayed unresolved, and the app stayed at "can't
reach" with the gate of step 2 closed, for ever.

- **A `forbidden` answer from the vault** to any request the app sends
  to decide an unresolved change or reset (those above, or any other
  request of the resolution) is a **definite outcome**: this phone is
  no longer the holder, so the change can no longer be decided or
  completed from it. The app **ends the unresolved change**: it clears
  the marker and the change's candidate (§11.14.1), leaves no PIN
  uncertain (step 3), and the gate of step 2 opens. This holds for a
  PIN change, a password change, a renew and a reset alike, and also
  when `credential.version` had already shown "applied" and a later
  `credential.get`, `credential.ack` or `credential.utk.get` is
  answered `forbidden`.
- **Telling the member.** The app then shows, as step 7 says, the text
  it already shows for a vault that moved to another phone (ANDROID-PLAN
  and IOS-PLAN name it), not a "changed" or "not changed" text: from
  this phone it cannot be known whether the change applied. It offers
  no retry that would send the PIN or a password again.
- **Only the vault's own answer counts**: an error response with code
  `forbidden` (§10.1) in the inner plaintext (§5.3) of a response to
  that request (`re` equal to its `id`, §8.1), opened under this
  device's end-to-end encrypted session with the vault. A transport
  error, a timeout, an HTTP status, an error of the relay, the member
  API or the host, an answer that does not open or answers another
  `id`, and anything else that is not from the vault is **no answer**:
  the change stays unresolved, and the app shows its "can't reach your
  vault" text (step 3, "No answer at all"). A faulty or hostile host can
  therefore delay a decision, as before, but cannot end a change.
- **Not a proof of replacement.** Ending the change erases nothing: the
  app keeps its keys and its local state, and erases them only on what
  already proves that this phone was replaced (the vault's own
  `device.unlinked{transferred}` or `device.unlinked{replaced}`,
  §11.14.10, §11.11.5).

The vault needs no change for this: it already answers `forbidden` to
a request that only the holder may make when it comes from another
device (§3.5.9), and caches every answer of a request, errors included,
under the request's `id` (§8.2).

#### 11.14.10 Transfer from release R

§6.7.1 holds, with these changes:

1. **The new phone's secret.** The new app creates its phone key and
   sends `unlock_secret` (epoch 1) in its `hs.init` (purpose `app`),
   which is sealed to the vault (§6.2). The vault keeps it **in memory
   only** until the holder's approval; if the vault locks first, the
   transfer ends and is started again.
2. **The approval** carries the PIN and the password, as before. The
   vault verifies both, takes the heavy-derivation permit (`busy`
   without one; nothing is spent but the UTK, the transfer stays open,
   and the old app tries again), opens the current wrap and makes a new
   `opener`, and replaces the DEK for the PIN and the new phone's secret
   in the order of writes of §11.14.2: the new phone's unlock key and app
   key in step 1's `next` part (`app_key_next`), the new device record
   and the removal of the old app in step 2, the promotion in step 3
   (`app_key`). The approval answer is `{"unlink": "after_new_unlock"}`
   (before release R, `{}`); a failed step 1 is answered `retry`.
3. **A new phone that unlocks before step 2 is stored** is answered
   `transfer_incomplete` and repeats nothing itself: the app says "The
   move to this phone did not finish. Approve it again on your old
   phone."
4. **The new phone finishes the move.** Right after `device.paired` and
   the credential fetch, the new app asks for the PIN and sends
   `vault.lock` and then `vault.unlock` with its own secret ("Finish the
   move"). That unlock reads the stored header and state, so it proves
   that both writes of the transfer are durable.
5. **The new phone waits 11 minutes** (owner decision, 2026-10-23). The
   vault's 10 minutes (§6.7.1, failures) count from the `hs.init` it
   receives; the new app counts from the moment it started its
   `hs.init`, which is earlier. The new app of a transfer therefore
   waits for `device.paired` or `device.pair.rejected` for **11
   minutes** after it started its `hs.init` (the vault's 10 minutes
   plus about a minute of grace), and only then drops its handshake, its
   attested key and its epoch-1 secret. With 10 on both sides an
   approval near the end could complete at the vault after the new phone
   had already dropped them, and the vault's app would be a phone that
   cannot open it. A `device.paired` that arrives within the 11 minutes
   is accepted. The vault's 10 minutes are unchanged, and so are those
   of a pairing of a desktop or an agent (§6.7).

   **Collect before drop** (owner decision, 2026-10-23). The 11 minutes
   are measured from the moment the app started its `hs.init`; it is one
   deadline, and no user action extends it. The app stores that moment with the transfer, so a restart keeps the same deadline. An app that is not running at the deadline (stopped, killed, the phone off) does this at its next start, before anything else: one collect, then the drop. At the deadline the new app
   **collects its mailbox once** before it drops anything. If that
   collect brings a `device.paired{transfer}` for this transfer, opened
   under the transfer's session, the app applies it and completes the
   move (it takes over the credential, as for an approval within the 11
   minutes) instead of dropping. Otherwise, or if the collect fails or
   times out, it drops its handshake, its attested key and its epoch-1
   secret as before and offers a new code. The collect is bounded: one collect with `wait=0` and `max` at its cap (RELAY-PROTOCOL §6.3), bounded by the app's request timeout and by 30 seconds in all, its transport retries included; if the app cannot
   reach the relay, that is no reason to keep the keys longer, and it
   drops them at once. A transfer whose `device.paired` has arrived
   (the move is paired) completes at any later start of the app,
   whatever its age; the deadline applies only to a transfer still
   waiting.

**The old phone's keys after a transfer** (decided by the owner on
2026-10-15). *This replaces the earlier rule that the old app erases
itself on `device.unlinked{reason: "transferred"}` sent at the
approval.* The old app deletes its keys **when it receives that notice,
sent only after the new phone's first unlock from storage, or, from 7
days after the approval, when its vault answers that this phone is no
longer its app (0.55.10, owner decision 2026-10-23), whichever comes
first.**

- At the approval the old app is removed from the vault exactly as
  before (its relay key denylisted, its unlock key and UTK pool removed;
  §7.4), but the vault **does not** send `device.unlinked` then. It
  keeps, in its state, a **pending unlink**: the old device's mailbox,
  the deposit token it issued to the vault, the `transfer_id` and the
  transfer's `dek_version` and (0.55.10) the old session's sending key,
  so that it can seal the notice when it delivers it. **Before it sends
  the approval the old app renews the standing token it issued to the
  vault for its own mailbox** (`relay.token.issued{kind: "standing", token}`, §7.1, §7.2; no new
  token class and no new message). It deposits that message to the
  vault's mailbox and waits for the relay's `201` before it deposits the
  approval, so that the vault, which takes its mailbox in arrival order
  (§8, §8.3), stores the fresh token before it processes the approval;
  it SHOULD NOT denylist the previous token's `jti` before the approval
  is answered. It renews again before each approval it sends (after
  `busy`, `retry` or (0.56.1) `stale_credential` too). The renewed
  token then has its full lifetime, at most 30 days, from the approval;
  the pending unlink keeps the newest token. (0.56.1) If the renewal
  fails, the old app still sends the approval, and the pending unlink
  keeps the previous token: the notice can then be delivered only while
  that token lives.
- **`device.unlinked{reason: "transferred", transfer_id}`** is deposited
  to the old app only after the vault's then current app has completed
  its **first successful unlock from the stored objects under that
  `dek_version` or a later one** (the "Finish the move" unlock, or any
  later one; a completed recovery's open counts the same, and sends it
  before its relay key switches, §11.14.6). The vault then deletes the
  pending unlink. (0.55.10, owner decision 2026-10-23.) **The vault
  keeps the pending unlink for the life of that token, not for 7
  days:** it is deleted unsent only when the token has expired, at most
  30 days after the approval, whatever the pending unlink's age. The
  notice is sealed **at delivery**, with the old session's sending key
  the vault kept, and not at the approval, so that §8.4's 16-day `ts`
  rule does not cut it short. The notice normally goes out minutes after
  the move ("Finish the move"). The vault can deposit it for up to 30
  days after the move; once deposited it waits in the old phone's
  mailbox for the relay's 14 days (`message_ttl_seconds`), and an old
  phone that does not collect it in that time keeps its keys until the
  member removes VettID. These are vault changes of release L (staging release 23),
  together with the old app's renewal of the token at the approval.
- The old app, once its approval was answered `{"unlink":
  "after_new_unlock"}`, keeps its phone key, device key, app key and local
  state, records the approval's time, and does nothing with the vault: it
  shows "Finish the move on your new phone". On
  `device.unlinked{transferred}` it deletes the phone key, the device
  key and the app key and erases its local state. **At or after 7 days
  after the approval it first checks with the vault** (see "The day-7
  check" below), and erases only on a definite answer. Until then it
  offers **"The move
  didn't finish"**: an unlock with its own keys and the PIN, which
  succeeds only if the transfer's state write was not stored, or after
  an operator restored the earlier state (§11.14.2, RUNBOOK); the old
  phone is then the vault's app again and the member starts a new
  transfer. A refused relay key alone is still not proof of removal
  (§6.7.1, the old app offline).
- **Why.** Until the new phone has unlocked, the old phone is the way
  back from the one write fault no order can fix (§11.14.2): if the new
  state is not durable the new phone cannot unlock, and the earlier
  header and state, restored in time, open with the old phone and the
  PIN. Once the new phone has unlocked from storage that case no longer
  exists. After 7 days no operator restore of §11.14.2 is possible, so
  the old keys serve nothing **once the vault has answered**; until it
  answers, the 7 days prove nothing about the move (0.55.10: a vault
  that was locked on day 7 used to erase the old phone even when the
  approval never took effect, or after the §11.14.2 restore, which
  would strand the vault), so the keys are kept until the vault
  answers.
- **The residual until then.** With an honest host the old phone opens
  nothing after step 3: its unlock key is gone, its secret opens no
  current wrap and the DEK was replaced. With a host that replays, the
  old phone, the PIN, the old header and the old state are a running copy
  of the vault as it was, with working relay and identity keys (§11.14.2,
  "What an old copy still holds"), **until the old phone deletes its
  keys**. The notice cannot shorten that against such a host: the host
  also carries the relay traffic and can withhold `device.unlinked`, and
  a pending unlink whose standing token has expired is deleted unsent.
  A host that replays can withhold both the day-7 answer and the
  notice, so the bound against it is the member removing or resetting
  VettID on the old phone, which the last screen and the waiting notice
  ask for; a phone that is off, or never opens the app again, keeps the
  keys until it is wiped. Against an honest host the notice usually arrives within minutes, at "Finish
  the move". The old phone's last screen says: "This phone keeps your
  vault's keys until your new phone has finished the move, and until
  your vault has confirmed it. Once your new phone works, you can remove
  VettID from this phone. Before you give this phone away, remove
  VettID from it or reset it."
- **The day-7 check** (0.55.10; owner decision, 2026-10-23, from the iOS
  review). At the first start, and at every start and foreground after
  that, 7 days or more after the approval, the old app sends the vault
  `device.list` before it erases anything. There are three results.
  1. **The vault answers, and this phone is no longer its app** (a
     definite answer): the app erases as for the notice.
  2. **The vault answers, and this phone is still its app** (the
     approval never took effect, or an operator restored the earlier
     state): the app erases nothing, ends the keep, and is the vault's
     app again, as after "The move didn't finish".
  3. **The vault does not answer** (locked, `lock_pending`, a timeout,
     offline, or a refusal that is not an answer of the vault itself,
     such as `token_revoked`, §8.6): the result is **not known: check
     again later.** The app NEVER erases on it. It keeps its keys, shows
     "Your vault has not confirmed the move to this phone. Once your new phone opens your vault, remove VettID from this phone.", and checks again at each
     start and foreground, until it gets a definite answer. A check that
     is cancelled or interrupted (the app is stopped, the phone locks,
     the process dies) never erases; the next start runs it again.
  A definite answer (results 1 and 2) is only the response to this
  check's own request: a `device.list` response opened under this
  phone's session with its vault whose `re` is the check's request `id`
  and whose `status` is ok. Any other message, an earlier `device.list`
  response among them, and any error status, is result 3. The phone is
  still the vault's app only if the list holds this phone's own device
  `id` with kind `app`; it is no longer the vault's app only if the list
  does not hold that `id`.
  The app erases only on `device.unlinked{transferred}`, or on result 1.
- **What a removed phone hears** (0.55.10). Once the approval took
  effect the old app is removed (§7.4): the relay refuses its deposits
  (`token_revoked`), the vault drops its messages, and an unlock gives
  unreadable bytes (§11.4). So a removed phone gets result 3 at every
  check, and erases on `device.unlinked{transferred}` (reliable for the
  life of the deposit token, above) or when the member removes VettID.
  Result 1 needs a vault that answers a removed device, which no release
  does yet; it is specified for forward compatibility. Result 2 occurs
  only while the relay still accepts the old key (for example when the
  approval's writes were not stored, §11.14.2).
- **Recording the check** (0.55.10). The app keeps, with its transfer
  record, a generation that every change of the record raises. Before it
  asks, it reads the record and notes the generation; after the await it
  re-reads the record. If the record is gone or its generation changed
  meanwhile (the notice erased it, "The move didn't finish" ended the
  keep, a lock or another check changed it), it acts on nothing and
  records nothing; the next start or foreground checks again while a
  keep remains. Otherwise it writes the result conditionally on the
  noted generation, and records "kept, not done", or acts on result 1 or
  2, only if that write succeeds. A failed write records nothing, and
  the check runs again.
- **The residual of the day-7 check** (0.55.10). A vault that never
  answers keeps the old keys on the phone indefinitely. With an honest
  host they are useless at the vault (the old app is removed, its relay
  key is on the denylist (§7.4) and its unlock key is gone) and, since
  the notice is kept for its token's 30 days, the notice erases them
  once the new phone has unlocked; past those 30 days, or with a host
  that withholds the notice, they stay on the phone until the member
  removes VettID or resets it, which the last screen and the waiting
  notice say. With a host that replays they stay the residual above.
- A vault stranded by that fault and restored in time (§11.14.2) needs
  the old phone or, with the credential backup on, a recovery after the
  restore. One that is not restored in time is lost, with or without the
  backup.

#### 11.14.11 What the member sees: status, audit, feed and emails

- **`vault.status`** gains, for the app,

  ```json
  "recovery": { "state": "armed|off|needs_check|change_required|unknown",
                "attempts": {"used": 0, "of": 10},
                "present_recorded_at": "<ts>", "counter": "ok|unavailable" }
  ```

  and `{state}` alone for desktops (agents: nothing). `off`: the backup
  is off. `needs_check`: the backup is on and the next owner check will
  arm. `change_required`: §11.14.3, §11.14.7. `unknown`: the counter
  could not be read; the app MUST NOT show that as zero attempts used.
  When `counter` has been `unavailable` at every read for 24 hours, the
  app shows it with the urgency of a used attempt and says why.
- **The record a host cannot drop.** The counter holds, for each
  generation, every attempt with its counter time and which one, if any,
  succeeded. Whenever the vault reads the counter's status while unlocked
  (each owner check, a completed recovery; at a completion the read is
  bounded to 10 seconds, and a failure there still answers `ok` and
  leaves the entries to the next owner check, 0.50.1), it writes one audit entry for
  each attempt it has not recorded: kind `recovery.attempt`, `at` = the
  counter's time, `ref` = `<generation>/<n>/<outcome>/counter`, where
  `<outcome>` is `success` or `not_success` (a wrong pair and a lost
  attempt look the same to the counter, which records before the test)
  and `counter` says where it comes from (0.50.0: the outcome and the
  source are in the `ref`; the entry has no other members, §10.9). An
  attempt first seen as `not_success` is written again when the counter
  later shows it succeeded. Each makes a feed item and shows in
  History. The item is **not** urgent only if the attempt is in the
  generation of the member's last completed recovery and its *n* is at
  most that recovery's own counted attempt *k*: those attempts are the
  member's, up to the one that succeeded. Every other attempt is
  `urgent`, a later one in the same generation included, since the
  vault stays armed in that generation after a recovery (0.50.1; until
  then every attempt in that generation was taken as the member's). The
  vault keeps the recovered attempt (generation, *k*) in its state, set
  at the completion or, for a repeat whose step 2 was not stored, from
  the `next` part (§11.14.6). A state or a `next` part from before
  0.50.1 has no such attempt, so its attempts are `urgent`. When
  `attempts.used` rises the vault also audits
  `recovery.attempts_used`, `ref` = `<generation>/<used>`.
- **The details a host can drop.** The header's recovery log (§11.11)
  also notes opens with their outcome as the enclave knew it, and the
  vault moves them into the audit log at the next resume (or at the
  completed recovery, then with `device_id` = the new phone) as their
  own entries (0.50.0): kind `recovery.open`, `at` = the open's time,
  `ref` = `<recovery_id>/<outcome>` or `<recovery_id>/<outcome>/<name>`.
  **The attempting phone's name** (owner decision of 2026-10-20; needs a
  vault release, the vault as built writes the two-part form):
  `<name>` is the `app.name` the phone gave in
  `vault.recovery.register` (§11.11.3), which the enclave keeps in the
  header's recovery record with the registered key; every open comes
  from that registered phone, so the enclave adds it to each open it
  notes. It is the name's UTF-8, with control characters (C0, DEL, C1)
  removed and cut to at most 64 bytes at a character boundary, encoded
  as base64url without padding (so a `/` in a name cannot break the
  `ref`); an empty or absent name writes the two-part form. The name is
  **self-reported**: the phone, and whoever holds it, chooses it freely,
  and nothing checks it. Apps show it only as such ("from a phone that
  calls itself “<name>”", ANDROID-PLAN §4 "Event titles"), never as a
  verified identity, and **the name never affects** a feed item's
  priority, a notification, the alarming title or any decision of the
  vault or an app. It is the one name the audit log holds, and the
  vault's search (§10.9 Search) does not read it. The outcomes written
  are `wrong`, `attempt_lost`, and `quiet`, `wait`, `exhausted` or
  `closed` when the decision after the spend refused (each of these
  counted an attempt), and `busy` and `wrong_again` (no attempt
  counted); the other refusals (before the spend, or with the counter
  unavailable) and a successful open write none. `recovery.attempt`
  entries carry no `recovery_id`, so the apps match each counted outcome to the
  nearest `not_success` attempt in time (ANDROID-PLAN §4 "Event
  titles"). A host that drops header writes removes these details, not
  the counter's entries; History shows "details not available".
- **The email trail.** The member API cannot read an open's outcome. For
  an open that was counted (`spent` or `lost`), the enclave's answer to
  the host carries the clear marker **`code: "recovery_attempt"`**, with
  `retry_at` and `expires` when a wait began, beside the sealed result
  (§11.5). It does not say whether the guess was right. The member API
  sends an email for each, and moves the recovery's `expires_at` to
  `expires` (MEMBER-API "Vault recovery"). **VettID can suppress every
  email**, and an attacker who is VettID needs none: the emails are a
  notice against an attacker who is someone else. A member with no
  device learns of attempts only by email.
- **New audit kinds** (§10.9): `recovery.attempt`,
  `recovery.attempts_used`, `recovery.armed` (`ref` = the generation),
  `recovery.generation_closed` (`ref` = `<generation>/<reason>`, the
  reason `pin`, `password`, `reset`, `backup_off`, `exhausted` or
  `delete`; 0.50.0: also `stale` and `rollback`, written when a PIN,
  password or credential change finds that the next generation is
  already known to the counter, and the vault moves past it (§11.14.3):
  **`rollback`** (owner decision of 2026-10-20; needs a vault release)
  for a next generation that already shows used attempts, which can
  only come from a host that served an older copy of the vault's
  recovery record (an older timeline); its attempts are never written as
  `recovery.attempt`, so this entry is their only trace, and the apps
  show it as an alarm; **`stale`** for each other generation closed
  there (one only already closed, as after a retry of a failed write,
  and the current one), which the apps hide; the vault as built writes
  `stale` for all of them; and the
  suffix `/unconfirmed` after `delete` when the counter did not confirm
  the close, the deletion going ahead), `recovery.presence_unrecorded`,
  `identity.rotation_failed` (`ref` = `recovery`),
  `identity.rotate_conflict` (§3.4), `device.secret_renewed`; and, as
  built (0.50.0), `vault.pin_changed`, `recovery.open` (above) and
  `recovery.completed` with `ref` = `<recovery_id>/resumed` when a
  later open finishes a recovery that stopped after its state was
  stored. Feed: `recovery.attempt` (as above), `recovery.change_required`
  (`high`; `ref` = `password` when the password is too weak to arm, or
  the generation whose attempts were used), `recovery.counter_unavailable`
  (`urgent`, after 24 hours), (0.50.0, owner decision of 2026-10-20)
  `recovery.generation_closed` with `ref` `<generation>/rollback`
  (`urgent`, written with the audit entry; apps notify on Security
  alarms), and (0.50.0) `vault.pin_changed`,
  `device.secret_renewed`, `credential.recovered`,
  `recovery.device_paired`, `recovery.completed`,
  `identity.rotation_failed` and `identity.rotate_conflict` (§10.9).

#### 11.14.12 What VettID can and cannot do from release R

**It can:** wait for a member's three-day absence, or cause one by not
running the service or by cutting the enclave's way to the counter, and
then test at most the attempts the schedule allows, each counted, shown
and mailed (mail it can suppress); use up a member's attempts without a
test (§11.14.6), which forces a change of secret and can leave a member
who then loses the phone without recovery; make recoveries wait by
keeping enclaves full (`busy`); see when each member was last present;
start a recovery, since it holds the recovery request key; delete any
present record older than its 96-hour lock, which can only make
recoveries refuse (a vault with no present record cannot be recovered);
delete any vault, as before (§13.5).

**It cannot,** for as long as the counter's guarantees hold: get an
eleventh attempt for a generation by replaying a header, running many
enclaves, registering more phones or starting more recoveries; test an
attempt against a member whose presence was recorded within the 72
hours before that attempt's own time; shorten a wait; learn which of
the two secrets was wrong; test a PIN against stored objects without the
member's phone.

**AWS acting for VettID.** If AWS removed locked records at VettID's
request, VettID could remove a generation's tokens, waits and close
records and test further pairs, and remove present records younger
than their lock, shortening the quiet period. The count would then be bounded only by the second record
outside AWS, which production requires (§11.14.13).

**A broken sealing.** Every vault's sealed header rests on a KMS key
whose policy lets no principal change it (§11.10.7). AWS's documentation
says that for a key nobody can manage, "you must contact AWS Support to
regain access to the KMS key". If AWS restored VettID's control of a
sealing key, VettID could open every sealed header of that release
outside an enclave and read the pepper; no counter is involved. What
remains is the cost of guessing offline (estimates, at about 4 seconds
and 1 GiB per guess through the recovery wrap and an assumed 0.04 US
dollars per core-hour; a determined attacker pays less):

| The attacker has | Ordinary data (messages, connections, profile, `data` and `secret` items) | Critical items' values |
|---|---|---|
| Before release R: a broken sealing, no phone | Every PIN against the stored state at 0.2 s each: about 56 core-hours, a few US dollars; the password is not needed | Then the password against the credential's own key (64 MiB): about 20,000 US dollars for a password at 10^10 guesses |
| Release R: a broken sealing, no phone | Only through the recovery wrap, PIN and password together: up to about 400,000 US dollars for a password at 10^10 guesses if the PIN is known, multiplied when it is not (a factor of 10 to 1,000 for chosen PINs, up to 1,000,000 for a random one) | The same single cost: the pair that opens the wrap opens the credential |
| Release R: a broken sealing and the phone's secret | As before release R: the PIN alone, a few US dollars | As before: the password at the credential's lighter setting |

"The phone's secret" means making the phone's hardware key compute it:
the phone itself and a way to run code as the VettID app on it, or a
break of its key store. (0.36.0) Code that ran as the app for a time
could compute the secrets of the epochs whose records existed then, not those of
epochs created after it stopped (§11.14.1); on Android with a form 1
record, every epoch of that phone key. A broken sealing still gives, in every case,
who the member is, the vault's size and activity times, the public keys
in the header and the tag of the last wrong recovery pair, which tests
guesses at a wrong pair only.

**The isolation the sealing needs.** Release R MUST also carry the
change that stops a compromised vault process from having another
vault's sealed header opened for it (§12.4); without it one vault's
compromise opens every header of the release, and no counter matters.

#### 11.14.13 Later records, and production

The counter interface allows several records that must agree, the
stricter answer winning. Two more are specified later:

- **Release "R2": a second record outside AWS.** The tokens and the
  close records are mirrored in **Google Cloud Storage under a locked
  object retention**, written before the guess is tested like the S3
  records; presence is **not** mirrored (losing present records would
  shorten the quiet period, not add attempts, and one write per attempt
  tells the outside party far less than one per vault per day); the
  wait goes outside as a time on the spent record. Requirements: no act
  open to VettID as a customer of AWS, and no act of AWS at VettID's
  request, can remove or reorder a record; answers are authenticated by
  TLS ending in the enclave under pinned roots, and the store's identity
  (the project's number and the bucket's creation time, which the
  provider vouches for) is pinned in the measured release; a store that
  cannot be reached is `unavailable`, and one that answers but is not the
  pinned one, or was created after the release was built, or holds fewer
  records than S3, counts as **every attempt used** (fail closed); the
  outside party learns only opaque names, write times and that the
  customer is VettID; its absence stops recovery opens and changes of
  secret, never an everyday unlock or owner check. Known weakness: the
  customer can remove the lien that protects the project from deletion,
  so the pinned identity must be something the customer cannot choose or
  carry over; that and the rest are tried before R2 is specified.
  Holding the outside account by an independent party, not VettID, would
  change who can ask the provider for an exception; it needs no code and
  can be added at any time. Azure confidential ledger is considered only
  if experiments show that its identity can be followed from a pinned
  start across a provider-side recovery.
- **Release "R3": the counter group.** A small group of enclaves keeping
  the table only in memory and replicating it, with its own document.
  A group that has lost its memory counts, for each generation it is
  asked about, as **one attempt used and a wait of 30 units**, not as
  "never again"; a replacement group is named in the signed release
  manifest, with a serial the enclave refuses to see go down. Under that
  rule the group is a second record and a 30-day delay against VettID
  with AWS's help, not a second bound; the bound that survives AWS
  acting for VettID is R2's.

**Production.**

- **Production release 1 MAY ship with recovery refused in the enclave**
  if release R and the outside store are not ready: its channel file then
  sets `recovery_offered` to `false` (§11.10.8), and the enclave refuses
  every recovery request without locking the vault, as for a vault with
  the backup off (§11.11.1), with the sealed refusal `error:
  "not_offered"` and the clear marker `recovery_unavailable` with the
  clear `reason: "not_offered"` (§11.5), which the member API can read
  (it cannot read the sealed refusal). (0.34.0) Its capabilities leave
  out `recovery_offered` (§11.10.9), so the app knows before the member
  tries. The account site and the app say
  the truth: "This vault's release does not offer recovery. Your vault
  gains recovery only after you move it to a release that does, which
  needs your phone (an update approved in the app)." A member who loses
  the phone first can only start over (§11.11.9). It MUST NOT ship
  with the recovery of §11.11.5: every vault sealed to a release stays
  open to that release's method until the release's sealing key is
  destroyed.
- **The first production release with recovery carries S3 and the
  outside store (R2)**; it does not wait for the counter group.
- **An earlier release stays a way around a later one until its sealing
  key is gone.** A vault that moves from one release to a stronger one
  leaves its old header sealed under the old key, and the old genuine
  image still runs. With the outside store in production's first release
  with recovery, this arises only when the group is added; the rule for
  ending the earlier release then is decided with R3 (VAULT-RELEASES
  §3.5). On staging the earlier release is ended and its key deleted
  after the 7-day window.

#### 11.14.14 Staging, build rules and tests

- **Build rules.** `recovery_wait_unit_seconds` and
  `recovery_quiet_seconds` are constants of the channel file (§11.10.8).
  A production build MUST fail if the wait unit is below 86,400, if the
  quiet period is below 259,200, or if a test clock can be set (the
  development stack's recovery clock, `RecoveryNow`, MUST NOT be
  reachable in a release image). The staging and production counter
  buckets have different pinned names and accounts. A test asserts all
  three on the production image, and (0.33.2) that it locks the counter's
  token, success and close records for 100 years. Staging uses a wait unit of 600 seconds
  and the production quiet period; one test runs in real time as far as
  the 96-hour wait. (0.43.0, approved by the owner 2026-10-18;
  STAGING-TIME-SCALE §5.4) From the release that ships `time_scale`,
  the quiet period's lower bound of 259,200 s is a production rule:
  staging's file states 259,200 / `time_scale` (10,800 s at 24) and the
  check refuses any other value there; the wait unit stays 600 s and is
  not divided again. A test asserts on the production image that
  `time_scale` is 1 and that the enclave's scale is 1 whatever the file
  says.
- **Minimum app version.** The release constant `android_min_version_code`
  is checked against the version code in the key attestation at a
  recovery's register (and at enrollment and a transfer's `hs.init`);
  an older app is answered `attestation`. No security rule depends on
  it: an app from before release R cannot unlock a vault of release R
  anyway, since it sends no secret.
- **Re-enrolment on staging.** Release R runs and a new test vault has
  enrolled; each earlier staging test vault is deleted; every earlier
  staging release that still has a sealing key is ended, which schedules
  its key's deletion after the 7-day window (until then the old headers
  of the test vaults can still be attacked with the earlier method; they
  hold test data only); the test vaults are enrolled again on release R
  with passwords that pass §11.14.7.
